neighbors.heading: a verse before the meal
neighbors.text: Today a meal began with God's name. Some Hindu families wait at the table for a verse too, before anyone eats. It comes from the Bhagavad Gita and begins brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman, what is offered is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. The meal becomes an offering, not just food.
neighbors.difference: The Gita verse sees the offering, the one who offers and the fire all as Brahman. Muslims begin in God's name, and Islam keeps a clear line between the Creator and the food He provides.
neighbors.shared: a meal can start by remembering where it came from.

neighbors.heading: a blessing over bread
neighbors.text: Today a meal began with God's name. Jews bless before eating too. Over bread, the blessing praises God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. The Talmud teaches that enjoying anything of this world without a blessing is like taking from something holy.
neighbors.difference: Jewish blessings change with the food: one for bread, others for fruit, wine or vegetables, and a longer grace after a meal with bread. Bismillah is one phrase for every beginning, from a meal to a drive.
neighbors.shared: food is a gift, so you say thank you first.
neighbors.sources: the blessing over bread, hamotzi (paraphrase) · Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seven times a day
neighbors.text: Today the day was cut into five prayers. Christians have kept hours of prayer too. A psalm says: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice." Another says, "Seven times a day do I praise thee." Some Christians, monks above all, still pray at set hours from dawn to night.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, the five daily prayers are required of every adult who is able. Among Christians, set hours are a treasured practice, kept closely by monks and clergy; others pray when and how they choose.
neighbors.shared: a day goes better with places to stop and pray.

neighbors.heading: prayers that bookend the day
neighbors.text: Today the day was cut into five prayers. Sikhs keep a daily rhythm of prayer too. Guru Ram Das wrote that one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru rises early, bathes and remembers the Name. Sikhs recite set prayers, Nitnem, at dawn, at evening (Rehras) and before sleep (Kirtan Sohila).
neighbors.difference: Salat moves the body: standing, bowing, forehead to the ground, facing Mecca. Sikh daily prayers are recited or sung from scripture, facing no set direction, and the dawn hours, amrit vela, are held especially dear.
neighbors.shared: the day can open and close with remembering God.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 305 (Guru Ram Das, paraphrase) · Sikh Rehat Maryada on Nitnem (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: prayer, fasting and alms
neighbors.text: Today a share of money was given, so the rest is purified. Catholics give alms too, and keep giving close to prayer. The angel Raphael says in the Book of Tobias: "Prayer is good with fasting and alms." In Lent, Catholics are asked to practice all three, and the Catechism calls giving to the poor a work of justice pleasing to God.
neighbors.difference: Zakat is a set share, usually a fortieth of savings held a year above a threshold, owed to named groups. Catholic almsgiving has no fixed percentage; each person gives as conscience and love move them.
neighbors.shared: giving to the poor belongs right next to prayer.
neighbors.sources: Tobias (Tobit) 12:8 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: if you knew the fruit of giving
neighbors.text: Today a share of money was given, so the rest is purified. Buddhists count giving, dana, as the first of the perfections. The Buddha is remembered saying that if people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without first sharing, not even their last bite.
neighbors.difference: Zakat is owed to the poor as their right, a set share each year. In Buddhism giving is freely chosen, often food for monks and nuns who live on alms, and it loosens the grip of craving in the giver.
neighbors.shared: an open hand makes a lighter heart.
neighbors.sources: Itivuttaka 26 (paraphrase) · the perfection of giving, dana (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a whole world
neighbors.text: Today one brother killed another, and a verse said one life is like all lives. The Qur'an says this was decreed for the Children of Israel, and Jewish teaching carries it. The Mishnah says Adam was created alone to teach that whoever destroys one life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life, a whole world.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an it is God's decree, told after the story of the two sons. In the Mishnah, judges say it to witnesses in a life-and-death case, so they tremble before testifying falsely.
neighbors.shared: every person you meet is a whole world.

neighbors.heading: one great body
neighbors.text: Today one life weighed as much as all lives. The Stoic Seneca reached for the same weight. He wrote that all we see is one: we are parts of one great body, and nature made us kin. Keep this line on your lips, he said, from the playwright Terence: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, each life's worth is set by God, who forbids taking it without right. For Seneca, our kinship comes from nature and shared reason, a bond he believed anyone can see without a revelation.
neighbors.shared: harm to one person is harm to all of us.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters 95.51–53 (paraphrase) · Terence, The Self-Tormentor (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: true then, true now
neighbors.text: Today a young man watched a star, the moon and the sun go down, and wanted what never sets. Sikh scripture opens on that same longing. Guru Nanak's Japji begins: "The True One was in the beginning; the True One was in the primal age." True now, it goes on, and true forever.
neighbors.difference: Ibrahim reasons from the sky up to its Maker, beyond all that sets. Gurbani sings of the One beyond creation and also present within all of it, known through the Guru's grace.
neighbors.shared: your heart can rest on what doesn't set.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, opening salok of Japji (Macauliffe 1909; the rest paraphrased)

neighbors.heading: from the unreal to the real
neighbors.text: Today a young man watched a star, the moon and the sun go down, and said he would not love what sets. An old Hindu prayer asks for the same turning. From the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to the deathless.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishads, the real is Brahman, often found as the Self within. Ibrahim turns from the sky to a Creator beyond everything He made, never one with the one who prays.
neighbors.shared: you're allowed to want something that doesn't fade.

neighbors.heading: angels unawares
neighbors.text: Today Ibrahim hurried to feed strangers who turned out to be angels. Christians read the same visit at Mamre and draw the same lesson. The Letter to the Hebrews says: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Jesus adds that whoever takes in a stranger takes him in.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus saying that welcoming a stranger is welcoming him. In Islam, the hadith ties honoring a guest to faith in God and the Last Day.
neighbors.shared: the knock at the door might be the best part of your day.

neighbors.heading: the hare in the moon
neighbors.text: Today Ibrahim hurried to feed strangers with the best he had. Buddhists tell of a hare with nothing to offer a hungry traveler but himself. He leapt into the fire to feed his guest, who was the god Sakka testing him. The fire did not burn, and Sakka drew the hare on the moon so his giving would be remembered.
neighbors.difference: The hare is told as the Buddha in an earlier life, practicing the perfection of giving. Ibrahim's guests come from God with news of a son, and his welcome is remembered as a prophet honoring the guest.
neighbors.shared: a hungry guest at the door is a gift, not a bother.

neighbors.heading: holy ground
neighbors.text: Today Musa saw a fire on the mountain and was told he stood in a sacred valley. Catholics read the same moment: "Come not nigh hither, put off the shoes from thy feet: for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." In a Catholic church, people mark holy ground too: holy water and a sign of the cross at the door, a knee bent toward the tabernacle.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the holiest presence in a church is Christ himself in the Eucharist, kept in the tabernacle; that's why they kneel. Muslims honor Isa as a prophet, and in a mosque nothing stands for God.
neighbors.shared: some places ask you to slow down and go quiet.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 3:5 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1378–1379 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: standing on the bare ground
neighbors.text: Today Musa went to fetch a coal and found himself in a sacred valley. Emerson wrote of moments like that in the woods: "Standing on the bare ground, my head bathed by the blithe air, and uplifted into infinite space, all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all."
neighbors.difference: Musa is spoken to by God, by name, and given a mission. Emerson's moment has no words and no task; he felt a larger life flowing through nature and himself, which he called the Universal Being.
neighbors.shared: wonder can find you on an ordinary walk.

neighbors.heading: true, kind and helpful
neighbors.text: Today Musa was sent to Pharaoh and told to speak gently. The Bhagavad Gita counts gentle speech as a discipline too. It calls words that cause no distress, words that are true, pleasant and helpful, the austerity of speech. An old Sanskrit saying puts it simply: speak the truth, and speak it kindly.
neighbors.difference: Musa's gentleness is aimed outward, so Pharaoh might take heed. The Gita treats kind, true speech as tapas, a discipline that steadies and purifies the one who speaks.
neighbors.shared: even a hard truth can be said softly.

neighbors.heading: a soft answer
neighbors.text: Today Musa was told to speak gently, even to Pharaoh. Jewish wisdom says it too. Proverbs teaches: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." And the sages held up Aaron, Moses' brother, as one who loved peace and pursued it.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, the gentle word is God's command for that one meeting. The Exodus scenes in the Torah don't carry that line; Jewish teaching on the soft word comes from Proverbs and the sages.
neighbors.shared: a gentle word can open a door anger keeps shut.

items.lessonTitle: The shirt and the false blood

neighbors.heading: patience, then hope
neighbors.text: Today a grieving father said: beautiful patience. Christians know that road. Paul wrote: "we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope." Ya'qub never stopped hoping for his son, and Christians, too, are taught that patience in pain can grow into hope.
neighbors.difference: Ya'qub's patience rests on trust in God's decree and never despairing of His mercy. Paul's hope rests on Christ, through whom, Christians believe, God's love is poured into their hearts.
neighbors.shared: patience isn't giving up; it's holding on with hope.

neighbors.heading: walking in the Will
neighbors.text: Today a grieving father chose beautiful patience. Sikhs speak of accepting God's will, bhana, with a steady heart. Guru Nanak's Japji asks how a person becomes truthful, and answers: walk in the way of the Hukam, the divine order, written with you. Sikhs call the spirit that follows chardi kala, rising spirits, even on hard days.
neighbors.difference: Ya'qub grieves out loud, but to God alone, and waits for Him to bring his son back. Sikh teaching asks the heart to find even loss sweet as the Hukam, with the Name on the lips.
neighbors.shared: you can grieve and still trust the road.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji pauri 1 (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394 (Guru Arjan, "your will is sweet", paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seventy times seven
neighbors.text: Today a brother said to the brothers who threw him in a well: no blame on you today. Catholics read Joseph forgiving his brothers in Genesis too. And Jesus, asked how often to forgive, said: "I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times." In every Our Father, Catholics ask to be forgiven as they forgive.
neighbors.difference: Yusuf forgives his brothers himself and asks God to forgive them. Catholics also bring their own wrongs to a priest in confession, the sacrament of Penance, trusting that God forgives through it.
neighbors.shared: letting go of an old hurt can bring a family home.

neighbors.heading: hatred ceases by love
neighbors.text: Today a brother forgave the ones who left him in a well. The Buddha taught that same release. The Dhammapada says: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." The verses before it name the thoughts that keep a grudge alive: he abused me, he beat me, he robbed me.
neighbors.difference: Yusuf forgives and asks God to forgive his brothers; mercy comes from God. The Buddha frames letting go of hatred as freeing your own mind, with no Creator's pardon involved.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to carry an old wrong forever.

items.lessonTitle: The gourd and the saved city

neighbors.heading: the city that turned
neighbors.text: Today the city Yunus walked away from turned back and was spared. Jews read Jonah's whole story on Yom Kippur afternoon, the Day of Atonement. The people of Nineveh fast and turn from evil, and God relents. The book ends on God's question to Jonah: you pitied a vine you never planted; should I not pity a great city?
neighbors.difference: The Hebrew book ends on God's question, with no answer from Jonah. The Qur'an tells that he was sent to them, they believed, and they were given comfort for a while.
neighbors.shared: no one is too far gone to turn around.

neighbors.heading: teach them, or bear with them
neighbors.text: Today the people Yunus gave up on turned around after all. Marcus Aurelius, an emperor who wrote notes to himself, kept a line for days when people let him down: "Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them." Elsewhere he wrote that we are made to work together, like hands and feet.
neighbors.difference: Yunus is a prophet sent by God, and the city turns to God. Marcus leans on reason and our shared nature; he has no message to deliver, only the daily work of patience with people.
neighbors.shared: people can surprise you, if you stay long enough to see.

neighbors.heading: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today a young merchant became the one Mecca trusted with its valuables. Sikhs prize that kind of trust. Guru Nanak taught that truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living. Sikhs are asked to earn an honest living, kirat karni, and to share what they earn.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, amanah is a trust from God, owed back whole to its owners. For Sikhs, truthful living is how a person lives in tune with the One whose name is Sat, Truth.
neighbors.shared: being trusted is worth more than being clever.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62 (Guru Nanak, Sri Rag, paraphrase) · kirat karni, honest work (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: truth alone prevails
neighbors.text: Today a young merchant became known as al-Amin, the one people trusted. Hindus hold truth high too. The Mundaka Upanishad says satyameva jayate: truth alone prevails, not falsehood, and by truth the road to the divine is laid.
neighbors.difference: Amanah is about what is left in your keeping, things and words, returned whole. Satya reaches further: in the Upanishads, Brahman itself is called truth, so living truthfully is also seeking the real.
neighbors.shared: your word is something people can lean on.

neighbors.heading: under the tree
neighbors.text: Today a man climbed to a small cave to think and pray alone. The Buddha's story has a seat like that. After years of searching, tradition says, Siddhartha sat beneath a tree and resolved not to rise until he understood. Buddhists still honor that quiet: a seat, a breath, a mind settling.
neighbors.difference: In the cave, the Prophet ﷺ was met by the angel Jibril with words from God. The Buddha's awakening came through his own insight, with no messenger and no Creator speaking.
neighbors.shared: big things can begin in a quiet place, alone.
neighbors.sources: the awakening under the bodhi tree, Jataka Nidanakatha (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 36 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: into the wilderness
neighbors.text: Today a man climbed to a cave above Mecca to be alone with God. Christians know that pull. The Gospel of Luke says of Jesus: "And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." Before he began teaching, he spent forty days in the desert, and he told his friends to come apart and rest awhile.
neighbors.difference: Christians see Jesus as the Son praying to his Father. Muslims honor the Prophet ﷺ as a human messenger who went to the cave to seek and came down carrying revelation from God.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the bravest thing is to step away and listen.

neighbors.heading: a good will
neighbors.text: Today every prayer began in the heart before the tongue. The philosopher Immanuel Kant put the heart's aim at the center too. He wrote that nothing in the world can be called good without condition except a good will. Even if it achieved nothing, he said, a good will would still shine like a jewel, by its own light.
neighbors.difference: Kant judged a will good when it acts from duty, by reason alone. The hadith says each person gets what they intended, and God, who looks at hearts, weighs it.
neighbors.shared: what you mean counts, even before anyone sees it.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the Lord beholdeth the heart
neighbors.text: Today every prayer began with what you mean. Catholics read the same about the heart. When Samuel looked for a king, God told him: "man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart." Some Catholics begin each day with a morning offering, giving God its prayers, works, joys and sufferings, so the whole day is meant.
neighbors.difference: Muslim scholars hold that a prayer or a fast needs its intention to count at all. Catholic teaching weighs any act by three things together: the act itself, the intention and the circumstances, so a good aim can't make a wrong act right.
neighbors.shared: God sees the heart before the hands move.
neighbors.sources: 1 Kings 16:7 (Douay-Rheims; 1 Samuel 16:7 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1750–1753 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the bow with eight limbs
neighbors.text: Today a forehead touched the ground, the closest a person gets. Hindus know a full bow too: sashtanga pranam, the bow with eight limbs, lying flat before God. In the Gita, Arjuna, overwhelmed by Krishna's vision, bows down, lays his body on the ground, and asks for his grace.
neighbors.difference: Hindus may bow fully before God present in a temple murti, and also touch the feet of parents and teachers in respect. Muslims prostrate to God alone, never to a person or an image.
neighbors.shared: the lowest bow can feel like the closest place.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 11.44 (paraphrase) · sashtanga pranam, the eight-limbed bow (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: falling on their faces
neighbors.text: Today a forehead touched the ground, the closest a person gets. Jews once bowed this way in the Temple. The Mishnah says that on Yom Kippur, when the people heard God's Name from the high priest, they knelt, bowed and fell on their faces. A psalm still sings: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker."
neighbors.difference: Muslims prostrate in every unit of every prayer. In most Jewish prayer today, full prostration is kept for the High Holy Days, when some congregations kneel to the floor; daily prayer bows from standing, or rests the head on an arm.
neighbors.shared: sometimes prayer needs your whole body, not just words.

neighbors.heading: peace be unto you
neighbors.text: Today a prayer ended by turning right, then left: peace be upon you. Christians pass peace too. The risen Jesus greeted his frightened friends with: "Peace be unto you." In churches that share the sign of peace, people turn to those beside them, often before communion, shake hands and say, peace be with you.
neighbors.difference: Christians share Christ's peace with the people around them, face to face. The taslim closes each Muslim prayer with a greeting to the right and left, which many read as including the angels beside each person.
neighbors.shared: a prayer can end by turning toward the people beside you.
neighbors.sources: John 20:19 (KJV) · the sign of peace in the liturgy (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good of all
neighbors.text: Today a prayer ended with peace to both sides. The Sikh prayer Ardas ends wider still. After remembering the Gurus and the community's history, it asks for chardi kala, rising spirits, and then: sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not just Sikhs, not just this room. Everyone.
neighbors.difference: The taslim is a greeting of peace that closes the prayer. Ardas is a standing request, led aloud with folded hands, and its last wish reaches past the room to all people, by God's will.
neighbors.shared: a prayer can end by wishing everyone well.

neighbors.heading: beads in the hand
neighbors.text: Today fingers counted subhanallah, thirty-three times. Catholics count prayers too, on the rosary. Each decade is ten Hail Marys, beginning with the angel's words: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." While the beads pass, Catholics think through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.
neighbors.difference: Tasbih glorifies God directly. The rosary joins the Our Father and Glory Be with asking Mary to pray for them, while meditating on Jesus, whom Catholics worship as God's Son; Muslims honor Maryam and Isa without praying to them.
neighbors.shared: counting slowly can turn your hands into a prayer.

neighbors.heading: a string of beads
neighbors.text: Today fingers counted subhanallah, thirty-three times. Some Buddhists count too, on a mala, a string of beads, often 108. With each bead they may repeat a mantra or recall the Buddha's qualities: the Blessed One, fully awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, teacher of gods and humans.
neighbors.difference: Tasbih glorifies God, the One beyond everything. Buddhist recollection steadies and clears the mind by remembering a teacher's qualities, without praising a Creator.
neighbors.shared: a few beads can bring a scattered mind home.
neighbors.sources: the recollection of the Buddha, Anguttara Nikaya (paraphrase) · the mala in Buddhist practice (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Ramadan: the fast of the tongue

neighbors.heading: the fast I have chosen
neighbors.text: Today the fast reached past the stomach to the tongue. Jews hear that on Yom Kippur morning, from Isaiah: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free." A fast with a cruel tongue or closed hands, the prophet says, misses the point.
neighbors.difference: Yom Kippur is one full day without food or water, a day of atonement. Ramadan is a month of daylight fasts, and the hadith says God has no need of a hunger that keeps false speech.
neighbors.shared: a fast is meant to change how you treat people.

neighbors.heading: if it is not true
neighbors.text: Today the fast reached the tongue: hold back false words, not just food. Marcus Aurelius kept a rule for himself that sounds like it: "If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it." He wrote it as a private reminder, a fast he could keep every day.
neighbors.difference: Marcus keeps his rule by reason, because truth fits a good life. The fast of the tongue is kept for God, and the hadith says God has no need of a hunger that keeps lying.
neighbors.shared: what leaves your mouth matters as much as what goes in.

neighbors.heading: in every heart
neighbors.text: Today a verse said: when my servants ask, I am near. Hindus hear nearness in the Gita too. Krishna says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, turning them all as if on a wheel. In another verse he says he is seated in everyone's heart, the source of memory and knowing.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus understand the Lord in the heart as the inner Self, in some schools one with Brahman. In Islam, God is near by knowing and answering, nearer than the jugular vein, yet never one with the one who prays.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to shout; the one you're calling is close.

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today a verse said: I am near, I answer. Sikhs sing that nearness too. Guru Tegh Bahadur asks why you go searching in the forest, when the One dwells everywhere and is always with you, like fragrance in a flower, like a reflection in a mirror. Look within, he says.
neighbors.difference: Gurbani sings of the One within every heart and pervading all, found through the Guru's word. The Qur'an speaks of God near and answering, nearer than the jugular vein, while beyond all He made.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to travel far to be heard.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684 (Guru Tegh Bahadur, Raag Dhanasari, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: near and far
neighbors.text: Today a prayer went out for a friend who wasn't in the room. Buddhists send good wishes outward too. The Metta Sutta asks for a heart like a mother's toward her only child, wishing every being well: the seen and the unseen, those near and those far, the born and those yet to be born. May all beings be happy.
neighbors.difference: The du'a asks God for a friend's good, and an angel answers: and for you the same. Metta asks no one; it trains your own heart to wish all beings well, until the wish has no edges.
neighbors.shared: you can do someone good from far away.

neighbors.heading: prayers for all men
neighbors.text: Today a prayer went out for someone absent, and an angel answered: and for you the same. Christians are asked to pray for others too. Paul wrote: "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men." Jesus went further: pray even for those who mistreat you.
neighbors.difference: Christians usually pray in Jesus' name, and Paul asks believers to pray for one another and for rulers. In the hadith, a du'a made quietly for someone absent brings an angel's reply: and for you the same.
neighbors.shared: praying for someone is a quiet way of loving them.

neighbors.heading: the voice that says wait
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said: sin is what wavers in your chest, so leave what makes you doubt. Socrates trusted a similar signal. At his trial, as Plato tells it, he said an inner sign had come to him since childhood, a kind of voice, that never told him what to do, only held him back.
neighbors.difference: Socrates' sign only warned, and he called it something divine without saying more. Islam calls the heart's unease a guide and pairs it with knowledge: ask, learn, and when still unsure, leave it.
neighbors.shared: that uneasy feeling is worth listening to.

neighbors.heading: written in their hearts
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said: sin is what wavers in your chest. Catholics speak of conscience in a similar way. Paul wrote of people who "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness." The Church calls conscience a person's most secret core and sanctuary, where they are alone with God.
neighbors.difference: Catholic teaching asks people to form conscience with Scripture and the Church, then follow its certain judgment. The hadith leans toward caution: when the heart wavers, step back and leave the doubtful thing.
neighbors.shared: you were given a quiet voice inside for a reason.
neighbors.sources: Romans 2:15 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1776, 1783–1790 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the world is one family
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet ﷺ said Jibril kept urging kindness to neighbors. Hindus have an old line about who counts as near. A Sanskrit verse says: this one is mine, that one a stranger, is how small minds count; for the large-hearted, the whole world is one family, vasudhaiva kutumbakam.
neighbors.difference: The hadith starts at the closest door, with duties to the household next to yours. The Sanskrit verse opens the circle all at once, to the whole earth as family.
neighbors.shared: kindness starts next door and doesn't have to stop there.

neighbors.heading: love thy neighbour
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet ﷺ said Jibril urged kindness to the neighbor so often he thought neighbors might inherit. The Torah says it in one line: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." A few verses later it widens: the stranger who lives with you, love as yourself.
neighbors.difference: The Torah frames it as love, sealed with God's name. The hadith frames it as a right so heavy it nearly became inheritance, and the Qur'an names the neighbor who is kin and the neighbor who is a stranger.
neighbors.shared: the people next door are part of your faith.

neighbors.heading: the Lord is one
neighbors.text: Today four short lines said who God is: One, needing no one, with none like Him. Christians confess one God too. Asked which commandment comes first, Jesus answered with the Shema: "Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord." The creed Christians say begins the same way: I believe in one God.
neighbors.difference: Christians confess the one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and call Jesus the Son of God. Al-Ikhlas says God neither begets nor was begotten, and Muslims honor Isa as a prophet.
neighbors.shared: you can say "one" with your whole heart.

neighbors.heading: Ik Onkar
neighbors.text: Today four short lines said who God is: One, needing no one, unbegotten, with none like Him. Sikh scripture opens with its own portrait of the One. The Mool Mantar, in an old translation: "There is but one God whose name is true, the Creator," and then, without fear, without enmity, timeless, unborn, self-existent.
neighbors.difference: Al-Ikhlas came, tradition says, when people asked the Prophet ﷺ to describe his Lord. The Mool Mantar opens Guru Nanak's Japji, and Sikhs teach the One is also present in all creation, known through the Guru's grace.
neighbors.shared: "one" can be the first word of a whole life.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (Macauliffe 1909; the rest paraphrased)

neighbors.heading: nothing true and holy
neighbors.text: Today a short surah said: to you your way, to me mine. The Catholic Church has its own words for meeting other faiths. The Second Vatican Council taught that the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions, and it speaks of Muslims with esteem, as people who worship the one God and honor Abraham.
neighbors.difference: The Church holds that the fullness of truth is found in Christ, and still esteems what is good elsewhere. Surah al-Kafirun draws a clear line in worship, and the Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion.
neighbors.shared: you can hold your own faith and still honor your neighbor's.

neighbors.heading: honor the other's path
neighbors.text: Today a short surah said: to you your way, to me mine. A Buddhist king said something close in stone. The emperor Ashoka had an edict carved: whoever praises their own faith and condemns others' only harms their own. Listen to one another's teachings, he urged, and honor them.
neighbors.difference: Ashoka urged people to learn and honor one another's teachings. Al-Kafirun is firmer about worship: the Prophet ﷺ would not join theirs, nor they his, and each was left free to keep their own.
neighbors.shared: you can be clear about your path and kind about theirs.

neighbors.heading: number our days
neighbors.text: Today the surah swore by time: people are in loss, except those who believe, do good, and urge each other to truth and patience. Jews pray over the same clock. A psalm headed "a Prayer of Moses" asks: "So teach us to number our days, that we may get us a heart of wisdom." And Rabbi Tarfon warned: the day is short, and the work is great.
neighbors.difference: Al-'Asr is Allah swearing by time and naming the way out: faith, good deeds, truth and patience, urged on one another. The psalm is a person asking God to teach the counting, and the rabbis answer with Torah study and the commandments.
neighbors.shared: the clock is a teacher, not an enemy.

neighbors.heading: long enough, if used
neighbors.text: Today the surah swore by time: people are in loss, except those who believe, do good, and urge each other to truth and patience. The Roman philosopher Seneca wrote a whole essay on the same alarm. Life isn't short, he said; we make it short by wasting it. Spent well, it is long enough for great things.
neighbors.difference: Al-'Asr names the way out as faith in Allah, good deeds, and urging truth and patience together. Seneca's answer is reason and time given to philosophy, and he points to no Day of reckoning beyond this life.
neighbors.shared: your hours are the one thing you can't earn back.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: you eat what you plant
neighbors.text: Today the surah said even an atom's weight of good will be seen. Sikhs hear a close line in Guru Nanak's Japji: you plant the seed, and you yourself eat its fruit. And another: by our deeds, each of us is weighed; true is the Lord, and true is His court.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, every deed is shown on one Day, and Allah judges. The Japji says deeds shape this birth, but the door of liberation opens by the Guru's grace, nadar, and the soul merges in the One.
neighbors.shared: small good is never weightless.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 20 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4) (paraphrase) · Japji Sahib, pauri 34 (Ang 7) (paraphrase) · Japji Sahib, pauri 4 (Ang 2) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no effort is lost
neighbors.text: Today the surah said even an atom's weight of good will be seen. Hindus have an old way of saying it. An Upanishad teaches: as a person acts, so they become; the one who does good becomes good. And in the Gita, Krishna promises that on this path no effort is wasted, and even a little of it protects from great fear.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, karma ripens across many lives, a law woven into things. In Islam there is one life and one Day, and the record is weighed by Allah, whose mercy is beyond the scale.
neighbors.shared: no kindness is too small to count.

items.lessonTitle: Ad-Duha: the orphan and the asker

neighbors.heading: the last bite
neighbors.text: Today the surah reminded the Prophet he had been an orphan once, so: don't oppress the orphan, don't drive the asker away. The Buddha said it from another side. If people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without giving, even their last bite, if someone needed it.
neighbors.difference: Ad-Duha grounds giving in Allah's care: He sheltered you, so shelter others. The Buddha speaks of no creator; giving loosens the grip of stinginess on the giver's own heart and ripens as good fruit.
neighbors.shared: an open hand is how a heart stays open.

neighbors.heading: turn not away
neighbors.text: Today the surah reminded the Prophet he had been an orphan once, so: don't oppress the orphan, don't drive the asker away. Jesus says it nearly the same way: "Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away." And James writes that pure religion is "to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction."
neighbors.difference: In Ad-Duha, Allah speaks to His prophet about his own orphan years. Christians hear these words from Jesus, whom they believe is God's Son, and say that what is done for the least is done for him.
neighbors.shared: the person asking might be you, a few years back.

neighbors.heading: care of the soul
neighbors.text: Today the surah swore by the soul: the one who purifies it succeeds. Socrates spent his life on that sentence. At his trial, in Plato's Apology, he says he went around Athens asking people why they cared so much for money and fame, and so little for making their soul as good as it could be.
neighbors.difference: The surah says Allah shaped the soul and inspired its sense of right and wrong. Socrates argues from reason, and calls care of the soul the work of wisdom, without pointing to a revelation.
neighbors.shared: your inner life deserves as much care as your wallet.

neighbors.heading: a clean heart
neighbors.text: Today the surah swore by the soul: the one who purifies it succeeds. Catholics pray the same wish in a psalm: "Create a clean heart in me, O God." And Jesus promises: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God."
neighbors.difference: In Islam, a person purifies the soul by remembering Allah, praying and doing good, with His help. Catholics believe the heart is made clean by God's grace through Christ, given in baptism and renewed in confession.
neighbors.shared: a heart can be made clean, and it's worth the work.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 50:12 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 51:10 in many Bibles) · Matthew 5:8 (Douay-Rheims)

neighbors.heading: i am the himalaya
neighbors.text: Today the surah asked: won't they look at the camel, the sky, the mountains, the earth spread out? In the Gita, Krishna points at the world too. Among things that stand unmoving, he says, I am the Himalaya; among lights, the radiant sun. Wherever you see glory and power, know it springs from a spark of my splendor.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, the camel and the mountains are signs pointing to their Maker, who is never one of the things He made. In the Gita, Krishna says the best of things are his own glories showing through.
neighbors.shared: the ordinary world is worth a second, slower look.

neighbors.heading: lift up your eyes
neighbors.text: Today the surah asked: won't they look at the camel, the sky, the mountains, the earth spread out? A Hebrew prophet asked the same: "Lift up your eyes on high, and see: who hath created these?" And a psalm answers: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth His handiwork."
neighbors.difference: The surah turns looking into a question meant to wake the listener. Jewish practice turns it into blessings said aloud: on seeing mountains, seas or deserts, a Jew blesses the One who makes the works of creation.
neighbors.shared: slow down and look: the world is a message.
neighbors.sources: Isaiah 40:26 (JPS 1917) · Psalm 19:2 (JPS 1917; 19:1 in many Bibles) · Mishnah Berakhot 9:2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: god is love
neighbors.text: Today the surah named Allah al-Wadud, the Loving. Christians treasure a short line in one of John's letters: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." The same letter goes on: "he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him."
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the Loving is one of Allah's beautiful names, shown in His mercy and care. Christians say God is love itself, shown above all in sending Jesus, whom they believe is His Son.
neighbors.shared: both call God loving, and both ask us to love back.

neighbors.heading: those who love
neighbors.text: Today the surah named Allah al-Wadud, the Loving. Sikhs sing of a love that finds God. Guru Gobind Singh wrote: hear, all of you, I tell you the truth: only those who love find the Lord. And Guru Nanak's Japji says the True Master's Name is spoken with endless love.
neighbors.difference: Al-Wadud names how Allah loves His servants. Sikh teaching puts its weight on the devotee's love, prem, for the One: loving devotion is itself the way to meet the Lord.
neighbors.shared: love is the road, and it runs both ways.
neighbors.sources: Tav-Prasad Savaiye, Dasam Granth (paraphrase) · Japji Sahib, pauri 4 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: bless us, o lord
neighbors.text: Today the surah said: let the human look at his food, the rain, the grain, the grapes and the olives. Catholics stop at the table to look too. The old grace goes: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen."
neighbors.difference: The surah makes the meal a sign pointing to Allah, who sends the rain. The Catholic grace asks God's blessing through Christ, and for Catholics the highest meal is the Eucharist, which they believe is Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: every plate has a long road behind it, and someone to thank.

neighbors.heading: before the first bite
neighbors.text: Today the surah said: let the human look at his food. Buddhist monks are taught to look before they eat. The Buddha told them to reflect wisely: this food isn't for fun or for vanity, only to keep this body going so the path can go on. In Zen, the Five Reflections before meals begin with all the work that brought the food.
neighbors.difference: The surah points from the meal to Allah, who sends the rain and grows the grain. The Buddhist reflection points inward, to eating without craving, and names no creator to thank.
neighbors.shared: a meal eaten with attention is a kinder meal.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (paraphrase) · the Zen Five Reflections at meals (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: lie down in peace
neighbors.text: Today the surah called sleep a sign: rest given to us, the night a covering. Jews end the day in that trust. A psalm says: "In peace will I both lay me down and sleep; for Thou, LORD, makest me dwell alone in safety." And another gives the reason: "He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep."
neighbors.difference: In the surah, sleep is one of Allah's signs, pointing to the Day of rising. Jewish bedtime prayer hands the night to God with the Shema, and the morning prayer thanks Him for returning the soul.
neighbors.shared: you can set the day down; you aren't holding up the world.

neighbors.heading: the work of sleep
neighbors.text: Today the surah called sleep a sign, rest built into us. Science keeps finding what that rest does. In a 1924 study, Jenkins and Dallenbach had two people learn nonsense syllables, then either sleep or stay awake. After sleeping, they remembered more. Sleep isn't wasted time; something in you keeps working while you let go.
neighbors.difference: The surah reads sleep as a sign from Allah, pointing to its Maker. Psychology treats it as biology to measure, and draws no conclusion about who made it.
neighbors.shared: rest is part of the work, not a break from it.
neighbors.sources: Jenkins & Dallenbach, "Obliviscence during sleep and waking" (1924) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a daily set
neighbors.text: Today you learned the three quls, said three times morning and evening. Sikhs keep a daily set too, the Nitnem: Japji Sahib among the morning prayers, Rehras Sahib at evening, Kirtan Sohila before sleep. Guru Ram Das wrote that one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru rises early and meditates on the Name.
neighbors.difference: The quls ask Allah for refuge, in words Muslims hold are Allah's own. The Nitnem is the Gurus' own hymns, the Guru's word, centered on remembering the Name, naam simran.
neighbors.shared: a short prayer, kept every day, becomes a home.
neighbors.sources: Gauri ki Var, Guru Ram Das (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 305) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: dawn and dusk
neighbors.text: Today you learned the three quls, said morning and evening. Hindus mark the day's meeting points too. Sandhya, the joining prayer, is said at dawn and dusk, and traditionally at noon too, and at its heart is the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda: may we meditate on the glorious light of the divine Sun; may it brighten our minds.
neighbors.difference: The quls seek refuge in Allah, who has no equal. The Gayatri asks Savitr, the divine light, to brighten the mind; Hindus read it in different ways, from one deity to the one Brahman.
neighbors.shared: dawn and dusk are good doors to step through on purpose.

neighbors.heading: overcome anger by love
neighbors.text: Today you heard a hadith: Allah wrote, My mercy prevails over My anger. The Buddha asked the same of people. In the Dhammapada: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good." And what it calls an old rule: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love."
neighbors.difference: The hadith describes Allah, whose mercy outruns His anger. The Buddha speaks of no creator here; he is training the human heart, where loving-kindness, metta, is grown on purpose.
neighbors.shared: anger is answered best by something softer than itself.

neighbors.heading: mercy rejoiceth
neighbors.text: Today you heard a hadith: Allah wrote, My mercy prevails over My anger. Christians sing it in a psalm: "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy." And the apostle James puts it in four words: "mercy rejoiceth against judgment."
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, Allah writes it about Himself, and His mercy reaches whoever turns back. Christians see mercy's fullest picture in Jesus dying and rising, so that judgment meets forgiveness at the cross.
neighbors.shared: mercy is meant to win, in heaven and at the kitchen table.

neighbors.heading: try again, gently
neighbors.text: Today Allah was al-Ghaffar, who forgives again and again. Psychologists found that going easy on yourself after a failure doesn't make you lazy. In studies by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen, people prompted to meet a mistake with self-compassion were more motivated to make amends and try harder than people prompted to boost their self-esteem.
neighbors.difference: Al-Ghaffar is Allah forgiving, a mercy that comes from beyond you. Self-compassion is something you give yourself, and the research makes no claim about any forgiveness beyond the human.
neighbors.shared: the kindest voice is the one that helps you try again.

neighbors.heading: seventy times seven
neighbors.text: Today Allah was al-Ghaffar, who forgives again and again, however often you come back. Peter once asked Jesus how often he must forgive his brother: "till seven times?" Jesus answered: "I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times." Catholics hear in it God's own patience, and come back to confession as often as they need.
neighbors.difference: Muslims turn to Allah directly in repentance, with no one in between. Catholics confess to a priest in the sacrament of Penance, believing Christ forgives through him.
neighbors.shared: coming back is never one time too many.

neighbors.heading: seated in the heart
neighbors.text: Today Allah was al-'Alim, who knows what the heart hides. In the Gita, Krishna says it from the inside: the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, Arjuna. Elsewhere he calls himself the knower of the field, present in every body, knowing it from within.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, Allah knows the heart completely and is "nearer than the jugular vein," yet never becomes the self. In the Gita, the Lord seated in the heart is one way Hindus speak of God within each being.
neighbors.shared: you're never as unseen as you feel on a lonely night.

neighbors.heading: search me
neighbors.text: Today Allah was al-'Alim, who knows what the heart hides. A psalm says it with wonder: "O LORD, Thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, Thou understandest my thought afar off." By the end, the psalmist asks for more: "Search me, O God, and know my heart."
neighbors.difference: In Islam, al-'Alim is one of Allah's names, a name to call on in prayer. The psalm gives God's knowing no title; it's one person talking to God, half amazed, then asking to be searched and led.
neighbors.shared: being fully known can feel like being held.

neighbors.heading: all things common
neighbors.text: Today strangers became brothers in Medina, each migrant paired with a helper who shared his home. The first Christians in Jerusalem did something close: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." They sold what they had and "parted them to all men, as every man had need."
neighbors.difference: The Medina brotherhood paired people one to one, by the Prophet's arrangement, in a season of migration. In Acts, the whole community pooled what it had, and Christians call that bond one body in Christ.
neighbors.shared: a stranger can become family the day you share your door.

neighbors.heading: no one is a stranger
neighbors.text: Today strangers became brothers in Medina, each migrant paired with a helper who shared his home. Sikhs build that welcome into every gurdwara: in the langar, anyone can sit and eat side by side, whatever their caste or faith. Guru Arjan sang: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone.
neighbors.difference: The Medina brothers were paired among believers, one household opening to another. The langar is a shared meal rather than a pairing, served by whoever is there to whoever walks in.
neighbors.shared: a stranger can become family over one shared meal.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Raag Kanara (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: anoint thy head
neighbors.text: Today fasting was prescribed, "even as it was prescribed for those before you." Catholics are among those who still keep it. In Lent, the forty days before Easter, they fast and give things up, following Jesus, who said: "when thou fastest anoint thy head, and wash thy face; that thou appear not to men to fast."
neighbors.difference: Ramadan is a full month with no food or drink from dawn to sunset. Catholic fasting is lighter in law, one full meal on set days like Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, joined to Christ's forty days in the desert.
neighbors.shared: an empty stomach can make room for a fuller heart.

neighbors.heading: nothing after noon
neighbors.text: Today fasting was prescribed, "even as it was prescribed for those before you." Under the old monastic rule, Buddhist monks and nuns keep a daily fast of their own: no food from noon until the next dawn. On observance days, uposatha, lay Buddhists can join them by keeping eight precepts. The Buddha said that eating once a day, he felt light, healthy and at ease.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the fast is commanded by Allah, a duty of Ramadan for every able adult. The Buddhist noon rule is monastic training to steady the mind; for lay people it is a practice taken on, not a command from God.
neighbors.shared: going without, on purpose, teaches what's enough.

neighbors.heading: regard the life of his beast
neighbors.text: Today you heard of a sinner forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog. Jewish law takes an animal's pain seriously too; the rabbis call it tza'ar ba'alei chayim. Proverbs says: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." And the Talmud teaches that you feed your animals before you sit down to eat yourself.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, one act of mercy to a dog brings Allah's forgiveness. Jewish teaching frames this care as law, a commandment owed every day; the Talmud even tells of a great rabbi who suffered for brushing off a frightened calf.
neighbors.shared: how you treat a thirsty animal says who you are.

neighbors.heading: can they suffer?
neighbors.text: Today you heard of a sinner forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog. The English philosopher Jeremy Bentham put the animal question in one line: "The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?" For him, a creature's pain counted, whoever's it was.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, kindness to an animal is seen by Allah and rewarded. Bentham argued from pain and pleasure alone, with no God keeping the record; the suffering itself is the reason.
neighbors.shared: a creature's thirst is reason enough to help.
neighbors.sources: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), ch. 17, note

neighbors.heading: where forgiveness is
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet stood before the people who drove him out and said: no blame on you today. Sikh scripture holds that same mercy. Kabir: where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself. And Baba Farid: do good to the one who does you evil, and don't carry anger in your heart.
neighbors.difference: At Mecca, forgiveness came from a prophet at the height of his power, echoing Yusuf before him. In the Guru Granth Sahib, forgiveness is part of any God-filled life, a quality asked of everyone, every day.
neighbors.shared: forgiving the one who hurt you is the strong move.
neighbors.sources: Salok Kabir (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372) (paraphrase) · Salok Farid (Ang 1382) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: forgiveness is truth
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet stood before the people who drove him out and said: no blame on you today. In the Gita, Krishna lists forgiveness, kshama, among the qualities of one born to a godly nature. And in the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira tells his angry wife that forgiveness is truth, and forgiveness holds the world together.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet forgave Mecca as Allah's messenger, a day Muslims look back to as history. In the Mahabharata, Draupadi argues back, and war still comes later; the epic lets the question stay hard.
neighbors.shared: letting go of what you're owed can free two people.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 16.3 (paraphrase) · Mahabharata, Vana Parva 29 (Ganguli numbering; 3.30 in the Critical Edition) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today, in his farewell sermon, the Prophet said no Arab is above a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab above an Arab, except by goodness. The Buddha said something close, to a world sorted by birth: not by birth is one an outcast, not by birth a brahmin; by deeds one becomes an outcast, by deeds a brahmin.
neighbors.difference: The sermon is about standing before Allah, who alone weighs goodness. The Buddha was taking apart the caste order of his day; by "brahmin" he meant anyone of pure conduct, with no God doing the weighing.
neighbors.shared: your worth is in how you live, not where you were born.

neighbors.heading: neither jew nor greek
neighbors.text: Today, in his farewell sermon, the Prophet said no Arab is above a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab above an Arab, except by goodness. Paul wrote to churches split over who belonged: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."
neighbors.difference: The sermon measures people by taqwa, mindful goodness before Allah. Paul grounds the oneness in Christ, through faith and baptism; the common ground is being in him.
neighbors.shared: no one at the table was born a step higher.

neighbors.heading: as if watched
neighbors.text: Today you heard ihsan: worship as though you see Him, for if you don't see Him, He sees you. Seneca passed on advice from Epicurus: "Cherish some man of high character, and keep him ever before your eyes, living as if he were watching you, and ordering all your actions as if he beheld them."
neighbors.difference: Ihsan is awareness of Allah, who truly sees. Seneca's watcher is an imagined good person, a standard to live up to; the Stoic doesn't claim anyone is actually looking.
neighbors.shared: you live differently when you remember you're seen with kindness.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 11.8 (tr. Gummere, 1917)

neighbors.heading: among the pots and pans
neighbors.text: Today you heard ihsan: worship as though you see Him, for if you don't see Him, He sees you. A Carmelite brother, Lawrence of the Resurrection, made a life of this in a monastery kitchen. He called it the practice of the presence of God: in the noise of his work, he said, he held God as calmly as if he were on his knees.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, Allah sees you but has no form to picture. Brother Lawrence spoke to God as a close friend, and Catholics believe God came near in Jesus, who can be seen and pictured.
neighbors.shared: the dishes can be prayer too, if you remember who's near.
neighbors.sources: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: love, not liberation
neighbors.text: Today Rabi'a prayed to love Allah for Himself, not for heaven and not from fear of hell. Hindu bhakti, devotion, has the same fire. In the Bhagavata Purana, Kapila teaches that true devotees, even when offered every kind of liberation, won't take it if it means giving up loving service to the Lord.
neighbors.difference: Rabi'a loved Allah, the One beyond every image. In bhakti, love is often poured out to a personal form of God, such as Krishna or Vishnu, through images, songs and names.
neighbors.shared: the best love doesn't keep a ledger.

neighbors.heading: not for the reward
neighbors.text: Today Rabi'a prayed to love Allah for Himself, not for heaven and not from fear of hell. An early Jewish sage, Antigonus of Sokho, taught: don't be like servants who serve the master to get a reward; be like servants who serve the master with no thought of reward. And let the fear of Heaven be upon you.
neighbors.difference: Rabi'a's words are a lover's, wanting only the Beloved, past both heaven and fear. Antigonus speaks as a servant before a Master, and keeps awe in the picture beside the service.
neighbors.shared: serving out of love asks for nothing back.

neighbors.heading: pray without ceasing
neighbors.text: Today you heard: everything has a polish, and the heart's polish is remembrance. A Christian letter puts cleaning and nearness together: "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded." And Paul gives a method in three words: "Pray without ceasing."
neighbors.difference: In the saying, remembrance itself is the polish. Christians believe the heart is cleansed by Christ's grace, and prayer keeps a person close to that grace rather than doing the cleaning alone.
neighbors.shared: the heart stays bright by turning back to God, often.

neighbors.heading: washed by the name
neighbors.text: Today you heard: everything has a polish, and the heart's polish is remembrance. Guru Nanak used a washing picture in the Japji: when hands are muddy, water washes them; when clothes are soiled, soap cleans them; when the mind is stained with wrongdoing, it is washed by the love of the Name.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, dhikr remembers Allah by His names and set phrases, often counted on beads. Sikh simran remembers the Name, Waheguru, often sung in the Guru's hymns with the congregation.
neighbors.shared: a heart gets clean the way a window does: again and again.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 20 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: by word or by letter
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an was kept two ways: written on palm stalks and bone, and carried in people's hearts. Catholics also hold the faith came down two ways. Paul wrote: "hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word, or by our epistle." The Church calls them Scripture and Tradition, passed hand to hand.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, what was written and what was memorized are the same words, the Qur'an itself. For Catholics, Tradition is more than the Bible's words: the Church's living teaching, which reads and hands on Scripture.
neighbors.shared: a sacred word lasts because people carry it, by hand and heart.

neighbors.heading: thus have i heard
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an was kept two ways: on palm stalks and bone, and in people's hearts. Buddhist tradition remembers that after the Buddha died, his monks met and recited his teachings together, Ananda speaking the discourses from memory. That's why so many begin: "Thus have I heard." Tradition says they were chanted long before anyone wrote them down.
neighbors.difference: Muslims hold the Qur'an is Allah's own word, every letter. The suttas are the Buddha's teaching as his followers heard and remembered it, and Buddhists don't hold them to be the speech of a God.
neighbors.shared: words worth keeping live in people before they live in books.

neighbors.heading: turn it and turn it
neighbors.text: Today you saw scholars explain the Qur'an by other verses, by hadith, by language and context. Jews love this work too. In the Mishnah, Ben Bag Bag says of the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. And Hillel, after giving the whole Torah in one line, said: the rest is commentary; go and learn.
neighbors.difference: Muslims explain the Qur'an through the Prophet's sunnah and the scholars who followed. Jews read Torah with the Oral Torah, held to be given at Sinai too, and the Talmud keeps even the losing side of an argument on the page.
neighbors.shared: an old text keeps opening if you keep asking it questions.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 5:22 (numbering varies by edition) (paraphrase) · Talmud Shabbat 31a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the parts and the whole
neighbors.text: Today you saw scholars explain the Qur'an by other verses, by hadith, by language and context. Philosophers who study how we understand texts call this the hermeneutic circle, a name tied to Friedrich Schleiermacher: you understand the parts through the whole, and the whole through its parts, going round until the meaning opens.
neighbors.difference: Tafsir reads a book Muslims hold to be Allah's word, guided by the Prophet's own explanations. The hermeneutic circle is a method for any text, a poem or a law, and assumes no divine author.
neighbors.shared: careful reading is a way of showing respect.

neighbors.heading: the unbroken reading
neighbors.text: Today you met the khatm, a whole reading of the Qur'an, often closed with a gathering. Sikhs know that joy too. In an Akhand Path, readers take turns through day and night, reading the entire Guru Granth Sahib without a break, front to back. At the end comes prayer, and karah prashad shared with everyone there.
neighbors.difference: A khatm can be read by one person across a month or by a group in parts. An Akhand Path must never stop, one reader handing to the next, and the Guru Granth Sahib is honored as the living Guru.
neighbors.shared: finishing a holy book together turns readers into family.
neighbors.sources: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on the Akhand Path (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seven days of listening
neighbors.text: Today you met the khatm, a whole reading of the Qur'an, often closed with a gathering. Hindus have whole readings too. The Bhagavata Purana is recited start to finish in seven days, a saptaha, with families gathering to listen; its own praise-chapters tell of a lost soul freed by hearing it through.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an is recited in its own Arabic, the exact words held to be Allah's. A Bhagavata saptaha is often led by a teller who reads, sings and explains, and for most who come, listening is the practice.
neighbors.shared: a whole book, start to finish, changes you more than a favorite page.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Mahatmya (Padma Purana), the story of Gokarna and Dhundhukari (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mirror
neighbors.text: Today you looked back down the hill at a whole year. The Buddha taught his son Rahula a looking-back habit, like using a mirror: before, while and after you do anything, look at it. Did it bring harm to me, to others, to both? If it was good, he said, go on in joy, training day and night.
neighbors.difference: Your lookout thanks Allah for what He gave this year. Rahula's mirror names no giver to thank; it looks at actions and their fruit, so the next step can be wiser.
neighbors.shared: looking back kindly is how you find the next step.

neighbors.heading: hitherto
neighbors.text: Today you looked back down the hill at a whole year. In the Bible, Samuel did that after a hard battle: he set up a stone, called it Ebenezer, and said, "Hitherto hath the LORD helped us." A psalm keeps the habit: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits."
neighbors.difference: Your lookout remembers what Allah gave through His prophets, the prayer and the Qur'an. Christians look back through Israel's story to Jesus, and keep their church year around his birth, death and rising.
neighbors.shared: every so often, stop and see how far you've been carried.

neighbors.heading: a world in a grain of sand
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said God isn't too proud to teach with a gnat. Poets have found the same in small things. William Blake opened a poem: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower." For Blake, looking closely at the smallest thing was a way of seeing everything.
neighbors.difference: For Blake, the vision comes through the seer's own opened imagination. In the Qur'an, the gnat is a likeness God himself chooses to strike, a sign pointing past itself to its maker.
neighbors.shared: the smallest thing can hold a lesson, if you look.

neighbors.heading: a mustard seed
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said God isn't too proud to teach with a gnat. Jesus taught with small things too: "The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field." The least of all seeds, he said, grows into a tree, and the birds come and dwell in its branches.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, Allah coins the likeness, answering people who scoffed at small examples. For Catholics, the one telling the parable is Jesus, whom they believe is God the Son made man, teaching with seeds, coins and lost sheep.
neighbors.shared: nothing is too small to show you something true.

neighbors.heading: come toward, be met
neighbors.text: Today God said, "remember Me, I will remember you." In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna makes a promise with the same two-way shape: in whatever way people come to me, in that same way I receive them. In japa, a name of God is repeated softly on a string of beads, a small way of turning toward.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God come in a human form, speaking face to face with Arjuna. In the Qur'an, Allah speaks through revelation and takes no form; remembrance turns to One beyond every likeness.
neighbors.shared: the one you remember is remembering you.

neighbors.heading: return, and be returned to
neighbors.text: Today God said, "remember Me, I will remember you." The Hebrew prophets heard a two-way promise too. In Malachi, God says: "Return unto Me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts." And a psalm asks, in wonder: "What is man, that Thou art mindful of him?"
neighbors.difference: In Malachi, the call goes to a people, Israel, to come back to the covenant after drifting. In al-Baqarah, remembrance follows a gift received, a prayer answered, and asks for thanks in return.
neighbors.shared: turning toward God is never a one-way road.
neighbors.sources: Malachi 3:7; Psalm 8:5 (JPS 1917; Psalm 8:4 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: neither slumber nor sleep
neighbors.text: Today the Throne verse said of God, "Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him." Christians pray a psalm with almost the same words: "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. The LORD is thy keeper." It ends: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in."
neighbors.difference: Christians pray this psalm to one God they know as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Muslims hear the Throne verse as the word of Allah, the One, with whom no one intercedes except by his permission.
neighbors.shared: someone keeps watch while you sleep.

neighbors.heading: the timeless one
neighbors.text: Today the Throne verse named God the Alive, the Eternal, never weary. Sikh scripture opens with the Mool Mantar, a short list of who God is: one; truth is the name; the creator; without fear; without hate; timeless in form; never born; self-existent. It's the opening of Japji Sahib, the morning prayer.
neighbors.difference: The Mool Mantar ends gur prasad: God is known by the Guru's grace, and Sikhs meet Waheguru through the Guru's word. The Throne verse goes on to God's Throne and his knowledge, which people grasp only as he wills.
neighbors.shared: you lean on someone who never gets tired.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, the Mool Mantar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said a gift held over someone is like soil washed off a rock. Jesus said something close: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth. That thy alms may be in secret, and thy Father who seeth in secret will repay thee."
neighbors.difference: Jesus' warning is about giving to be seen by others. The Qur'an warns against that too, and adds the afterwards: bringing the gift up to the one who received it, holding it over them.
neighbors.shared: a gift is lightest when you don't keep score.

neighbors.heading: giving without holding on
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said a gift held over someone is like soil washed off a rock. Buddhists call giving dana, and count it among the perfections. In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha teaches that a bodhisattva should give without clinging to anything at all, and that giving like that brings merit beyond measure.
neighbors.difference: In the Diamond Sutra, the point is letting go of the very idea of a giver and a gift. In the Qur'an, the gift is given for God's sake, and its reward is kept with the Lord.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts come with no strings at all.

neighbors.heading: a time for everything
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the days take turns among people, and neither good days nor bad ones stay. Ecclesiastes says it in a list: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." And then: "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance."
neighbors.difference: Ecclesiastes sets the turning seasons beside a hard question: what lasts? The Qur'an speaks to grief right after a lost battle and gives a purpose: in the turning days, God makes known who stays faithful.
neighbors.shared: the hard day you're in is not the last day.

neighbors.heading: the river of days
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the days take turns, and neither good ones nor bad ones stay. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote in a notebook to himself that time is like a river of things happening, a strong current: one thing is seen and swept away, another takes its place, and it too will be carried off.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, the turning is simply nature's way, to be met with a calm mind. The Qur'an sees a hand in it: God turns the days, and through them shows who holds on.
neighbors.shared: nothing, not even a bad season, stays forever.

neighbors.heading: no stranger
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said everyone comes from a single soul, so every person you meet is family. Guru Arjan sang it in the Guru Granth Sahib: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. In the langar, the Sikh free kitchen, anyone who walks in eats side by side.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an roots it in one first soul and its mate, and in honoring the ties of the womb, your kin. Guru Arjan's line comes from the company of the holy, and from seeing the one God in everyone.
neighbors.shared: every face you pass today belongs to your family.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Kanra, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the world is one family
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said everyone comes from a single soul, so every person you meet is a relative. An old Sanskrit verse agrees: only narrow minds count this one as mine and that one as a stranger; for the generous-hearted, the whole earth is one family. In Sanskrit: vasudhaiva kutumbakam.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an traces the family to one first soul and its mate, made by God. The Sanskrit verse is about the heart's width: kinship is how the generous see. Some Hindu schools add that one Self lives in every being.
neighbors.shared: nobody you meet is really a stranger.

items.lessonTitle: The near neighbor and the far

neighbors.heading: near or far
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked kindness for the neighbor who is near and the one who is far. The Buddha's Metta Sutta wishes well to every being: seen or unseen, living near or far away, born or yet to be born. It asks for a love like a mother's, who would guard her only child with her life.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an names people one by one and makes being a neighbor a duty before God. The Metta Sutta widens loving-kindness to every living being, animals and unseen ones too, as a practice that frees the heart.
neighbors.shared: your circle of care can always get a little wider.

neighbors.heading: who is my neighbor?
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked kindness for the neighbor who is near and the one who is far. A lawyer once asked Jesus, "And who is my neighbour?" Jesus answered with a story: a Samaritan, a stranger, stops on the road for a wounded man the others passed by. Then he said: "Go, and do thou likewise."
neighbors.difference: Jesus turns the question around: not who counts as my neighbor, but who acted like one. The Qur'an lists the neighbors in order, near and far, in a verse that begins with worshipping God alone.
neighbors.shared: the stranger on your road is your neighbor too.

neighbors.heading: don't become like them
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said don't let hatred of a people push you into being unjust. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote a note to himself: "The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer." Being wronged, he thought, is never a reason to do wrong.
neighbors.difference: Marcus grounds it in reason and self-command: your own character is the one thing you control. The Qur'an grounds it in God: stand as witnesses for Allah in fairness, because justice is nearer to taqwa.
neighbors.shared: someone else's wrong never has to become yours.

neighbors.heading: love your enemies
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said don't let hatred of a people push you into being unjust. Jesus spoke to the same pull, in the Sermon on the Mount: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you."
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an's command here is justice: deal fairly with people you dislike, and don't let feeling bend the scales. Jesus' command is love and prayer for the enemy. Each is asked when it's hardest.
neighbors.shared: the people you struggle with still deserve your fairness.

neighbors.heading: the one who knows
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said not a leaf falls without God knowing. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says something close: I know all beings, those that were, those that are, and those still to come, but no one knows me. Later the Gita adds that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the one who knows also lives in every heart, and many Hindus see God as within the world and beyond it. In the Qur'an, God knows every leaf, yet no creature shares his being.
neighbors.shared: nothing about you goes unseen, not even the small things.

neighbors.heading: you have searched me
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said not a leaf falls without God knowing. A psalm says it about one person: "O LORD, Thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising." It goes on: there is nowhere to go from God, not the heavens, not the sea, not the dark.
neighbors.difference: The psalm speaks from inside one life, in wonder at being known so fully. The Qur'an's verse widens to the whole earth: every leaf, every grain in the dark, written in a clear record.
neighbors.shared: you're known, all the way down to the small things.

neighbors.heading: the hidden person of the heart
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the best clothing is the garment of piety. A New Testament letter says real beauty is not "that outward adorning", but "the hidden man of the heart... even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit." And Paul writes: "Put on therefore... kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness."
neighbors.difference: Christians also speak of putting on Christ himself, clothed in him at baptism. In the Qur'an, the inner garment is taqwa, mindfulness of God, and outer clothing is called a gift too.
neighbors.shared: what you wear inside is what people remember.

neighbors.heading: a thread that won't wear out
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the best clothing is the garment of piety. Sikhs tell how the boy Nanak was offered a sacred thread and asked for a different one. His hymn says: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, self-control the knot, truth the twist. A thread like that won't break, get dirty, or burn.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak's hymn asks for virtues in place of an outward thread. The Qur'an keeps both garments, calling clothing and finery a gift, and names taqwa, mindfulness of God, the best.
neighbors.shared: the clothes that matter most are the ones nobody sees.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Asa di Var, Guru Nanak (paraphrase); the Janamsakhis (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: gather up the fragments
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said eat and drink, but don't waste. After Jesus fed the crowd with five barley loaves, the Gospel adds a small, practical line: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." They filled twelve baskets with what was left. Even after a miracle, nothing was thrown away.
neighbors.difference: Catholics read this meal as a sign pointing to the Eucharist, the bread they receive at Mass as Christ himself. The Qur'an's verse is about ordinary eating and drinking: enjoy the good things, and stay inside the limit.
neighbors.shared: enjoy what's on your plate, and let nothing go to waste.

neighbors.heading: knowing the measure
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said eat and drink, but don't waste. The Buddha found his path between indulgence and starving himself, and called it the middle way. The Dhammapada says one who lives moderate in food, steady and faithful, can't be blown over by the tempter Mara, any more than wind can topple a rocky mountain.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, good food is Allah's gift to enjoy with thanks, and excess is what he doesn't love. For Buddhists, moderation is training: eating just enough keeps the mind clear for the path.
neighbors.shared: enough is a kind of freedom.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 7–8 (paraphrase); Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the middle way (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: proclaim peace first
