neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said if the other side leans toward peace, lean toward it too. The Torah has a rule for war: "When thou drawest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it." And a psalm turns peace into a chase: "seek peace, and pursue it."
neighbors.difference: The Torah asks Israel to offer peace first, before any fight. The Qur'an speaks to the moment the other side offers it, and meets the fear of a trick: trust in Allah; he is enough.
neighbors.shared: when peace is offered, reach for it.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 20:10; Psalm 34:15 (JPS 1917; Psalm 34:14 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: leave room for peace
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said if the other side leans toward peace, lean toward it too. The philosopher Immanuel Kant, writing on how nations could reach a lasting peace, set one rule even for wartime: never do anything that would make trust impossible once the fighting stops. Keep the door to peace open, even mid-fight.
neighbors.difference: Kant builds peace on reason and on rules nations could agree to. The Qur'an builds it on trust in God: incline to peace, and if they mean to deceive you, Allah is enough for you.
neighbors.shared: even in a fight, leave a door open.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Toward Perpetual Peace (1795), sixth preliminary article (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: your will is sweet
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet was told to say, God is enough for me, even if people turn away. Guru Arjan sang a line Sikhs carry into hard days: tera kiya meetha laagai, whatever you do feels sweet to me. Sikh tradition remembers him at peace even during his martyrdom in Lahore.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan's line is about accepting God's hukam, his will, as sweet. The Qur'anic line is tawakkul: leaning your whole weight on Allah, Lord of the Throne, even when people turn away.
neighbors.shared: even when plans fall apart, you're not empty-handed.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Asa, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: take refuge in me alone
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet was told to say, God is enough for me, even if people turn away. Near the end of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna: let go of every other support and take refuge in me alone; I will free you; do not grieve. Some Hindu traditions call that full leaning on God prapatti, surrender.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God in a human form, standing beside Arjuna on the battlefield. In the Qur'an, Allah is beyond every form; trusting him means leaning on One no eye can see.
neighbors.shared: you can set the whole weight down.

neighbors.heading: the moon out of the clouds
neighbors.text: Today the people of Yunus turned in time and were spared. Buddhists tell of Angulimala, a killer whose name means finger-garland. He met the Buddha, stopped, and became a monk. The Dhammapada says one whose wrong deeds are covered by good ones lights up the world, like the moon freed from clouds.
neighbors.difference: In the sutta, no one lifts the results from outside: Angulimala still met the fruits of his past deeds, karma at work. In the Qur'an, the town turned to God, and God himself lifted what was coming.
neighbors.shared: no one is too far gone to change.

neighbors.heading: the same city
neighbors.text: Today the people of Yunus turned in time and were spared. Christians read the same story in the book of Jonah. Nineveh fasted and cried out, "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." Jesus later pointed to it: the men of Nineveh "repented at the preaching of Jonas."
neighbors.difference: In Jonah, the prophet preaches in the city and is angry when it's spared, and God teaches him mercy. In the commentators' telling of the Qur'an, Yunus had already left, and the people turned without him.
neighbors.shared: it's not too late to turn around.

neighbors.heading: love even the wrongdoer
neighbors.text: Today you met Yusuf, who said to the brothers who sold him: no reproach on you today. Marcus Aurelius wrote in his notebook: "It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong." He reminded himself that the wrongdoer is kin, acting in ignorance, and can't make your own mind worse.
neighbors.difference: Marcus forgives by reasoning: they acted in ignorance, and your mind is still your own. Yusuf forgives as one who trusted God through the well and the prison, and he asks God to forgive his brothers too.
neighbors.shared: forgiving them can be how your own story heals.

neighbors.heading: i am Joseph, your brother
neighbors.text: Today you met the story the Qur'an calls the best: Yusuf and his brothers. Catholics read it in Genesis. When Joseph finally reveals himself, he says: "I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Be not afraid." Later he tells them: "You thought evil against me: but God turned it into good."
neighbors.difference: Genesis tells it across many chapters, and Catholics also read Joseph as a sign pointing ahead to Christ. The Qur'an tells it whole in one surah, with Yusuf a prophet, and his words: no reproach on you today.
neighbors.shared: a betrayal doesn't have to be the end of the story.

neighbors.heading: a lamp where no wind blows
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said hearts find rest in remembering God. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the one who knows him as the friend of all beings attains peace. And it pictures the settled mind as a lamp in a windless place that doesn't flicker. In japa, a name of God is repeated softly until the mind grows still.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the settled mind comes through practice and devotion to Krishna, God in a form many Hindus picture and love. In the Qur'an, remembrance turns to Allah, beyond every image, through his words and names.
neighbors.shared: a mind can learn to rest, one remembered word at a time.

neighbors.heading: my soul waits in stillness
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said hearts find rest in remembering God. A psalm says it almost the same way: "Only for God doth my soul wait in stillness; from Him cometh my salvation." And another speaks to its own heart: "Return, O my soul, unto thy rest; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee."
neighbors.difference: The psalms speak as one person, often in trouble, talking to their own soul and to God. The Qur'an names a practice for every believer, dhikr: short phrases of remembrance through the day.
neighbors.shared: a restless heart can come home and settle.

neighbors.heading: more than can be numbered
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said if you tried to count God's favor, you couldn't. A psalm tries anyway, and happily gives up: "Many, O LORD my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done... they are more than can be numbered." An old hymn turns it into a practice: "Count your blessings, name them one by one."
neighbors.difference: Christians count Jesus himself as God's greatest gift: "Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift." The Qur'an's verse closes on God's forgiveness and mercy, even toward people who forget his favors.
neighbors.shared: start counting your blessings, and you'll never reach the end.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 40:5; 2 Corinthians 9:15 (KJV); "Count Your Blessings," Johnson Oatman Jr. (1897)

neighbors.heading: no end to the giving
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said if you tried to count God's favor, you couldn't. Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib says it in a long, joyful list: no end to God's praises, no end to the ways of telling them, no end to the gifts, no end to the giving. Many try to find the limit, it says, and none can.
neighbors.difference: Japji speaks of Waheguru, beyond all limits, known through the Guru's grace. The Qur'an's verse looks at the favors from the human side, and closes on God's forgiveness for those who forget them.
neighbors.shared: there's always more to be grateful for than you can count.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib, pauri 24 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: patience as a fruit
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said your patience comes only through God. Catholics say something close: patience is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, grown in you, not forced. Paul lists it: "the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace, patience." And Jesus told his friends: "In your patience you shall possess your souls."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, patience grows from the Holy Spirit, worshipped with the Father and the Son as one God. In the Qur'an, sabr is given by Allah, the One, and asked of the Prophet in a grief commentators place after Uhud.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to find all your patience on your own.

neighbors.heading: patience, the highest austerity
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said your patience comes only through God. The Buddha counted patience, khanti, among the perfections. A verse of the Dhammapada calls patient endurance the highest austerity. And in one teaching, he asks for a heart of goodwill even toward bandits sawing you limb from limb.
neighbors.difference: For Buddhists, patience is trained in your own mind, a practice that cools anger at its root. In the Qur'an, the command to be patient comes with a promise: you can't hold steady alone; Allah gives the steadiness.
neighbors.shared: a steady heart can be grown, even on hard days.

neighbors.heading: what a day may bring
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an taught: never say I'll do it tomorrow without adding, if God wills. Proverbs says: "Boast not thyself of to-morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth." A plan may come with a small Hebrew phrase: im yirtzeh Hashem, if God wills, or b'ezrat Hashem, with God's help.
neighbors.difference: Inshallah comes straight from a Qur'anic command, which commentators tie to a promised answer that came late. In Judaism, im yirtzeh Hashem is a cherished custom of speech, not a command in the Torah.
neighbors.shared: make your plans, and hold them with open hands.

neighbors.heading: if nothing gets in the way
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an taught: never say I'll do it tomorrow without adding, if God wills. The Stoic Seneca taught something close. The wise person, he wrote, starts every plan with a quiet clause: if nothing prevents it. So when something does, they aren't thrown; they never claimed the future was theirs.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's clause leans on fate and reason: the world isn't yours to command. Inshallah turns to God: every plan sits inside the will of Allah, who knows what you don't.
neighbors.shared: plan boldly, and leave room for what you can't control.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, On Tranquility of Mind 13; On Benefits 4.34 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a thief hears a hymn
neighbors.text: Today a page of the Qur'an changed Umar on his way to do harm. Sikhs tell of Sajjan, a man who welcomed travelers and then robbed them. The story goes that Guru Nanak sang him a hymn: bronze shines bright, but rub it and the black shows. Sajjan saw himself, fell at the Guru's feet, and changed his life.
neighbors.difference: Sajjan was turned by the Guru himself, singing face to face. Umar was turned before he ever reached the Prophet, by the words of the Qur'an on a page in his sister's house.
neighbors.shared: one true word can turn a whole life around.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Suhi, Guru Nanak (paraphrase); the Janamsakhis (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the robber who became a poet
neighbors.text: Today a page of the Qur'an changed Umar on his way to do harm. Hindus tell of Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana. Tradition says he was once a robber. The sage Narada asked him: will your family share the weight of your crimes? They wouldn't. Shaken, he sat repeating Rama's name, and became a sage.
neighbors.difference: Valmiki's change, in the telling, came slowly, through long practice repeating a name. Umar's, in the sirah's telling, came in one sitting, reading the opening of Ta-Ha in his sister's house.
neighbors.shared: nobody is beyond a change of heart.
neighbors.sources: the Valmiki legend in later Ramayana retellings and popular tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: both edges of the day
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said glorify God before the sun rises and before it sets. In many Buddhist monasteries, the day has two edges too: chanting in the morning and the evening, recalling the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha. The Dhammapada says the Buddha's disciples stay wide awake, their minds on the Buddha day and night.
neighbors.difference: Buddhists recall the Buddha as a teacher who woke up, not as a creator to be worshipped, and the chanting trains the mind. In the Qur'an, tasbih glorifies Allah, the Lord, and brings contentment from him.
neighbors.shared: the edges of the day are good for remembering what matters.

neighbors.heading: from the rising of the sun
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said glorify God before the sun rises and before it sets. A psalm Christians pray says: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD's name is to be praised." The Book of Common Prayer sets out a Morning Prayer and an Evening Prayer for every day.
neighbors.difference: Many commentators read the two edges of the day as Fajr and 'Asr, part of the daily prayer asked of every Muslim. In much of Christianity, morning and evening prayer is a rhythm many keep, not a duty for all.
neighbors.shared: you can bookend the day with praise.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 113:3 (KJV); Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning and Evening Prayer

neighbors.heading: attention is prayer
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an praised khushu': stillness in prayer, not rushing, coming to rest. The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer. For her, slowing down and looking without grabbing for answers mattered most, and she said even schoolwork could train it.
neighbors.difference: For Weil, attention is an open, waiting stillness that study can train, and at its height it turns toward God. In the Qur'an, khushu' is stillness before Allah, kept in a prayer with set movements, each held until you're at rest.
neighbors.shared: slower can be deeper.
neighbors.sources: Simone Weil, Gravity and Grace, "Attention and Will" (paraphrase); "Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let thy words be few
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an praised khushu': stillness in prayer, and turning from idle talk. Ecclesiastes gives similar counsel: "let not thy heart be hasty to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few." Catholics also keep quiet hours of adoration.
neighbors.difference: In Catholic adoration, the stillness is before Christ, whom Catholics believe is truly present in the consecrated bread. In the Qur'an, khushu' is stillness before Allah, kept in the bows and prostrations of salah.
neighbors.shared: fewer words, and more of you present.

neighbors.heading: by his light, all shines
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pictured God's light as a lamp in a niche, light upon light. The Katha Upanishad says of the highest: the sun doesn't shine there, nor the moon and stars, nor lightning, let alone this fire. When he shines, everything shines after him; by his light all this is lit.
neighbors.difference: Some Hindu schools read this light as one with your own deepest Self, the atman. In the Qur'an, God's light guides the heart, but the lamp is a likeness, and God stays beyond what he lights.
neighbors.shared: every light you see points back to a deeper one.

neighbors.heading: the lamp of the LORD
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pictured God's light as a lamp in a niche, light upon light. Proverbs has its own lamp: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inward parts." And a psalm sings: "For with Thee is the fountain of life; in Thy light do we see light."
neighbors.difference: In Proverbs, the human spirit is the lamp God uses to search a person. In the Qur'an, the lamp is a likeness for God's own light, which commentators read as shining into the believer's heart.
neighbors.shared: some light in you was lit from beyond you.
neighbors.sources: Proverbs 20:27; Psalm 36:10 (JPS 1917; Psalm 36:9 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: blessed are the meek
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the servants of the Merciful walk gently, and answer a hothead with peace. Jesus blessed the same people: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth." "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." And Proverbs adds: "A soft answer turneth away wrath."
neighbors.difference: Many Christians hear the Beatitudes as Jesus' own portrait, the way he himself walked. The Qur'an paints its portrait of the servants of the Merciful as a list of habits a person grows into.
neighbors.shared: gentle isn't weak; it's strength that doesn't need to win.

neighbors.heading: sweetness and humility
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the servants of the Merciful walk gently, and answer a hothead with peace. Guru Nanak sang: sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue. And Baba Farid, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, says: answer evil with good; don't let anger fill your heart.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, humility, nimrata, belongs to a whole life lived in the Guru's way, with Waheguru's name at its center. The Qur'an names the servants of the Merciful by how they walk and how they answer.
neighbors.shared: a calm word can end a fight before it starts.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470 (Guru Nanak) and Ang 1382 (Baba Farid) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: into the desert to pray
neighbors.text: Today you met i'tikaf: staying in the mosque in the last ten nights, to draw near. Jesus did something like it: "And he retired into the desert, and prayed." Catholics keep the practice in retreats, days set apart for silence and prayer, and in Lent, which remembers his forty days in the desert.
neighbors.difference: I'tikaf is kept in a mosque, above all in the last ten nights of Ramadan, waiting for the Night of Power. A Catholic retreat can be any quiet place and any season, often guided by a priest.
neighbors.shared: sometimes stepping away is how you come close.

neighbors.heading: staying put for the rains
neighbors.text: Today you met i'tikaf: staying in the mosque in the last ten nights, to draw near. Buddhist monks and nuns keep a retreat too, called vassa. For the rainy season they stay in one place instead of wandering, deepening meditation and study, and lay people come to the monastery to practice with them.
neighbors.difference: Vassa began with a practical rule: no wandering in the rains, so crops and small creatures aren't trampled. I'tikaf is devotion to Allah in a house of prayer, timed to seek one night, Laylat al-Qadr.
neighbors.shared: pausing in one place can help you go deeper.
neighbors.sources: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga III, the rains retreat (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: eat, be satisfied, and bless
neighbors.text: Today you met the days of tashriq: days of eating, drinking and remembering God. The Torah puts food and blessing together the same way: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." And for the festivals: "thou shalt rejoice in thy feast."
neighbors.difference: From Deuteronomy 8:10, Jews draw Birkat Hamazon, the grace said after a meal. The days of tashriq belong to Eid al-Adha and the Hajj, with takbir said aloud after the prayers.
neighbors.shared: a good meal can be a way of saying thank you.

neighbors.heading: grace before everything
neighbors.text: Today you met the days of tashriq: days of eating, drinking and remembering God. The writer G. K. Chesterton noticed that people say grace before meals, and asked why not before a concert, a walk, a swim, a good book too. For him, thanks was the right answer to simply being alive.
neighbors.difference: Chesterton's thanks were a Christian writer's, aimed at God, but he made them a habit anyone could borrow. The days of tashriq set thanks in a shared calendar: a whole community eating and saying takbir on the same days.
neighbors.shared: joy and thanks belong at the same table.
neighbors.sources: G. K. Chesterton, notebook lines quoted in Maisie Ward's biography (1943) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the breaker of sorrow
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked who answers the cornered one when he calls. Sikhs call on God with a name made for that moment: Dukh Bhanjan, the breaker of sorrow. A hymn by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, comes back to it again and again: your Name is the destroyer of pain.
neighbors.difference: The verse is about a single cry, in any words, from someone with nowhere left to turn. The Sikh hymn is sung, set to a raag, and the Name it praises is remembered every day, not only in the corner.
neighbors.shared: a cry from the corner is never too small to be heard.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Raag Gauri Majh, Guru Granth Sahib ("Dukh bhanjan tera naam ji"; paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the one in distress
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked who answers the cornered one when he calls. Hindus hear an echo in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna names four kinds of good people who turn to him, and the first one named is arta, the one in distress. Not only the wise or the learned: the one with nowhere else to go is counted too.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna in the Gita speaks as God come to earth, and goes on to call the wise devotee the dearest. In the Qur'an, God hears from beyond every form, and the cornered one's answered call is simply set among His signs.
neighbors.shared: you don't need perfect words to call. hurting is enough.

neighbors.heading: ways to honor a spouse
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an put a marriage among God's signs: rest, love and mercy between you. Buddhists keep a talk where the Buddha advises a young man, Sigala, on everyday duties. A husband honors his wife, never looks down on her, stays faithful, trusts her with the home, and gives her gifts. She runs the home well, welcomes both families, stays faithful, guards what they have, and works with skill.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, love and mercy are placed between spouses by God, as a sign of Him. The Buddha's advice names no creator; it treats marriage as part of lay life, a set of duties both people practice and keep up.
neighbors.shared: a home is built from small kindnesses, kept up every day.

neighbors.heading: not good to be alone
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said spouses were made of one kind, to find rest in each other. Christians open their Bible to a matching scene. God looks at the first man and says: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him." Later, Paul tells husbands to love their wives "even as Christ also loved the church."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, a marriage can picture Christ's self-giving love for the church, and Catholics and Orthodox count it a sacrament. In Islam, marriage is a sacred contract, and the love and mercy in it are one of God's signs.
neighbors.shared: love is meant to be somewhere you can rest.

neighbors.heading: the gratitude visit
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an saw a mother's weakness upon weakness, and joined thanks to God with thanks to parents. Psychologist Martin Seligman tested a simple practice: write a letter to someone who helped you and was never properly thanked, then read it to them in person. In his studies, people who did it felt happier for weeks afterward. Saying the thanks out loud changed the one saying it.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, thanks to parents comes in the same breath as thanks to God, as a duty owed. The gratitude letter needs no belief at all; it's offered as a practice that does the giver good, whoever they thank.
neighbors.shared: somebody carried you here. it's never too late to say so.
neighbors.sources: Martin Seligman and colleagues, the gratitude visit, American Psychologist (2005; paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the groanings of thy mother
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an remembered a mother carrying her child in weakness upon weakness. Catholics read a tender line in Sirach: "Honour thy father, and forget not the groanings of thy mother." It goes on: remember you would not have been born but through them, and repay them as they did for you. The Catechism calls honoring parents gratitude for the gift of life.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, honoring parents is the fourth commandment, and Sirach is part of their Bible. In Islam, the duty comes in God's own voice in the Qur'an, and it holds even when parents differ about faith: keep their company kindly.
neighbors.shared: remember what was carried, so you could be here.
neighbors.sources: Ecclesiasticus 7:29–30 (Douay-Rheims; Sirach 7:27–28 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2215 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: when the flute played
neighbors.text: Today the hills and birds echoed Dawud's praise. Hindus tell of a song that nature answers too. In the Bhagavata Purana, the cowherd girls describe Krishna playing his flute in the forest: the peacocks dance, the cows lift their ears to drink it in, the birds close their eyes, and the rivers swirl, stirred by the sound.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God himself, and the forest is answering its Lord. In the Qur'an, Dawud is a prophet and a man, a smith who ate from his own work; the hills glorify God with him, never him.
neighbors.shared: when someone sings to God, the whole world can join in.

neighbors.heading: let the mountains sing
neighbors.text: Today the hills echoed Dawud's praise. Jews know him as David, "the sweet psalmist of Israel," and the Psalms are full of a world that sings back: "Let the floods clap their hands; let the mountains sing for joy together." An old Jewish text, Perek Shirah, gives every creature its own verse of praise: the sea, the wind, the dove, even the frog.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the Psalms, which tradition links to David, are their own scripture, still prayed aloud. Muslims honor Dawud as a prophet given the Zabur, which they connect with the Psalms, and pray with the Qur'an.
neighbors.shared: praise is a song the hills are waiting to sing back.

neighbors.heading: let there be light
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said that when God wills a thing, He says only, "Be!" and it is. Christians open the Bible with the same quiet power: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." A psalm says it plainly: "For he spake, and it was done." No tools, no struggle, only a word.
neighbors.difference: John's Gospel adds something Christians hold dear: the Word that made all things "was made flesh" in Jesus. In Islam, God's command is never a person, and His "Be!" is unlike any speech of ours.
neighbors.shared: you exist because you were called into being.

neighbors.heading: one word, and rivers
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said God need only say, "Be!" and it is. Sikhs pray something close in Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib, their morning prayer. With one word, it says, God made the whole wide expanse, and from it hundreds of thousands of rivers began to flow. The same hymn admits no one can describe how vast that making is.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the divine Word, the Shabad, is also the Guru, living now in the scripture the community bows before. In Islam, the Qur'an is God's speech, deeply honored, and "Be!" points to His power alone.
neighbors.shared: one word was enough to start the rivers running.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Japji Sahib, pauri 16, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 3 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no sin too big
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said: don't despair of God's mercy; He forgives all sins. Catholics hear the same wide door. Jesus says there shall be joy in heaven "upon one sinner that doth penance, more than upon ninety-nine just who need not penance." The Catechism adds that there is no offense, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive.
neighbors.difference: Catholics receive this forgiveness through Christ, above all in the sacrament of confession with a priest. In Islam, there's no one in between: the sinner turns straight to God, and the turning itself is the way back.
neighbors.shared: it is never too late to come home.
neighbors.sources: Luke 15:7 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 982 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the moon from behind clouds
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an told people who had done terrible things not to despair. Buddhists tell of Angulimala, a killer who met the Buddha on a forest road, stopped, and became a monk. The Dhammapada says: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds."
neighbors.difference: In Buddhism there is no God who forgives; past deeds still bear fruit, and Angulimala's peace came through practice and insight. In Islam, a merciful God forgives, and the one who turns back is met by Him.
neighbors.shared: nobody is too far gone to begin again.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 173, tr. Max Müller 1881 · Angulimala Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 86 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: an enemy made a friend
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said: repel evil with what is better, and an enemy may become a warm friend. Jews keep the same hope. Proverbs says: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat." And an old rabbinic teaching asks who is the mightiest of the mighty, and answers: the one who turns an enemy into a friend.
neighbors.difference: The rabbis frame it as might, a hero's work, and the Torah makes it practical law: help lift your enemy's fallen donkey. The Qur'an frames it as patience, a gift given only to those who endure.
neighbors.shared: kindness can turn an enemy into a friend.

neighbors.heading: kindness is invincible
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said to answer harm with something better. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote himself a note on the same idea: kindness is invincible, if it's genuine and not a fake smile. What can the most violent person do to you, he asked, if you stay kind, and gently set him right at the very moment he tries to hurt you?
neighbors.difference: Marcus grounds it in reason and our shared nature: people are made to work together, like two hands. The Qur'an grounds it in God, who promises a great portion to the patient who answer evil with good.
neighbors.shared: a kind answer is harder to beat than a hard one.

neighbors.heading: five thieves in the house
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked about someone who makes their own desire their god. Sikh scripture pictures the body as a house with five thieves living inside: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. They plunder what's precious, and the one led by their own mind doesn't notice. Sikhs call that person a manmukh, and someone turned toward the Guru a gurmukh.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the cure is the Guru's word and remembering the Name, which tames the ego, haumai. In Islam, the cure is putting God back in the top place, with desire allowed its rightful place below Him.
neighbors.shared: wanting makes a good servant and a poor master.
neighbors.sources: Guru Amar Das, Raag Sorath, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 600 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the enemy within
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked about someone whose desire has taken God's place. In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks what drives a person to do wrong, almost against their will. Krishna answers: it is desire, and anger born from it, never satisfied. Know it as the enemy here. Like smoke over a fire, it covers wisdom.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's answer is to master the senses and act without craving the fruits, offering every act to him. In the Qur'an, desire isn't the enemy in itself; the wrong is letting it rule in God's place.
neighbors.shared: you can want something without letting it run your life.

neighbors.heading: a quiet mind
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said calm was sent down into troubled hearts after Hudaybiyyah. Buddhists prize that stillness too. Calm, passaddhi, is one of the qualities the Buddha named on the way to awakening. The Dhammapada describes someone who has found freedom: "His thought is quiet, quiet are his word and deed."
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, sakinah comes down from God, a gift into hearts that couldn't calm themselves. In Buddhism, calm is grown from within, through mindfulness and practice, with no giver from above.
neighbors.shared: stillness can find you even in a room full of disappointment.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 96, tr. Max Müller 1881 · the factors of awakening, Samyutta Nikaya 46 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: peace past understanding
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said God sent calm into the hearts of a camp full of disappointed people. Christians know that gift. Paul writes: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."
neighbors.difference: Christians receive this peace through Christ Jesus, who promised his friends a Comforter, the Holy Spirit. In Islam, sakinah comes from God directly, adding faith to faith, with no one in between.
neighbors.shared: peace can be a gift, not only an achievement.

neighbors.heading: meeting changes minds
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said people were made nations and tribes so they could know one another. Psychologist Gordon Allport studied prejudice and came to a hopeful idea: contact. When people of different groups meet as equals, work toward shared goals, and have support around them, suspicion tends to ease. Distance turns strangers into stereotypes; meeting turns them into neighbors.
neighbors.difference: Allport's idea needs no God; it's about how minds work. The Qur'an makes difference itself part of God's plan, then takes away every visible ranking: the noblest is the most mindful of Him.
neighbors.shared: difference is an introduction, not a wall.
neighbors.sources: Gordon Allport, The Nature of Prejudice (1954; paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: made of one
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said humanity is one family, made into nations to know one another. Catholics hear Paul in Athens: God "hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth." The Church's teaching on other religions opens the same way: all peoples are one community, with one origin and one final goal, God.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, that one family is gathered in Christ, and the Church sees itself as a sign of that unity. In Islam, the family is one through Adam and Hawwa, and nobility is measured by mindfulness of God alone.
neighbors.shared: every stranger is family you haven't met yet.

neighbors.heading: the wheel of riches
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the poor have a right in your wealth, the one who asks and the one too proud to ask. A hymn of the Rig Veda praises the generous: truly bountiful is the one who gives to the hungry who comes asking. Riches roll like a chariot wheel, it says, coming now to one, now to another.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, the poor's share is a right owed to them, later fixed as zakat. The Vedic hymn praises giving as noble, and Hindu teaching treats dana, the generous gift, as a duty that brings merit to the giver.
neighbors.shared: what you hold today may be someone else's tomorrow.

neighbors.heading: the corners of the field
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the poor have a right in your wealth. The Torah builds that right into the harvest. Don't reap the corners of your field, or gather every grape: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I am the LORD your God." The Hebrew word for giving, tzedakah, shares a root with tzedek, justice.
neighbors.difference: Jewish law spells these gifts out field by field, and Maimonides ranked ways of giving, with helping the poor stand on their own at the top. The Qur'an names the one who asks and the silent one, and Muslim law fixes a yearly share, zakat.
neighbors.shared: giving can be paying what's owed, not doing a favor.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 19:9–10 (KJV) · Maimonides, Gifts to the Poor 10 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a great while before day
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pointed to the hour when the stars fade, a time to praise God. Christians find Jesus there too. Mark's Gospel says: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." A psalm says: "in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus is the Son praying to his Father, and morning prayer takes many forms. In Islam, the dawn prayer is one of the five daily prayers, and the two units before it are a cherished sunnah.
neighbors.shared: the hour before dawn has always been good company for prayer.

neighbors.heading: the ambrosial hours
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pointed to the hour when the stars fade. Sikhs call that time amrit vela, the hours of nectar before dawn. Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib says: in the ambrosial hours, speak the true Name and reflect on God's greatness. The Sikh code of conduct asks Sikhs to rise early, bathe, and recite their morning prayers.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the early hours are for remembering the Name, recited or sung, with no fixed set of postures. In Islam, the dawn hour holds a prayer of standing, bowing and prostrating, at a time set by the sky.
neighbors.shared: dawn is a door that opens before the day gets loud.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Japji Sahib, pauri 4, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 2 (paraphrase) · Sikh Rehat Maryada (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the word endureth
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said everything on earth passes, and only the face of your Lord remains. Catholics read the same pair in Isaiah: "The grass is withered, and the flower is fallen: but the word of our Lord endureth for ever." On Ash Wednesday, many hear it as ashes mark their foreheads: remember that you are dust, and to dust you will return.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, what remains has a human face too: the Word made flesh, who rose from the dead. In Islam, God's face is unlike anything created, and what remains is God, and whatever was done for His sake.
neighbors.shared: what passes can still point to what remains.
neighbors.sources: Isaiah 40:8 (Douay-Rheims) · Genesis 3:19, the Ash Wednesday words (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all made things pass
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said everything on earth passes away. The Buddha taught it as a truth to see clearly. The Dhammapada says: "'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity." His last words, as the scriptures remember them: all made things decay, so strive on with care.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an sets one thing against the passing: the face of the Lord, which remains. Buddhism points to nibbana, the unconditioned, with no creator; seeing impermanence clearly is itself part of the path to freedom.
neighbors.shared: seeing that things pass can make you gentler with them.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 277, tr. Max Müller 1881 · Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: The water you drink, the fire you light

neighbors.heading: a blessing for water and fire
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked: have you seen the water you drink, the fire you light? Jews answer with blessings. Before a sip of water, a short blessing praises God, by whose word all things came to be. And at Havdalah, as Shabbat ends, a braided candle is lit, hands are held up to its glow, and God is blessed for creating the lights of fire.
neighbors.difference: Jewish blessings use the rabbis' set words, said before the sip or over the flame. The Qur'an asks a question instead and leaves the thanks to the listener; Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after.
neighbors.shared: the tap and the flame are gifts too.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Berakhot 6 and 8 (paraphrase) · the Havdalah blessings

neighbors.heading: noticing the gift
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked if you've really looked at the water you drink and the fire you light. Psychologist Robert Emmons, who studies gratitude, describes it in two steps: first you affirm there's good in your life, then you recognize that the good came, at least partly, from outside you. Even tap water counts. Something brought it here.
neighbors.difference: Emmons leaves open where the good comes from: other people, nature, or God. The Qur'an names the Giver plainly, and asks its question to lead you to thanks: why don't you give thanks?
neighbors.shared: the most ordinary things are quietly given.

neighbors.heading: water for everyone
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an praised the Helpers who put others first, even in need. Sikhs remember Bhai Kanhaiya, who carried water across a battlefield to the wounded of both sides. When others complained he was helping the enemy, tradition says Guru Gobind Singh asked him why. He answered that he saw the Guru's face in everyone. The Guru gave him salve for their wounds too.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, seva, selfless service, is everyday life, from the battlefield to the langar, the free kitchen where all sit together. In the Qur'an, ithar is praised as a high grace: preferring others even when you yourself are poor.
neighbors.shared: a cup of water doesn't check what side you're on.
neighbors.sources: the story of Bhai Kanhaiya, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the king who gave his last meal
neighbors.text: Today a hadith told of a couple who fed a guest while their own children went to bed hungry. Hindus tell of King Rantideva, who gave everything away and went hungry for days. When food and water came, guest after guest arrived, a priest, a poor man, a man with his dogs, and he gave it all, down to the last cup. He asked only to take on others' suffering.
neighbors.difference: In the Bhagavata, the gods reveal themselves at the end, and Rantideva's reward is pure devotion to Vishnu. In the hadith, no one saw what the couple did, but God did, and marveled.
neighbors.shared: sometimes love looks like an empty plate.

items.lessonTitle: Why say what you don't do?

neighbors.heading: a flower without scent
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked believers why they say what they don't do. The Buddha used a picture for that gap. The Dhammapada says: "Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly." The very next verse gives the other kind: a flower with color and scent, words matched by deeds.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an names the gap as hateful in God's sight. The Buddha names it as fruitless: words without deeds bear no fruit, for you or anyone, and the fix is practice, not a judge.
neighbors.shared: a promise kept smells sweeter than a promise made.

neighbors.heading: doers of the word
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked why people say what they don't do. Christians feel the same sting in the letter of James: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." Jesus warned about teachers who "say, and do not," and told of a son who answered his father, "I go, sir," and never went.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the gap is closed by grace as much as effort: Christ at work in a person through faith. In Islam, the believer is called to close it by effort, with God's help, and the gap itself is named hateful to God.
neighbors.shared: words are promises; deeds are where they come true.

neighbors.heading: a little every day
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked for mindfulness as much as you can, and the Prophet loved small deeds done steadily. Psychologist William James wrote about habit and gave advice that sounds the same: "Keep the faculty of effort alive in you by a little gratuitous exercise every day." Small, regular, chosen. That, he said, is how a character gets built.
neighbors.difference: For James, steady habits shape a person's nerves and character over time. The Qur'an asks for consistency for God's sake, and promises He doesn't burden a soul beyond what it can bear.
neighbors.shared: small, done daily, adds up to a life.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 4, "Habit" · Qur'an 2:286

neighbors.heading: the little way
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked for mindfulness as much as you're able, and the Prophet loved small deeds done steadily. Catholics have a saint of exactly that: Thérèse of Lisieux, who called her path the little way: no great feats, just ordinary things done out of love. Jesus said: "He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater."
neighbors.difference: Thérèse saw her littleness as a child's trust, lifted to God in Christ's arms like an elevator. In Islam, the measure is your real capacity, and God asks no more of a soul than it can bear.
neighbors.shared: nothing done with love is too small to count.
neighbors.sources: Luke 16:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the scribe who writes it all
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pictured a person handed the book of their deeds. Hindus tell of Chitragupta, the scribe who sits beside Yama, lord of death, and writes down the deeds of every life. When a soul arrives, the stories say, Chitragupta reads out the record. Some Hindu families honor him on a festival day by worshipping pen, ink and account books.
neighbors.difference: In Hindu teaching, the record feeds karma, shaping the next birth, until the soul is freed. In the Qur'an, there is one life and one Day, and the book is handed over once, to the right hand or the left.
neighbors.shared: every day writes a page; it can be one worth showing.
neighbors.sources: Garuda Purana, on Chitragupta and Yama (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all your deeds in a book
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pictured a person handed the record of their deeds. Jews keep the same image. The Mishnah teaches: know what is above you, an eye that sees and an ear that hears, and all your deeds are written in a book. On the High Holy Days, the prayer Unetaneh Tokef pictures God opening the book of memories, and in it, each person's own signature.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish teaching, the books are opened on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur, every year, and repentance can change what's written. In the Qur'an, the book is handed over on the Last Day, though turning back is open all through life.
neighbors.shared: the pen is still in your hand today.

neighbors.heading: the birds of the air
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the human was created anxious, fretful in harm, clutching in good. Jesus spoke to that worry on a hillside: "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them." And then: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow."
neighbors.difference: Jesus points worried people to their Father's care, and to seeking his kingdom first. The Qur'an names anxiety as built into the human, then points to steady prayer and giving as the way out of both panic and clutching.
neighbors.shared: worry is human. you weren't meant to carry it alone.

neighbors.heading: why plot and plan?
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the human was created anxious. Sikhs pray a hymn by Guru Arjan in their evening prayer that speaks right to it: why, my mind, do you scheme and worry, when God himself takes care of you? It points to creatures living in rocks and stones, and says their food was set before them.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the answer to worry is trust in God's will, hukam, and remembering the Name. The Qur'an asks for trust too, and names the practice right after: constant prayer, and a known share given to those in need.
neighbors.shared: your worry isn't the only thing holding the world up.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Raag Gujri, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 10, in Rehras Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the examen
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an swore by the self that blames itself, the small voice at eleven at night. Catholics give that voice a daily appointment. Saint Ignatius taught the examen: at day's end, thank God, look back over the hours, notice where you fell short, ask pardon, and resolve to do better tomorrow. The Church calls conscience a person's secret core, where they are alone with God.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, serious sins found in that look back are brought to a priest in confession, and forgiven in Christ's name. In Islam, the blaming self turns straight to God, and is meant to grow toward the self at peace.
neighbors.shared: the voice that blames you is trying to bring you home.
neighbors.sources: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises 43, the examen (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1776 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mirror
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an swore by the self that blames itself. The Buddha taught his young son Rahula a practice for that voice. What is a mirror for? For reflecting. So before, during and after any act of body, speech or mind, reflect: does this lead to harm, for me or for others? If it did, admit it to a wise friend, and hold back next time.
neighbors.difference: In Buddhism, the reflecting isn't before a God; it's seeing clearly what causes harm, then confessing to a teacher or fellow monk. In the Qur'an, the blaming self stands before God, and its oath sits beside the Day of Resurrection.
neighbors.shared: looking honestly at yourself is a kind of kindness.

neighbors.heading: when neither knows the other
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an praised people who fed the hungry, the orphan and the captive, saying: we want no reward or thanks from you. Jewish teaching prizes the same quiet. Maimonides lists levels of tzedakah, and near the top is giving where the giver doesn't know who receives, and the poor person doesn't know who gave. The Temple, he says, had a quiet room for it.
neighbors.difference: For Maimonides, the very highest gift helps someone stand on their own, through a loan, a partnership or a job. The Qur'an's verse praises giving that costs you, done for God's sake alone, even to a captive from the other side.
neighbors.shared: a gift is lighter when no thanks is owed.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7–8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: forget you gave
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an praised givers who wanted no thanks. The Roman philosopher Seneca wrote a whole book on giving and said much the same: the giver should forget the gift at once, while the receiver should never forget it. Some gifts, he said, are best given in secret, so the person in need isn't shamed.
neighbors.difference: Seneca gives because virtue is its own reward, needing no witness. In the Qur'an, the giver wants no thanks from people because they give for God's face, and hope for His reward alone.
neighbors.shared: the gift is finished the moment it's given.

neighbors.heading: water, the father
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an showed water flowing through the whole book as mercy. Sikhs close Japji Sahib with a line by Guru Nanak: air is the Guru, water the father, and earth the great mother of all. Elsewhere he says water came first, the life that makes everything green. At Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple, the gurdwara stands in a pool of water.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the sacred pool, the sarovar, is a place to bathe and remember the Name, and nature itself is family. In the Qur'an, water is God's mercy and sign, and washing, wudu, prepares the body for prayer.
neighbors.shared: every glass of water is a small mercy.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Japji Sahib, closing salok, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 8 · Asa di Var (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the waters, like mothers
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an showed water as mercy, from creation to the rivers of the Garden. A hymn of the Rig Veda praises the waters as bringers of strength and joy, and asks them to share their kindest sap, like loving mothers. Hindus bathe in sacred rivers like the Ganga, and in the rite called achamana, water is sipped from the palm to purify before worship.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, rivers like the Ganga are holy in themselves, honored as goddesses. In Islam, water is a creation and a mercy of God, and God alone is worshipped, never the river.
neighbors.shared: you can hold mercy in your cupped hands.

neighbors.heading: the raft
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said God strikes parables, even of a gnat. The Buddha taught in pictures too. In one, a man crosses a flood on a raft he built from grass and branches. Safe on the far shore, should he carry the raft on his head? No, the Buddha says. The teaching is like that raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's parables point to the end of suffering, and even the teaching is set down at the far shore. The Qur'an's parables come as God's own words, to be kept, recited and lived, never set down.
neighbors.shared: a good picture can carry a truth farther than an argument.

neighbors.heading: he spoke in parables
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said God isn't embarrassed to coin a parable, even of a gnat. Jesus taught the same way, with seeds, a lost coin, and a mustard seed that grows into a tree. Matthew says: "All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus tells the parables himself, as the one who brings God's kingdom near. In Islam, the parables are God's speech in the Qur'an; the Prophet received and recited them, and was never their author.
neighbors.shared: small things can hold big truths.

neighbors.heading: belief can't be forced
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said there is no compulsion in religion. The philosopher John Locke argued the same in his Letter Concerning Toleration. The mind, he said, can't be forced into believing anything by outside pressure. Punish a person and you may change what they say, but not what they truly think. Forced faith isn't faith at all.
neighbors.difference: Locke argued from the nature of the mind and the limits of government. The Qur'an argues from God: He could have made everyone believe and chose not to, so faith must be chosen freely.
neighbors.shared: a heart has to open from the inside.
neighbors.sources: John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: faith is a free act
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said there is no compulsion in religion. The Catholic Church says it in its own words. In its teaching on religious freedom, the Second Vatican Council declared that no one may be forced to act against their conscience in matters of religion. Faith, it said, is by its very nature a free act, an answer no one can be made to give.
neighbors.difference: Catholics root religious freedom in human dignity and in Christ, who invited and never forced. Muslims root it in the Qur'an's own words: God could have made all believe, and left faith to be chosen.
neighbors.shared: faith freely chosen is faith truly held.

neighbors.heading: a cry from deep water
neighbors.text: Today Yunus called out from the dark inside the fish. Hindus tell of Gajendra, a king of elephants caught by a crocodile in a lake. He pulled and fought until his strength was gone. Then, with nothing left, he prayed to the Lord beyond all. When Vishnu came, Gajendra lifted a lotus to him with his trunk, and Vishnu pulled him out.
neighbors.difference: Gajendra's prayer is surrender with no strength left, and Vishnu comes in person to rescue him. Yunus's prayer also confesses: I was wrong. In the Qur'an, God answers from beyond every form, never coming down in a shape.
neighbors.shared: no water is too deep for a call to reach.

neighbors.heading: out of the belly of the fish
neighbors.text: Today Yunus prayed from inside the fish. Jews know him as Jonah, and the Book of Jonah gives his prayer from the depths: "I called out of mine affliction unto the LORD, and He answered me." The whole book is read in synagogue on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, a day for saying, like him, I was wrong.
neighbors.difference: In the Book of Jonah, his prayer is mostly thanks for rescue, and the book ends with God asking about mercy for Nineveh. The Qur'an gives his cry as three short clauses, ending in a confession.
neighbors.shared: it's never too late to say i was wrong.
neighbors.sources: Jonah 2:3 (JPS 1917; 2:2 in many Bibles) · Talmud Megillah 31a, on reading Jonah on Yom Kippur (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: forget not all his benefits
neighbors.text: Today Sulayman, the king Christians know as Solomon, smiled at an ant and asked God to keep him grateful. Christians pray the same to their own soul in a psalm: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." Paul writes: "In every thing give thanks." In both, gratitude is something you ask to be kept in.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the greatest gift to give thanks for is Christ himself, and their central worship is called the Eucharist, thanksgiving. In Islam, thanks goes to God directly, in a prophet's own words: for me, and for my parents.
neighbors.shared: gratitude is easier to keep when you ask for help with it.

neighbors.heading: may I never forget
neighbors.text: Today Sulayman asked God to keep him grateful, not trusting himself to stay that way. Guru Nanak asks something close in Japji Sahib: Guru, give me this one understanding, that there is one Giver for all living beings. May I never forget Him. The line comes back a second time, like a request made twice to be sure.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak asks the Guru, the teacher who gives understanding, to keep the one Giver in mind. Sulayman asks God directly, and names his parents as part of the gift he's thankful for.
neighbors.shared: remembering the Giver keeps the gift from going to your head.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Japji Sahib, pauri 5–6, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a restless heart
neighbors.text: Today a few Meccans looked at the idols and kept looking for the God of Ibrahim. Catholics treasure a seeker's prayer too. Saint Augustine, after years of searching, opened his Confessions to God with: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The Church teaches that the longing for God is written in the human heart.
neighbors.difference: The hanifs turned toward the one God of Ibrahim before any revelation came to them. Augustine found his rest in Christ and his Church, and Catholics read an honest search as already drawn by grace.
neighbors.shared: the search itself can be a way of turning toward home.
neighbors.sources: Augustine, Confessions I.1 (Pusey 1838) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 27 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the noble search
neighbors.text: Today Zayd ibn Amr walked away from what everyone around him did, and kept asking. Buddhists remember a search like it. Before his awakening, the Buddha told of studying with two respected teachers, mastering what they taught, and leaving each one because it wasn't yet the answer. He called it the noble search: looking for what doesn't age, sicken or die.
neighbors.difference: The hanifs were looking for the one God of Ibrahim, the Lord of the House. The Buddha's search wasn't for a creator; it was for freedom from suffering, which he taught is found by seeing clearly.
neighbors.shared: it takes courage to keep asking when everyone else has stopped.

neighbors.heading: don't stand by
neighbors.text: Today the young Prophet stood with men who swore to side with anyone wronged in Mecca, even a stranger. The Torah gives Jews the same duty in one line: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." The rabbis read it broadly: if you see someone drowning, or robbed, and you can help, you must.
neighbors.difference: The league was a pact clans chose to make, and the Prophet later said he'd still answer its call. For Jews the duty is a command from God at Sinai, binding on each person whether or not anyone else signs on.
neighbors.shared: a stranger with no one should still find someone on their side.

neighbors.heading: decide before the moment
neighbors.text: Today a group promised in advance to stand with anyone wronged. Psychologists found why that matters. In experiments by Bibb Latané and John Darley, people alone helped someone in trouble far more often than people in a group, where each one waited for someone else. A promise made ahead of time may help break that waiting.
neighbors.difference: The league was sworn in a house in Mecca, and the Prophet later tied it to a call from God to stand for justice. The psychology describes how people act; it doesn't say who calls us to act.
neighbors.shared: someone has to go first; you can decide now it'll be you.
neighbors.sources: Darley and Latané, "Bystander intervention in emergencies," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today Mecca called him al-Amin, the trustworthy, a man whose word matched what happened. Sikhs hold the same ideal high. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says truth is above everything, and higher still is truthful living. For Sikhs, being honest isn't only what you say; it's how you earn, trade and treat people every day.
neighbors.difference: Mecca's name for him was praise from his neighbors, even his opponents, before the message came. For Sikhs, truthful living is the path itself, part of remembering God, who in the Mool Mantar is named as Truth.
neighbors.shared: the people who know you best can say: your word holds.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: speak the truth
neighbors.text: Today he was known as al-Sadiq, the truthful, long before he made any claim. Hindus have a teacher's farewell to students that starts the same way. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, the teacher's first words of advice to those leaving his school are: speak the truth, practice dharma. Another Upanishad says truth alone wins, words India later put on its national emblem.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, the Prophet's truthfulness was the ground people stood on when he spoke of God. In the Upanishads, satya, truth, is also woven into the order of the world itself, dharma, which a life is meant to keep.
neighbors.shared: a life that tells the truth becomes a voice people trust.

neighbors.heading: the quiet place first
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet went up to Hira for nights alone, with Khadijah keeping him in food. Buddhists remember a seat like his cave. Before his awakening, the Buddha went to a quiet grove beside a river and sat down to strive, and later he sent his monks to the forest, to the roots of trees, to sit.
neighbors.difference: At Hira the Prophet worshiped in the way of Ibrahim, and the angel came to him there. The Buddha sat in meditation, not prayer to a God, and awakening came from seeing the mind clearly.
neighbors.shared: some things can only be heard once the noise goes quiet.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 26, Ariyapariyesana Sutta (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 19 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: up the mountain to pray
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet climbed to a cave and came back, again and again. Christians know that rhythm from Jesus. Luke says: "he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God." Mark adds: "rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed."
neighbors.difference: Muslims honor the Prophet as a human messenger seeking God before revelation came to him. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God, praying to his Father in a closeness they understand as unique to him.
neighbors.shared: the people who carried the most went off alone to pray first.

items.lessonTitle: The sun in my right hand

neighbors.heading: not for sale
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet said that even the sun in one hand and the moon in the other couldn't buy his message. Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote about that kind of refusal in his essay Self-Reliance: "Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind." For Emerson, what you hold true isn't something to trade for comfort or approval.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet refused because the message was from God, not his to give away. Emerson places the last word in a person's own honest mind, and the essay leans on no scripture.
neighbors.shared: some things aren't for sale, and saying no can still cost tears.

neighbors.heading: the whole world
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet turned down an offer as big as the sky. Catholics hear Jesus ask a question close to it: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" Catholics also remember Saint Thomas More, who kept his conscience even when the king's favor and his life were the price.
neighbors.difference: In the sirah, the Prophet is refusing to give up the message God gave him to deliver. Jesus speaks of every disciple's own soul, and Catholics hear it as the cost of following him.
neighbors.shared: what's worth everything can't be traded for anything.

neighbors.heading: the boy who kept the name
neighbors.text: Today Bilal, under a rock in the sun, could only say: One, One. Hindus tell of a boy who held on like that. In the Bhagavata Purana, young Prahlada's father, a demon king, tries again and again to break his devotion to Vishnu. The boy is threatened and thrown into danger, and still he keeps remembering the Lord, until Vishnu himself comes to protect him.
neighbors.difference: Bilal's "One" refused every partner beside God. Prahlada's devotion is to Vishnu, whom he sees present everywhere, even in a pillar; and his rescue comes from Vishnu himself, while Bilal's came through a friend's money.
neighbors.shared: when you've almost no breath left, it can still hold what you love.

neighbors.heading: one, until the last breath
neighbors.text: Today one word was Bilal's whole answer: ahad, one. Jews say the sister of that word twice a day: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The Talmud tells how Rabbi Akiva, tortured by the Romans, recited it, and drew out the last word, echad, one, until his soul left him.
neighbors.difference: Bilal lived; Abu Bakr bought his freedom, and he became the voice of the call to prayer. Akiva died, and Jews remember him among martyrs who sanctified God's name. Each tradition prays its own words.
neighbors.shared: one word, said under pressure, can say everything you are.

neighbors.heading: the same Mary
neighbors.text: Today a Christian king wept to hear the Qur'an's chapter about Mary. Christians know her story from Luke: "And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." No wonder the court was moved. They heard someone they loved honored in another people's scripture.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an honors Mary and the virgin birth, and Jesus as a prophet and servant of God. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God. The two books tell her story in their own ways.
neighbors.shared: it's moving to hear someone you love honored by a stranger.

neighbors.heading: a book with room
neighbors.text: Today a king heard holy words from another faith and recognized something true. Sikhs built that recognition into their scripture. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the hymns of the Sikh Gurus beside the verses of bhagats from other backgrounds, among them Kabir and the Muslim Sufi Sheikh Farid. Sikhs sing their words as gurbani, the Guru's word, and bow before them.
neighbors.difference: The Negus heard Christian figures told in the Qur'an's own words, then protected the people who recited them. The Guru Granth Sahib places other saints' words inside the Sikh scripture itself, to be sung as its own.
neighbors.shared: truth can sound like home even in a neighbor's voice.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, hymns of Sheikh Farid and Bhagat Kabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: they know not
neighbors.text: Today, offered revenge on the worst day of his life, the Prophet said no and hoped for his enemies' children instead. Catholics hear something close from the cross. Luke remembers Jesus, praying for the people who were killing him: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." The Church calls forgiving enemies a high point of Christian prayer.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet turned down the power to destroy and looked to the faith of generations not yet born. Jesus, Catholics believe, gave his life on that cross, and asked his Father to forgive the very people who put him there.
neighbors.shared: the hardest day can still end without a curse.
neighbors.sources: Luke 23:34 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2844 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hatred doesn't end hatred
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet could have had the mountains close over Mecca, and refused. Buddhists have a verse for it. The Dhammapada, early in its first chapter, says: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Answering hate with more hate only keeps it going.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet's mercy hoped that God would bring believers out of his enemies' line. The Dhammapada speaks of a law of the mind and heart, with no God sending angels or judging the outcome.
neighbors.shared: mercy on a bad day keeps a door open for people not yet born.

neighbors.heading: we will do
neighbors.text: Today twelve men promised a way of living: no stealing, no slander, no harming their children. Jews remember a people's promise at Sinai. When Moses read them the book of the covenant, they answered: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." The rabbis loved that they said "we will do" before anything else.
neighbors.difference: At Aqaba, twelve men pledged to the Prophet personally, and the reward was left with God. At Sinai, a whole people entered a covenant with God through Moses, which Jews understand as binding on their children ever after.
neighbors.shared: faith gets real in your hands, your tongue and your home.

neighbors.heading: be one
neighbors.text: Today's pledge wasn't about armies or money; it was about how to live, day to day. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, wrote himself a note in that spirit: "No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such." For the Stoics, a good life is something you practice, not just admire.
neighbors.difference: The twelve made their promise to a prophet, before God, and the hadith leaves room for God's forgiveness when they slip. Marcus wrote to himself; his reminder rests on reason and habit.
neighbors.shared: a good life is mostly small promises, kept.

neighbors.heading: why should I fear?
neighbors.text: Today, with searchers at the mouth of the cave, the Prophet asked: what of two, when God is their third? Sikhs sing a hymn of the same trust. Guru Arjan calls God father, mother, relative and brother, and says: when You are my protector everywhere, why should I fear or worry?
neighbors.difference: In the cave, God is the unseen third, close but beyond the two friends. In Sikh teaching, the one God is also the light within every heart, and the hymn speaks to God as family.
neighbors.shared: fear gets smaller when you know you aren't alone in it.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 103, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: do not grieve
neighbors.text: Today, in the cave, the Prophet told his friend: grieve not, God is with us. Near its close, the Bhagavad Gita has the same words. Krishna tells the frightened Arjuna to let go of every other support and take refuge in him alone: I will free you from every wrong; do not grieve.
neighbors.difference: In the cave, the words pass between two friends, and God is unseen. In the Gita, Krishna speaks them himself, face to face on a battlefield chariot, honored by many Hindus as God come to earth.
neighbors.shared: you can be careful and still let the fear go.

neighbors.heading: the bowl and the teaching
neighbors.text: Today the poorest believers lived on a bench inside the mosque, fed by gifts and listening close. Buddhist monks and nuns live by a similar trade. In many Buddhist lands they own almost nothing and eat what lay people put in their bowls, and the Buddha said the two help each other: the givers offer food and robes, and the monastics offer the teaching.
neighbors.difference: The people of the bench were poor because they had no family or wealth to fall back on, not by a vow. Buddhist monastics choose to give up possessions as part of their training.
neighbors.shared: the ones with the least can be the ones who remember the most.

neighbors.heading: all things common
neighbors.text: Today the poor were fed in the middle of the mosque, not at the edge of town. Christians remember the first church in Jerusalem doing something like it: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need."
neighbors.difference: In Medina, the Prophet sent charity to the bench and shared gifts with them. In Acts, the believers pooled what they owned, and Christians have lived that out in different ways since.
neighbors.shared: the people with the least belong in the middle of the room.

neighbors.heading: sing while you dig
neighbors.text: Today the whole city dug a trench, and the Prophet sang out a line while the diggers sang back. Psychologists have studied that. In one study by Oxford researchers, adults who joined a singing class felt close to each other faster than people who joined other group classes. Singing together seems to knit strangers into a team.
neighbors.difference: At the trench, the songs were prayers: asking God for forgiveness, calm and firm feet. The research measures the closeness people feel and doesn't ask who, if anyone, is listening.
neighbors.shared: hard work gets lighter when everyone sings the same line.
neighbors.sources: Pearce, Launay and Dunbar, "The ice-breaker effect," Royal Society Open Science, 2015 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the leader in the dirt
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet carried earth until the dust covered his belly. Catholics see their Lord kneel, too. At the Last Supper, Jesus washed his disciples' feet and said: "If then I being your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; you also ought to wash one another's feet." On Holy Thursday, many priests still kneel and wash people's feet.
neighbors.difference: At the trench, the Prophet worked beside everyone on a shared job. In John, Jesus does a servant's job for his disciples alone, and Catholics read it as a sign of the gift he gives on the cross.
neighbors.shared: the one in charge is not too big for the dirty work.

neighbors.heading: the right resolve
neighbors.text: Today Wahshi, Hind and Ikrimah, who had fought him, came back and found the door open. Hindus hear a door like that in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna says that even someone who has done great wrong, if they turn to him with an undivided heart, should be counted good, because they have made the right resolve.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet received the people who came to him, and the grief stayed real, as with Wahshi. In the Gita, Krishna speaks as the Lord himself, and the turning is devotion to him.
neighbors.shared: where you're headed can matter more than where you've been.

neighbors.heading: turn and live
neighbors.text: Today people who had done real harm walked back in, and weren't turned away. Jews call that turning teshuvah. God asks through the prophet Ezekiel: "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD; and not rather that he should return from his ways, and live?" The days before Yom Kippur are kept for that return.
neighbors.difference: In the stories, the Prophet welcomes people who come to him and to Islam. Jewish teshuvah is turning back to God, and for wrongs against a person, Jewish law asks you to make it right with them first.
neighbors.shared: the way back is there before you start walking it.

neighbors.heading: one blood
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet told a vast crowd that all people are children of Adam, and no color or nation is above another. Christians hear Paul in Athens say it too: God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Elsewhere Paul writes that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek.
neighbors.difference: In the sermon, the only measure of nobility is mindfulness of God. Paul goes on, in both places, to speak of Christ, and Christians hear the oneness of people fulfilled in him.
neighbors.shared: every face you meet comes from the same family.

neighbors.heading: one light
neighbors.text: Today: no Arab over a non-Arab, no light skin over dark. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps a hymn of Bhagat Kabir that even uses the name Allah. First God made the light, he sings; from that one light came everyone. So who is good, and who is bad? Sikhs see it in the langar, where all sit and eat in rows as equals.
neighbors.difference: The sermon names one measure of rank before God: mindfulness of Him. Kabir and the Sikh Gurus press hard against caste, and Sikhs teach that the same divine light shines in every person.
neighbors.shared: no one was made from a better batch of clay.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1349, Bhagat Kabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a cup of cold water
neighbors.text: Today Uthman bought a well and made its water free, his bucket beside everyone's. Catholics count "give drink to the thirsty" among the works of mercy, and Jesus said: "whosoever shall give to drink to one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward."
neighbors.difference: Uthman's well is sadaqah jariyah, flowing charity whose good keeps going after he dies. Jesus speaks of a single cup given in his name; Catholics see Christ himself in the one who receives it.
neighbors.shared: water given away keeps doing good long after the giving.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 10:42 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: goodness that grows
neighbors.text: Today a well became a gift that kept flowing. The Buddha said almost the same about wells. Asked whose merit keeps growing, he answered: those who plant groves and orchards, build bridges, give wells and places to drink, and shelter for travelers. Their goodness, he said, grows day and night.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, flowing charity carries its reward to the giver from God, even after death. In Buddhism, merit comes from the act itself and the giving heart, with no God keeping the account.
