neighbors.shared: the best gifts keep working while you sleep.

neighbors.heading: she reaches out her hands
neighbors.text: Today the "longest hand" turned out to be the giving one: Zaynab worked with her hands and gave from it. On Friday nights, many Jewish homes sing of a woman like her, from Proverbs: she works wool and flax with her own hands, and "She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy."
neighbors.difference: Zaynab's riddle came true in one real woman Aisha remembered. The woman of valor in Proverbs is a portrait, sung at the Shabbat table to honor the women of the house.
neighbors.shared: the longest reach belongs to the hands that give.

neighbors.heading: giving feels better
neighbors.text: Today the wives measured their arms, and the answer was charity. Psychologists have measured something too. In a study by Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues, people handed a little money were happier by evening if told to spend it on someone else than if told to spend it on themselves. Giving seems to come back to the giver.
neighbors.difference: Zaynab gave for God, and the riddle pointed to her place beside the Prophet after death. The study measures one evening's happiness and makes no promise beyond it.
neighbors.shared: giving tends to fill the hands that give.
neighbors.sources: Dunn, Aknin and Norton, "Spending money on others promotes happiness," Science, 2008 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember, remember
neighbors.text: Today Fatimah, worn from the mill, was given words to repeat at night instead of a servant. Sikhs know that gift. The Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, opens by asking you to remember God, remember, and remember, and so find peace. Sikhs pair it with honest work: remember the Name, earn by your own labor, share what you have.
neighbors.difference: Fatimah's words are counted: praise, thanks and God's greatness, in set numbers, before sleep. Sikh simran centers on the Name, often Waheguru, repeated through the day, with no count required.
neighbors.shared: tired hands can still hold a few holy words.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the offering of repeating
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet gave his daughter words to count, better for her than a servant. Hindus count holy words too, often on a string of beads. It's called japa. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna lists the ways he shows himself in the world, and says that among all offerings, he is japa, the quiet repeating of a sacred name.
neighbors.difference: Fatimah's words praise the one God, counted at day's end. Japa is often a name of a deity, like Rama or Krishna, or the syllable Om, and many Hindus count it on beads at any hour.
neighbors.shared: a few words, repeated, can carry a long day.

neighbors.heading: water or blood?
neighbors.text: Today Hasan had an army like mountains, and chose a settlement instead. Buddhists tell of the Buddha stepping between two clans, his own Sakyans and the Koliyans, armed and ready to fight over a river's water. He asked them which was worth more, the water or the lives of the warriors. They put down their weapons.
neighbors.difference: Hasan gave up a claim to rule, and Sunni and Shia Muslims read his choice in different lights. The Buddha wasn't giving up anything of his own; he reasoned with both sides until they saw the cost.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the strongest move is the one that keeps everyone alive.

neighbors.heading: the peacemakers
neighbors.text: Today a grandson was named a peacemaker before he was grown, and became one. Christians hear Jesus say it on the mount: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Christians have long read it as an active calling: not only avoiding fights, but making peace between others.
neighbors.difference: Hasan's peace was a hard settlement between two armies, praised in a hadith. Jesus' blessing names peacemakers "children of God," which Christians hear as sharing the life of his Father.
neighbors.shared: making peace can take more strength than winning.

neighbors.heading: rich in what you let go
neighbors.text: Today a perfumed young man gave up everything, and left the world in a cloak too short to cover him. Henry David Thoreau, who went to live simply by a pond, wrote: "a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone." For Thoreau, freedom grew as wants grew smaller.
neighbors.difference: Mus'ab gave up comfort for his faith and died at Uhud for it. Thoreau's simplicity was an experiment in living, chosen for freedom and clear sight, without a promise of reward after death.
neighbors.shared: what you can let go of can't own you.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (Thoreau)

neighbors.heading: Francis gave back his clothes
neighbors.text: Today Mus'ab traded fine clothes for a patched cloak. Catholics love a young man who did that: Saint Francis of Assisi, a rich merchant's son, gave back even the clothes he wore to his father, in front of the bishop, to follow Christ in poverty. He was answering a call Jesus gave: "go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor."
neighbors.difference: Mus'ab was cut off by his family for his faith and kept nothing back. Francis chose poverty as a way of imitating Christ, and founded a brotherhood that still takes that vow.
neighbors.shared: the ones who gave the most up are remembered with the most love.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 19:21 (Douay-Rheims) · Bonaventure, Life of Saint Francis, ch. 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: four places to look
neighbors.text: Today Mu'adh gave his order: the book, then the Prophet's example, then careful reasoning. Hindus know a ladder like it. The Manusmriti names four marks of dharma, of what's right: the Veda, the remembered tradition, the conduct of good people, and, last, what satisfies your own inner self.
neighbors.difference: For Mu'adh, reason works inside the book and the sunnah, never against them. Hindu sources are many and its schools weigh them differently, and the inner self in the list is a conscience shaped by that tradition.
neighbors.shared: start with what's been handed down, then think hard and honestly.

neighbors.heading: it is not in heaven
neighbors.text: Today: the book first, then the sunnah, then your own careful reasoning. Jews read the Torah through the oral tradition and the arguments of rabbis. Moses tells Israel the commandment "is not in heaven." The Talmud tells of rabbis who quoted that line to keep deciding by reasoning and majority, even when a voice from heaven spoke up.
neighbors.difference: In the Mu'adh report, reasoning is the last step, when the book and sunnah are silent. Talmudic debate keeps minority opinions on the page and makes argument itself a holy study.
neighbors.shared: the old words are given to us to think with, not around.

neighbors.heading: the persecutor preaches
neighbors.text: Today the man whose horsemen broke the lines at Uhud became "the sword of God." Christians know a turn like that. Saul hunted the first Christians, until he met Jesus on the road to Damascus. Afterward the churches said in wonder: "he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed."
neighbors.difference: Khalid came to Medina, and the Prophet taught that Islam wipes out what came before it. For Christians, Paul's turn began with Jesus himself appearing to him, and Paul wrote that anyone in Christ is a new creature.
neighbors.shared: people change, and a community can make room for them.

neighbors.heading: Sajjan the thug
neighbors.text: Today an old enemy came in and became a defender. Sikhs tell of a man named Sajjan, whose name means friend. He welcomed travelers to his inn and then robbed and killed them. Guru Nanak stayed the night and sang a hymn about things that shine outside and are dark within. Sajjan fell at his feet, confessed, and began to serve travelers instead.
neighbors.difference: Khalid's past was in battle, and he turned when he came to Islam in Medina. Sajjan's story comes from the janamsakhis, the Sikh life stories of Guru Nanak, and his change came through one hymn and one night.
neighbors.shared: nobody's worst chapter has to be their last.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Guru Nanak and Sajjan (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: sick, and you visited me
neighbors.text: Today a woman kept a tent for the wounded, right in the mosque. Catholics count caring for the sick as a work of mercy, because Jesus said the one in need is him: "sick, and you visited me." That line helped inspire hospitals, and orders of sisters who gave their lives to nursing.
neighbors.difference: Rufaydah's tent stood beside the place of prayer, and she served wounded believers. Catholics hear Jesus saying that in caring for the sick, they care for Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: healing belongs right beside prayer, not behind it.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:36 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: tend the sick
neighbors.text: Today Rufaydah did the unglamorous part: wounds, water, care. Buddhists tell of the Buddha finding a monk lying sick in his own filth, with no one helping. He and Ananda washed him and laid him on a bed. Then he told the monks: whoever would care for me should care for the sick.
neighbors.difference: Rufaydah's care is remembered as service to God's people, close to the Prophet. The Buddha taught that monks have no mother or father to nurse them, so they must nurse each other; tending the sick is how they tend him.
neighbors.shared: the person no one is helping is the one to help first.

neighbors.heading: honor thy mother
neighbors.text: Today the one deed the Prophet named for Uways was his care for his mother. Jews hear the commandment at Sinai: "Honour thy father and thy mother." The Talmud tells of a gentile, Dama ben Netina, who passed up a huge sale rather than wake his sleeping father for the key. The rabbis held him up as the model.
neighbors.difference: For Uways, care for his mother is remembered as what kept him from ever meeting the Prophet. In the Torah, honoring parents is one of the Ten Commandments, with a promise of long days attached.
neighbors.shared: caring for a parent is holy work, even when no one sees it.

neighbors.heading: from my mother
neighbors.text: Today Uways stayed home for his mother, and was honored for it. Marcus Aurelius, ruler of an empire, began his private notebook by thanking the people who made him, and his mother is near the top: "From my mother, piety and beneficence." He goes on to thank her for teaching him to live simply.
neighbors.difference: Uways cared for his mother with his days, and the Prophet tied it to God's favor. Marcus wrote thanks for what she gave him, as part of a practice of seeing clearly where his good came from.
neighbors.shared: who we are started with someone who took care of us.

neighbors.heading: Guru and disciple
neighbors.text: Today a new leader said: I'm not the best of you; if I go wrong, set me right. Sikhs remember a leader who bowed like that. Sikh tradition says that after Guru Gobind Singh gave amrit to the first five of the Khalsa, he knelt and asked those five to give it to him too. Sikhs praise him as both Guru and disciple.
neighbors.difference: Abu Bakr was chosen by pledge and set obedience to God as the limit of his own. Guru Gobind Singh was the Guru himself, and in Sikh belief he later passed guidance to the scripture and the Khalsa together.
neighbors.shared: a good leader asks to be corrected, out loud.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of the first amrit (paraphrase) · Bhai Gurdas II, Var 41 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the people's good is the king's
neighbors.text: Today a leader said the weak would be strong in his eyes until he got them their right. Hindus know a ruler's duty like that, rajadharma. The Arthashastra, an old Indian manual on governing, says a king's happiness lies in his people's happiness, and his good in their good, not in what pleases him.
neighbors.difference: Abu Bakr invited the people to correct him and set God's command as the limit. The Arthashastra speaks to kings born to rule, and grounds their duty in dharma, not in the people's pledge.
neighbors.shared: power is a trust, and the weakest are the test of it.

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today a governor's son thought his father's name made him untouchable, and Umar answered: their mothers bore them free. The Buddha said something like it to a proud man who called him an outcast. Not by birth is anyone an outcast, he said, and not by birth is anyone a brahmin. By what you do, you become one or the other.
neighbors.difference: Umar's line rests on birth itself: everyone is born free, and justice must be evenhanded before God. The Buddha's point is that worth comes from your actions, not from family or caste.
neighbors.shared: nobody's name makes them more of a person than you.

neighbors.heading: no respect of persons
neighbors.text: Today a Christian from Egypt crossed a desert, and the caliph took his side over a governor's son. Christians have a letter that warns against just that kind of favoritism: "My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons." James goes on: don't seat the rich man well and the poor man on the floor.
neighbors.difference: In the story, a Muslim ruler judges by the Qur'an's call for evenhanded justice. James writes to Christians about their own gatherings, tying fairness to faith in Christ.
neighbors.shared: justice that bends for the powerful isn't justice.

neighbors.heading: Socrates stayed
neighbors.text: Today Uthman, surrounded, sent his defenders home rather than let blood be shed for him. Socrates faced a choice like that. Condemned to death in Athens, he was offered an escape his friend Crito had arranged. Socrates refused: he had lived under the city's laws all his life, and would not answer an unjust verdict with a wrong of his own.
neighbors.difference: Uthman read his choice through the Prophet's words about a trial and a shirt, and readers still argue about it. Socrates reasoned his way there in conversation, out of loyalty to justice and his city.
neighbors.shared: sometimes holding your ground means refusing to fight for yourself.

neighbors.heading: put up thy sword
neighbors.text: Today Uthman forbade anyone to fight for him. Catholics remember the night Jesus was arrested. A disciple drew a sword to defend him, and Jesus said: "Put up again thy sword into its place: for all that take the sword shall perish with the sword." Then he let himself be led away.
neighbors.difference: Uthman refused to let Muslims kill Muslims for his sake, and Muslims remember the years after as a time of strife. Catholics believe Jesus went freely to the cross to save the world.
neighbors.shared: refusing to shed blood for yourself is its own kind of courage.

neighbors.heading: dharma, the king of kings
neighbors.text: Today a caliph stood before his own judge and lost. An old Hindu text puts a law above every ruler. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says dharma was made the power above power, nothing higher than it, so that even a weak person can stand up to a strong one through dharma, as if a king stood with them.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, dharma is the right order woven into the world, and a king's duty is to uphold it. In Islam, justice is a command from Allah in the Qur'an, and the judge answers to Him.
neighbors.shared: no crown sits above what is right.

neighbors.heading: even the king stands
neighbors.text: Today a caliph stood before his own judge and lost. The Torah sets the same scale: "thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor favour the person of the mighty." The Talmud tells of King Yannai called into court, and the sage Shimon ben Shetach telling him to stand: you stand not before us, but before the One who spoke and the world came to be.
neighbors.difference: In the Talmud, the other judges look down in fear, and afterward the sages rule that such kings neither judge nor are judged, since judging them proved dangerous. In the Muslim report, the caliph walks into court himself and accepts the loss.
neighbors.shared: the one with the most power still stands before the law.

neighbors.heading: lay not this sin
neighbors.text: Today Husayn fell on the tenth day, and the Qur'an says those slain in God's way are not dead. Christians keep their martyrs' days too. Stephen, whom they call the first martyr, prayed as the stones fell: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." And Jesus said: "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, a martyr's death follows the pattern of Jesus' own cross, which they believe saves the world. For Muslims, Husayn's death is a stand for truth, mourned deeply, especially by Shia Muslims, and each soul still carries its own account.
neighbors.shared: some people give everything rather than give up what is right.

neighbors.heading: your will is sweet
neighbors.text: Today Husayn fell on the tenth day, thirsty, and the Qur'an says such people are not dead. Sikhs remember their shaheeds, their martyrs, too. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was put to death in Lahore. Sikh tradition says he met the torture calmly, and his hymn is sung in his memory: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs mark Guru Arjan's day with his calm, accepting hymns, and often hand out cool sweet water to passersby in the summer heat. For many Shia Muslims, Ashura is the year's deepest mourning, with gatherings, elegies and tears.
neighbors.shared: courage remembered keeps courage alive.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394 (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition of Guru Arjan's martyrdom

neighbors.heading: one Lord, one faith
neighbors.text: Today two lists side by side showed more shared than split. Catholics keep a list like that too. Paul wrote: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." And the Church teaches that Christians separated from it, baptized and believing in Christ, are still its brothers and sisters, joined to it in a real, if imperfect, communion.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, full unity means communion with the pope and bishops, and the hope is to heal the split. Sunni and Shia Muslims have no single head over both; the shared prayer, Book and qiblah are their common ground.
neighbors.shared: a family that disagrees can still pray as one family.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 4:5 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 818, 838 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: three refuges, many schools
neighbors.text: Today two lists side by side showed more shared than split. Buddhists can make that list too. A Theravada monk in Thailand and a Mahayana nun in Taiwan practice in very different ways, yet both take refuge in the same three: the Buddha, the Dharma, his teaching, and the Sangha, the community. Both say the old words: I go for refuge.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist schools grew apart over monastic rules, teachings and texts, carried to different lands. The Sunni and Shia split began with who should lead after the Prophet. And Buddhists take refuge in an awakened teacher, not in a God who sent him.
neighbors.shared: what you share can run longer than what divides you.

neighbors.heading: the accounting of the soul
neighbors.text: Today Hasan al-Basri taught: hold yourself to account. The rabbis of the Mishnah taught a close watchfulness: know what is above you, an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book. Later Jewish teachers called the practice cheshbon hanefesh, the accounting of the soul, and Bahya ibn Paquda gave it a whole gate of his Duties of the Heart.
neighbors.difference: Bahya wrote in Arabic, in Muslim Spain, and scholars note he drew on Sufi writers. But Jewish self-accounting is measured against the Torah's commandments, and Muslim muhasaba against the Qur'an and the Prophet's way.
neighbors.shared: the first person to watch is the one in the mirror.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 2:1 (paraphrase) · Bahya ibn Paquda, Duties of the Heart, Gate of Self-Accounting (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the lamp goes out
neighbors.text: Today Hasan al-Basri taught: hold yourself to account. The Roman philosopher Seneca kept a nightly version. When the lamp was taken away, he wrote, he went over his whole day, his words and deeds, asking: what fault did I cure today, what did I resist, where am I better? He said he hid nothing from himself and passed nothing by.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's review answers to reason and his own conscience; he sits as his own judge. For Hasan, the account is kept before Allah, who is nearer than the jugular vein, and the heart is watched because He sees it.
neighbors.shared: a quiet look back at your day can change tomorrow.

neighbors.heading: voices from many homes
neighbors.text: Today Baghdad gathered wisdom from Greek, Persian and Sanskrit books. The Guru Granth Sahib gathers too. Beside the Gurus' own hymns, it holds words of saints from other backgrounds: Kabir the weaver, Ravidas the leatherworker, Namdev, and verses known as Sheikh Farid's, a Sufi of Punjab. Sikhs bow before all of it as one Guru.
neighbors.difference: In Baghdad, foreign books were studied, argued with and corrected, while the Qur'an stood apart as revelation. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the saints' words are scripture itself, sung in worship and honored as the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: wisdom can come from someone who isn't like you.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, bhagat bani of Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sheikh Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: from every side
neighbors.text: Today Baghdad gathered wisdom from many languages. A Vedic prayer asks for that open door. A verse of the Rig Veda begins, in a well-loved rendering: let good thoughts come to us from every side. And wisdom traveled the other way too: the Panchatantra, Indian animal fables, went through Persian into Arabic as Kalila and Dimna.
neighbors.difference: The Vedic verse is a prayer to the gods for every kind of blessing. The Qur'an names Allah alone as the giver of wisdom, and Baghdad's scholars weighed each foreign book against their faith.
neighbors.shared: a good idea is welcome, whatever door it comes through.
neighbors.sources: Rig Veda 1.89.1 (paraphrase) · Ibn al-Muqaffa, Kalila wa Dimna

neighbors.heading: whoever would tend me
neighbors.text: Today a hospital opened its door to all who came. A Buddhist story opens the same door. The Buddha found a monk sick with dysentery, lying in his own filth, with no one caring for him. With Ananda, he washed the monk and laid him on a bed. Then he told the monks: whoever would tend me should tend the sick.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha spoke to monks who had left their families and had no one else to nurse them. The bimaristan grew from the Prophet's command to visit the sick, and the hope that Allah sent a cure for every disease.
neighbors.shared: the sick person in front of you is the one to serve.

neighbors.heading: I was sick, and ye visited me
neighbors.text: Today a hospital opened its door to all who came. Jesus gave a list close to the Prophet's. In Matthew he says: "I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." Asked when, he answers that what they did for the least of his brothers, they did for him. Many Christian hospitals trace their work to those words.
neighbors.difference: In Matthew, Jesus says the sick person stands in for him, and Christians believe he is God's Son. In a Muslim hadith, Allah asks, "I was sick and you did not visit Me," then explains: He is found with the one who is sick.
neighbors.shared: visiting the sick is never just a visit.

neighbors.heading: the starry heavens
neighbors.text: Today astronomers studied the sky so prayers would come on time. Philosophers have looked up for their own reasons. Immanuel Kant wrote that two things filled his mind with ever new wonder and awe, the more often he thought about them: the starry heavens above him, and the moral law within him.
neighbors.difference: For Kant, the stars turned his thoughts to the mind and to duty, with no set hour or direction. For Muslims, the sky is a clock and a compass God appointed, and reading it serves a prayer owed to Him.
neighbors.shared: the sky still asks us to pay attention.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Critique of Practical Reason, conclusion (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the heavens shew forth
neighbors.text: Today the new moon set the start of Ramadan. Catholics read the sky for a feast too. Easter falls on the Sunday after the first full moon of spring, and a pope reformed the calendar to keep Easter in its season. The Church still runs an observatory. A psalm sings: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God."
neighbors.difference: Easter's date comes from tables worked out in advance, so Latin Catholics everywhere keep it on the same day. Many Muslim communities still wait for a human eye to see the crescent, and the start can differ from place to place.
neighbors.shared: the sky has long kept time for prayer.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 18:2 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 19:1 in many Bibles) · Pope Gregory XIII, Inter gravissimas (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the offering of knowledge
neighbors.text: Today a student's walk to class counted as worship. Hindus call study an offering too. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the offering of knowledge is greater than an offering of things, and that nothing in this world purifies like knowledge. Some students begin their books with a prayer to Saraswati, goddess of learning.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the highest knowledge sees the true Self and frees a person from the cycle of rebirth. In Islam, knowledge sought with a good intention is a path to the garden, by Allah's mercy.
neighbors.shared: learning can be a way of bowing.

neighbors.heading: equal to them all
neighbors.text: Today a student's walk to class counted as worship. For Jews, study sits close to prayer. The Mishnah lists good deeds whose fruit a person enjoys in this world, like honoring parents, acts of kindness and making peace between people, then ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all. Many Jews still learn in pairs, out loud, in the house of study.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish teaching, Torah study is itself a commandment, and the text studied is the Torah and the rabbis' discussion of it. Muslim scholars differ on whether the hadith means religious knowledge first, or any useful knowledge sought with a good intention.
neighbors.shared: an open book can be a way toward God.

neighbors.heading: who is my neighbour?
neighbors.text: Today Jews, Christians and Muslims shared cities in al-Andalus, sometimes in friendship, sometimes in fear. Jesus was asked: "And who is my neighbour?" He answered with a story: a man beaten on the road, passed by, then helped by a Samaritan, a stranger from a people his listeners distrusted. "Go, and do thou likewise," Jesus said.
neighbors.difference: Jesus' story asks one person to cross a line for one stranger, and Christians hear it as a command to love. The Qur'an speaks of whole peoples, made nations and tribes to know one another, and al-Andalus shows how hard that knowing can be.
neighbors.shared: a neighbor can come from the people you were taught to fear.

neighbors.heading: no one is a stranger
neighbors.text: Today Jews, Christians and Muslims shared cities in al-Andalus, sometimes in friendship, sometimes in fear. Guru Arjan sang of a heart that has let that fear go: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. And Sikh tradition says a Sufi, Mian Mir, was invited to lay the foundation stone of the Golden Temple.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan describes an inner change, once jealousy of others is gone, in the company of the holy. Al-Andalus is a story of laws and rulers: protected communities, real limits and hard years, set down in the histories.
neighbors.shared: a stranger is a neighbor you haven't met yet.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299 (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition of Mian Mir and the Harmandir Sahib

neighbors.heading: the pilgrim road
neighbors.text: Today a young man left Tangier for Mecca and kept going. Catholics walk pilgrim roads too. On the Camino to Santiago de Compostela, pilgrims carry a scallop shell and sleep in hostels along the way, eating at the tables of strangers. A pilgrim psalm sings: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, pilgrimage is a loved devotion, not a duty, and there are many shrines to walk to. For Muslims, the Hajj to Mecca is a pillar, owed once in a lifetime by everyone able to make it.
neighbors.shared: on the road, strangers become hosts and guests.

neighbors.heading: the monk who walked west
neighbors.text: Today a young man left Tangier for Mecca and kept going for years. A Chinese monk, Xuanzang, made a long journey of his own. He left China, against the emperor's order, to find Buddhist texts in India, studied at the monastery of Nalanda, and came home with scriptures. Like Ibn Battuta, he told his travels to a helper, who wrote them down.
neighbors.difference: Xuanzang's journey was a search for texts and teachers, and Buddhist pilgrimage, to places like Bodh Gaya, is a devotion, not a duty. Ibn Battuta set out first for the Hajj, a pillar every able Muslim owes.
neighbors.shared: the road can be a teacher too.
neighbors.sources: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rejoice not
neighbors.text: Today a sultan won a city and let many go free. Jewish tradition watches the winner's heart too. Proverbs says: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." And the Talmud tells that when the Egyptians drowned in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, and God stopped them: the work of My hands is drowning, and you would sing?
neighbors.difference: The Talmud's story is about the heart in victory, with God himself grieving for the fallen. The Qur'an speaks to what the winner does: an answer may match the wrong, but pardon is praised, and its reward is with Allah.
neighbors.shared: winning is a test of the heart too.

neighbors.heading: with malice toward none
neighbors.text: Today a sultan won a city and let many go free. Near the end of a terrible civil war, with victory close, Abraham Lincoln asked his country for mercy in winning: "With malice toward none, with charity for all." He spoke of binding up the nation's wounds and caring for the widow and the orphan.
neighbors.difference: Lincoln spoke as a president to a nation that had to live together again. The Qur'an speaks to every believer, and pardon there is an act before Allah, with its reward from Him, not only a way to heal a country.
neighbors.shared: mercy matters most when you could choose otherwise.

neighbors.heading: a shelter for another faith
neighbors.text: Today a Christian king sheltered Muslim refugees and would not hand them over. Sikh memory holds a mirror image. Tradition says Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus pressed to convert, came to Guru Tegh Bahadur for help. He took up their cause, though it was not his own faith's, and gave his life for it. His son wrote that he did it to protect their sacred mark and thread.
neighbors.difference: The Negus sheltered Muslims in his own land, and they lived to come home. Guru Tegh Bahadur went to the ruler's court on the Pandits' behalf and was executed in Delhi; Sikhs remember him as a martyr for others' freedom of faith.
neighbors.shared: you can protect people whose prayers aren't yours.
neighbors.sources: Guru Gobind Singh, Bachittar Natak (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition of the Kashmiri Pandits

neighbors.heading: the guest as a god
neighbors.text: Today a Christian king sheltered refugees from across the sea. A Hindu teaching tells the host how to see such a guest. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students home with words still loved today: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be as a god to you. And a Parsi tradition remembers a Hindu ruler in Gujarat taking in Zoroastrians who came by sea.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad teaches a duty of every household: honor any guest as divine. The Negus was a king giving protection to a persecuted people of another faith, and Muslims remember him for it with gratitude.
neighbors.shared: the stranger at the door is owed a welcome.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (paraphrase) · Qissa-i Sanjan (Parsi tradition, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: written on leaves
neighbors.text: Today families in Timbuktu kept handwritten books safe for generations. Buddhists know that care. Their chronicles say that in Sri Lanka, monks who had carried the Buddha's teaching by memory wrote it down on palm leaves, so it would not be lost. And at Dunhuang, in China, a sealed cave kept a great library of scrolls safe until it was found, long after.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist teaching was memorized and chanted long before it was written, and monasteries kept it. Timbuktu's pages were kept by scholars and families in their own homes, beside a Qur'an that was memorized from the first.
neighbors.shared: a page is safe when someone loves it enough to keep it.

neighbors.heading: especially the parchments
neighbors.text: Today families in Timbuktu kept handwritten books alive. Christians know that care. Paul, near the end of his life, wrote asking a friend to bring "the books, but especially the parchments." Later, monks and nuns copied the Bible and older books by hand, and the scholar Cassiodorus praised the copyist for preaching with the hand and fighting evil with pen and ink.
neighbors.difference: Christian copying was often done by monks and nuns living together under a rule. Timbuktu's books were kept by scholars and families at home, in a trading city where books were among the costliest goods.
neighbors.shared: copying by hand is a slow kind of love.

neighbors.heading: like feet, like hands
neighbors.text: Today Sa'di said the children of Adam are limbs of one body. A Roman emperor and philosopher, Marcus Aurelius, used the same picture. Reminding himself each morning that he would meet rude and difficult people, he wrote: "we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth."
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, the bond comes from a shared reason running through all people and nature. Sa'di builds on the Prophet's picture of believers as one body, and widens it to everyone made from Adam's clay, created by Allah.
neighbors.shared: when one of us hurts, the rest can't really rest.

neighbors.heading: if one member suffer
neighbors.text: Today Sa'di said that when one limb is in pain, the others cannot rest. Paul wrote nearly the same to the church at Corinth: "And if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it; or if one member glory, all the members rejoice with it." Catholics call the Church the Body of Christ, where the hand and the foot both count.
neighbors.difference: Paul's body is the Church, joined in Christ, whom Catholics believe is its head. Sa'di widens the body to every child of Adam, of any faith, joined by being made from the same clay.
neighbors.shared: no one's pain is only their own.
neighbors.sources: 1 Corinthians 12:26 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 787–795 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the all-maker
neighbors.text: Today Sinan built domes so a crowd could pray under one sky. Hindu builders have a patron too. In the Rig Veda, Vishvakarman is praised as the all-maker who shaped heaven and earth, and later stories make him the architect of the gods' cities. Traditional temple builders still follow old texts on how a sacred space should be laid out.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, a temple is a home for the deity, whose image is installed at its heart. A mosque holds no image and is not God's home; it is a place to bow together, its beauty pointing past itself.
neighbors.shared: a well-made building can help people go quiet.

neighbors.heading: called by name
neighbors.text: Today an architect was remembered for space and light. The Torah names a craftsman too. For the tabernacle, God says: "See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri... and I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." A builder's skill, named as a gift.
neighbors.difference: Bezalel built a portable sanctuary in the wilderness, to the pattern God showed Moses. Sinan's domes came from his own craft and study, serving a prayer that a Muslim may offer anywhere clean.
neighbors.shared: skilled hands can serve something holy.

neighbors.heading: call the poor
neighbors.text: Today the pots at Ajmer fed whoever came, and the Qur'an praised those who feed for God alone, wanting no thanks. Jesus said: "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee." Many churches keep soup kitchens and open tables in that spirit.
neighbors.difference: Jesus promises the reward "at the resurrection of the just," and Christians see Christ in the poor. At Ajmer, the open pots also honor a saint's memory, a practice some Muslims treasure and others question.
neighbors.shared: the best table has room for people who can't pay you back.

neighbors.heading: the langar
neighbors.text: Today the Chishti shrines kept their pots full for anyone. Sikh gurdwaras keep an open kitchen too, the langar, which tradition traces to Guru Nanak: anyone may sit on the floor, in a row, and eat the same meal, free. And the Guru Granth Sahib holds verses Sikhs know as Sheikh Farid's, a Sufi of the same Chishti line.
neighbors.difference: In the langar, everyone sits at one level, and the meal is part of the gurdwara's worship, cooked and served by volunteers. At the Sufi shrines, the food is tied to a saint's memory and blessing, which some Muslims treasure and others question.
neighbors.shared: a full pot and an open door say welcome in any language.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Sheikh Farid (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition of Guru Nanak and the langar

neighbors.heading: in a scholar's robe
neighbors.text: Today Javanese saints taught a new faith through shadow puppets and gamelan songs. Catholic missionaries tried a similar door. In China, the Jesuit Matteo Ricci learned Chinese, dressed as a scholar and wrote in the style of the classics. The Second Vatican Council later taught that the Church does not impose one rigid uniformity in worship, but respects the gifts of each people.
neighbors.difference: Catholic adaptation is weighed by bishops and Rome, and Ricci's methods were long argued over. Java's saints are remembered in local tradition, and historians still sort out how much of their story is history.
neighbors.shared: a new teaching can wear a familiar coat.

neighbors.heading: in your own tongue
neighbors.text: Today Java's saints taught in the island's own songs and stories. The Buddha set a pattern like it. In the Vinaya, two monks worry that people are spoiling his words by saying them in their own dialects, and ask to put them into old learned verse. He refuses, and allows each to learn the teaching in their own language.
neighbors.difference: In Buddhism, the teaching itself may be carried in any language. Muslims recite the Qur'an in Arabic in prayer everywhere, even as teachers explain it in the local tongue, and sometimes in local music.
neighbors.shared: a teaching travels best in the listener's own language.

neighbors.heading: only a voice
neighbors.text: Today a child asked why a mosque has no pictures. A child in a synagogue might ask too. The Ten Commandments say: "Thou shalt not make unto thee a graven image, nor any manner of likeness." Moses reminds the people that at Sinai they heard a voice but saw no form. So the ark holds a scroll of words, not an image.
neighbors.difference: Jewish law forbids images made for worship, yet some ancient synagogue floors held mosaics with people and animals. Muslim scholars read the hadith in different ways, and the mosque keeps living figures out.
neighbors.shared: God is beyond any picture we could make.

neighbors.heading: the most sublime passage
neighbors.text: Today pattern pointed past itself. The philosopher Immanuel Kant thought a missing picture could be the strongest thing in the room. He wrote that perhaps no passage is more sublime than the command against graven images, because when the eye has nothing to hold, the mind reaches toward what no picture can contain.
neighbors.difference: For Kant, the sublime is a feeling in the human mind, stretched past what the senses can grasp. For Muslims, the bare wall honors Allah, of whom "naught is as His likeness," and heeds the Prophet's warning.
neighbors.shared: sometimes what's left out says the most.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Critique of Judgment, General Remark after §29 (paraphrase) · Qur'an 42:11 (Pickthall 1930)

neighbors.heading: a bed beside the langar
neighbors.text: Today caravanserais turned a stranger into a guest for the night. Sikh gurdwaras keep that door open. Beside the langar's free meal, larger gurdwaras keep a sarai, rooms where travelers and pilgrims can sleep, often without paying. Sikh tradition says Guru Nanak himself spent years on the road, taken in by strangers.
neighbors.difference: In a gurdwara, the welcome comes in the Guru's presence: travelers cover their heads and rest near a place of worship. The caravanserai was also a market and warehouse, built for trade as much as for rest.
neighbors.shared: a tired traveler deserves a place to rest.
neighbors.sources: Sikh practice of the gurdwara sarai · janamsakhi tradition of Guru Nanak's journeys (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: turn no one away
neighbors.text: Today road houses gave travelers a night's rest. Hindu pilgrims know the dharamshala, a rest house near temples and on pilgrim roads, often built as a gift by someone with means. The Taittiriya Upanishad gives the rule behind it: do not turn away anyone who comes asking for a place to stay. That is the vow.
neighbors.difference: Building a dharamshala is often seen as earning merit, good karma that shapes this life and the next. A Muslim waqf is a gift set aside for Allah's sake, its reward hoped for from Him on the Day of Judgment.
neighbors.shared: the road is kinder when someone builds a door.

neighbors.heading: not without sharing
neighbors.text: Today an imaret fed the hungry every morning. The Buddha spoke about that shared bowl. In the Itivuttaka, he says that if people knew, as he knows, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without giving, not even their last mouthful. Each morning, in many lands, monks walk with bowls, and lay people fill them.
neighbors.difference: On the Buddhist alms round, lay people feed monks, and giving loosens the grip of craving. The imaret was paid for by an endowment for Allah's sake, and fed the poor, students and travelers, wanting no thanks.
neighbors.shared: a meal tastes different when it's shared.

neighbors.heading: the daily ministration
neighbors.text: Today a building fed the poor every day, whether anyone felt generous or not. The first Christians faced that need too. In Acts, widows were being missed "in the daily ministration," the daily sharing of food. So the apostles had the believers choose seven trusted men to see it was done fairly. Many churches trace their deacons to that story.
neighbors.difference: In Acts, the feeding was run by the believing community for its own widows, growing from Jesus' command to love. The imaret was a gift set in a legal endowment, paying for bread and soup long after the giver had died.
neighbors.shared: feeding people works best when someone plans for tomorrow too.

neighbors.heading: the same skies
neighbors.text: Today Malcolm X saw pilgrims of every color in one row. The Roman philosopher Seneca, writing in a world built on slavery, told a friend: "Kindly remember that he whom you call your slave sprang from the same stock, is smiled upon by the same skies, and on equal terms with yourself breathes, lives, and dies."
neighbors.difference: Seneca argued from shared human nature, in a letter to a friend, without changing the laws of his day. In the Hajj, equality is acted out before Allah, in plain pilgrim dress and the same rows, with mindfulness of God the only measure.
neighbors.shared: under the same sky, no one stands higher by birth.

neighbors.heading: neither Jew nor Greek
neighbors.text: Today Malcolm X saw pilgrims of every color in one row. Catholics hear a line like that from Paul: "There is neither Jew nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free: there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus." At Mass, people of every color and class come forward to the same altar.
neighbors.difference: For Paul, the oneness comes through baptism into Christ. In the Hajj, it is lived out in plain pilgrim dress, men in two white cloths, before Allah, where mindfulness of God is the only rank.
neighbors.shared: every color fits in one row.

neighbors.heading: Gargi's two arrows
neighbors.text: Today Aisha's questions and corrections opened a long line of women scholars. The Upanishads remember a woman in the hall of debate. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Gargi Vachaknavi questions the sage Yajnavalkya before the king's assembly, pressing deeper and deeper, until he warns her not to ask too far. Later she rises again, with two questions she likens to arrows.
neighbors.difference: Gargi is remembered as a seeker in a debate about the ground of all things. Aisha is remembered as a narrator, keeping and checking what the Prophet said and did, so others could live by it.
neighbors.shared: a woman's question can open a door for everyone.

neighbors.heading: sins, not sinners
neighbors.text: Today Aisha corrected people who reported the Prophet wrongly. The Talmud remembers Bruriah, a learned woman, correcting her husband, Rabbi Meir. Troubled by cruel neighbors, he prayed that they would die. She pointed him to a psalm: let sins cease from the earth, not sinners. Pray that they turn back, she said. He did, and they did.
neighbors.difference: The Talmud records only a few learned women by name, Bruriah among them. Aisha stands among the main narrators of hadith, and a long line of women teachers of hadith followed after her.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the wisest correction comes from across the table.

neighbors.heading: a great while before day
neighbors.text: Today a drummer walked a dark street, calling names to wake people before dawn. Christians know that hour too. Mark's Gospel says of Jesus: "in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." In monasteries, a bell still wakes monks and nuns for prayer in the dark.
neighbors.difference: The monastery bell wakes a community to pray before dawn. The musaharati wakes a street to eat before the fast begins, so the waking itself serves the fast.
neighbors.shared: the dark before dawn can be a gift, not just an alarm.

neighbors.heading: the ambrosial hour
neighbors.text: Today a drummer woke a sleeping street before dawn. Sikhs have a name for that hour: amrit vela, the ambrosial time. Guru Nanak's Japji says to spend it with the True Name, reflecting on God's greatness. In many gurdwaras, the day's prayers begin while it is still dark.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the early hour is for meditation on the Name, not tied to a fast. The musaharati wakes people to eat suhur, as Bilal's night call once let sleepers rise before the fast began at dawn.
neighbors.shared: before the sun is up, the heart is quieter.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, pauri 4, Ang 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a grandmother's faith
neighbors.text: Today a sweeper with no name was honored by the Prophet. Catholics hold up small, hidden faith too. Paul writes to Timothy of "that faith which is in thee unfeigned, which also dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and in thy mother Eunice." And Saint Thérèse of Lisieux called her path a little way: small things, done with great love.
neighbors.difference: Catholics name some ordinary people as saints and ask for their prayers. Islam honors the unnamed sweeper through what the Prophet did, and leaves the final weighing of every heart to Allah alone.
neighbors.shared: faith mostly travels through kitchen tables, not thrones.
neighbors.sources: 2 Timothy 1:5 (Douay-Rheims) · Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the potter's kitchen
neighbors.text: Today a sweeper with no name was honored by the Prophet. A Buddhist discourse honors an ordinary man too. The Buddha tells of Ghatikara, a village potter who cared for his blind parents and kept the precepts so faithfully that the Buddha of his day once helped himself to rice from his kitchen while he was out, and the potter was glad.
neighbors.difference: In the Buddhist story, the potter's quiet goodness carries him toward awakening by his own practice. In Islam, Allah looks at hearts and deeds, and the sweeper's worth is weighed by Him, who sees what histories miss.
neighbors.shared: the quiet ones keep a faith alive.

neighbors.heading: thou art the man
neighbors.text: Today Muslim historians wrote down their own worst day. The Hebrew Bible does the same with its greatest king. After David takes another man's wife and has him killed, the prophet Nathan tells him of a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb. David is furious, and Nathan says: "Thou art the man." David answers: "I have sinned against the LORD."
neighbors.difference: In the Bible, a prophet sent by God confronts the king, and scripture itself keeps the story. In Islam, no prophet comes after Muhammad, so scholars and historians had to speak up, and some paid for it.
neighbors.shared: saying "I was wrong" is where healing starts.

neighbors.heading: I will gladly change
neighbors.text: Today the tradition named its own failures, from the inside. A Roman emperor, Marcus Aurelius, wrote in his private notebook: "If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no man was ever injured." An emperor, asking to be corrected.
neighbors.difference: Marcus wrote to train his own mind, alone, by reason. In Islam, the standard is Allah's, in the Qur'an: justice even against yourself, and the words "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves" are said to Him.
neighbors.shared: being corrected can be a kind of gift.

neighbors.heading: the same light
neighbors.text: Today every Muslim's learning ran back, link by link, to the companions. Sikhs speak of their Gurus in a similar way. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, the bards Satta and Balwand sing that from Guru Nanak to the next Guru, the light was the same and the way was the same; only the body changed.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the line of human Gurus ended with the tenth, who named the scripture itself as Guru. The isnad is a chain of witnesses, not of prophets: each link only passes on what the Prophet said, weighed for honesty.
neighbors.shared: the light passes from hand to hand.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali ki Vaar of Satta and Balwand, Ang 966 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: handed down in succession
neighbors.text: Today every Muslim's learning ran back, teacher before teacher, to the companions. Hindus call that kind of line parampara. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says he taught this yoga long ago, and it was handed down from king to king, until in time it was lost, so he tells it again to Arjuna. Many students still name their teachers' line.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the line begins with Krishna, whom Hindus honor as God, and he restores it himself when it breaks. The isnad begins with the Prophet, a human messenger, and scholars guarded it link by link.
neighbors.shared: you were taught by someone who was taught by someone.

neighbors.heading: the wish to be seen
neighbors.text: Today a man's prayer grew beautiful only when someone walked in. The Buddha's teaching names that pull too. The Dhammapada pictures a foolish monk who wants a reputation he hasn't earned, first place among the monks, and honor from people outside. His wishing, the verses say, only feeds his craving and his pride. The path it points to is the quiet one.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, showing off is a hidden partner set beside God in an act of worship owed to Him alone. Buddhist teaching names no creator; the wish for praise is craving and pride, a knot that keeps a person bound.
neighbors.shared: good done for applause loses something on the way.

neighbors.heading: the left hand
neighbors.text: Today a hadith praised someone who gave so secretly that the left hand didn't know what the right hand gave. Jesus used the same picture. In the Sermon on the Mount he says: "Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them." And: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth."
neighbors.difference: Jesus warns that praise from people can be the whole reward, and promises the Father who sees in secret. Islamic teaching also gives it a name: worship done for an audience is a lesser shirk, a partner set beside God.
neighbors.shared: the kindest gifts are the ones nobody sees you give.

neighbors.heading: this very moment
neighbors.text: Today a son spoke the words of faith softly near his dying mother, and bedtime became a rehearsal for last words. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote himself a similar reminder: "Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly." For him, remembering death wasn't gloom. It was a way to live each hour well.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, death is nature's change, met calmly, with no promise of what comes after. In the hadith, last words of faith open onto a meeting with God and the hope of the garden.
neighbors.shared: the words you live by are the ones you'll want at the end.

neighbors.heading: the hour of our death
neighbors.text: Today a son gently prompted his dying mother with the words of faith. Catholics carry their own last words all through life. Every Hail Mary ends: "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death." And to the dying, the Church brings Communion as viaticum, food for the journey.
neighbors.difference: Muslims prompt the dying with the testimony that God is one, said to God alone. Catholics also ask Mary to pray for them, and receive the Eucharist, which they believe is Christ himself, given for the last road.
neighbors.shared: no one should have to cross that last door alone.
neighbors.sources: the Hail Mary (traditional English) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1524 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one mind, gathered
neighbors.text: Today two roommates chose to pray side by side instead of in separate rooms. One of the Rig Veda's last hymns asks for that togetherness. It calls people to come together, speak together, and let their minds be of one accord, with a shared purpose and hearts in agreement. Hindus still gather this way in temples and singing circles.
neighbors.difference: The hadith pictures straight rows behind one imam at the five set prayers. The Vedic hymn asks for one mind among the gathered, and Hindu worship lives in many shapes: home shrines, temples, and singing together.
neighbors.shared: something grows when people turn toward the holy side by side.

neighbors.heading: ten in a room
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said prayer together outweighs prayer alone. Jewish prayer gathers too. The Talmud asks how we know God is present when ten pray together, and answers with a psalm: "God standeth in the congregation of God." A group of ten is called a minyan, and certain prayers, like the mourner's Kaddish, are said only with one.
neighbors.difference: Jewish law sets a number, ten, for certain communal prayers. The hadith sets no count; it simply weighs together against alone.
neighbors.shared: you pray differently with a shoulder beside yours.

neighbors.heading: i will give you rest
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet said, "give us rest by it, Bilal": prayer as the rest, not the chore. Jesus spoke of rest too. In Matthew's Gospel he says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Christians bring that line to prayer on the days they're most worn out.
neighbors.difference: Christians find that rest in Jesus himself, whom they believe is God the Son. In the hadith, the rest is found in the prayer, worship of Allah alone, with the Prophet as the one who shows how.
neighbors.shared: the thing you pray toward can be the place you rest.

neighbors.heading: the jewel of peace
neighbors.text: Today prayer was called rest, not a task to get through. Sikhs have a long prayer by Guru Arjan whose name speaks of peace: Sukhmani, often rendered the jewel of peace. It opens by asking you to remember God, again and again, and find peace. Many Sikhs recite it in the morning or when life feels heavy.
neighbors.difference: Sukhmani's peace comes through simran, remembering the Name, read or sung at length. The rest in the hadith comes inside the salah, the set prayer of standing, bowing and prostrating at its fixed times.
neighbors.shared: remembering God can be where the tired heart sits down.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Sukhmani Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: alms that cleanse
neighbors.text: Today zakat meant both purifying and growing, and it was the giver who was purified. In the Book of Tobit, the angel Raphael says: "For alms delivereth from death, and the same is that which purgeth away sins, and maketh to find mercy and life everlasting." The Church names almsgiving, with prayer and fasting, as a form of penance.
neighbors.difference: Zakat is a pillar with a measure: a set share of wealth above a threshold, owed each year. Catholic almsgiving has no fixed rate; the Church asks each person to help the poor and the Church according to their means.
neighbors.shared: what you give away cleans something in you, too.
neighbors.sources: Tobit 12:9 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1434, 2043, 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not without sharing
neighbors.text: Today giving was described as a cut that helps the plant grow fuller. The Buddha taught the same strange arithmetic. In the Itivuttaka he says that if people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without sharing, not even their last bite. In the Buddha's step-by-step teaching, generosity, dana, comes first.
neighbors.difference: In Buddhist teaching, giving loosens the giver's own grasping, on the road to freedom from craving. Zakat is owed to God and is the poor's right, set by His command, and it purifies the giver too.
neighbors.shared: an open hand is lighter than a closed one.

neighbors.heading: with a kind face
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an called the poor's share a right, and warned against gifts followed by hurt. Jewish teaching holds both too. The Torah says: "thou shalt surely open thy hand unto him." Maimonides added that giving with a sour face loses the merit, and placed highest on his ladder of giving the help that lets a person stand on their own.
neighbors.difference: Maimonides ranks eight degrees of giving and puts self-sufficiency at the top. The Qur'an's frame is that the share already belongs to the poor, so the giver hands over a right, not a favor.
neighbors.shared: a gift should leave the other person standing taller.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 15:8 (JPS 1917) · Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:4, 10:7 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the hand that feeds us
neighbors.text: Today a woman left a food pantry with a bag of groceries and the feeling of having been looked at. Ralph Waldo Emerson noticed that sting long ago. In his essay "Gifts" he wrote: "We do not quite forgive a giver. The hand that feeds us is in some danger of being bitten." Receiving, he saw, can cost a person their pride.
neighbors.difference: Emerson is an essayist describing human pride, and offers no law. The Qur'an makes it a duty: the share is the poor's right, and gifts must not be spoiled by reminders or hurt.
neighbors.shared: how you give can matter as much as what you give.
neighbors.sources: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Gifts," Essays: Second Series (1844)

neighbors.heading: laughing, eating, free
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet talked a companion down from fasting every day: your body has a right over you. Sikh teaching guards that balance too. Guru Arjan writes that when you meet the True Guru you find the perfect way, and are set free even while laughing, playing, dressing and eating. Devotion lives inside an ordinary, full life.
neighbors.difference: In Sikh practice ritual fasting isn't kept as a way to God; the balance is remembering the Name while working, eating and living. In Islam, fasting itself is worship, and the fast of Dawud is its balanced rhythm.
neighbors.shared: devotion lasts when it leaves room to eat, sleep and laugh.

neighbors.heading: not too much, not too little
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet gave an eager companion a rhythm: fast a day, break a day; sleep, and rise to pray. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna the same kind of advice. Yoga isn't for someone who eats too much or too little, he says, or sleeps too much or too little. For the one who keeps balance in food, rest and work, it ends sorrow.
neighbors.difference: Krishna, for many Hindus God come as a teacher, speaks of yoga, the steady discipline of the mind. The fast of Dawud is a set rhythm of fasting, taught by the Prophet and named for a prophet, David.
neighbors.shared: a steady practice outlasts a heroic one.

neighbors.heading: the middle way
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet said it isn't righteousness to fast on the road until others must shade you. The Buddha learned that in his own body. The suttas tell how he starved himself until he was skin and bone, then took food again. In his first teaching he named two extremes, indulgence and self-torment, and called the path between them the middle way.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha set harsh fasting aside as a dead end for awakening. In Islam, fasting stays a pillar, and the ease is built into God's command: the sick and the traveler may break it and make it up.
neighbors.shared: a practice is there to keep you whole, not wear you out.
neighbors.sources: Mahasaccaka Sutta, MN 36 (paraphrase) · Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, SN 56.11 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: made for people
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet raised a cup of water on a journey and drank, so the people watching knew they could stop. Jesus made a similar point when his disciples picked grain on the Sabbath and were criticized. He answered: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." A holy practice serves the people keeping it.
neighbors.difference: Jesus goes on to call himself Lord of the Sabbath, which Christians read as the authority of God's Son. In Islam, the ease comes from Allah's own command, shown in practice by His messenger.
neighbors.shared: the rules of worship are there for your good.

neighbors.heading: a new wearer of clothes
neighbors.text: Today men on pilgrimage left behind the clothes that said who they were and put on two plain cloths. Henry David Thoreau, who went to live simply in the woods, distrusted fancy dress too. In Walden he wrote: "I say, beware of all enterprises that require new clothes, and not rather a new wearer of clothes." What matters is the person changing inside.
neighbors.difference: Thoreau chose plainness on his own, as a private experiment in living simply. Ihram is a shared state entered with an intention at the boundary, with set rules from the Qur'an and the Prophet, so a whole crowd stands alike before God.
neighbors.shared: what changes on the inside matters more than what you wear.

neighbors.heading: a white garment
neighbors.text: Today two white cloths made rich and poor look alike. Catholics put on white at the start of faith. At baptism the newly baptized receive a white garment, a sign they have "put on Christ." Saint Paul goes on: "There is neither Jew nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free: there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus."
neighbors.difference: The baptismal garment marks a new life Catholics believe is given in Christ, once, at the start. Ihram is a state pilgrims enter and leave again, for Hajj or umrah, standing before Allah alone.
neighbors.shared: before God, the labels we wear come off.
neighbors.sources: Galatians 3:27–28 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1243 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said the meat and blood of the sacrifice don't reach God; the devotion does. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says something with the same heart. Whoever offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, with devotion, he accepts it. The offering is small; the love inside it is what's received. Then it's often shared as prasad.
neighbors.difference: Hindu offerings are often food, flowers or water, received back as blessed prasad, and many Hindus keep from meat. At Mina, an animal is sacrificed in Allah's name and the meat shared with the poor.
neighbors.shared: what reaches God is the love inside the offering.

neighbors.heading: mercy, not sacrifice
neighbors.text: Today a sacrifice turned into a meal shared with the poor, and the Qur'an said devotion is what reaches God. The prophet Hosea heard God say: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." After the Temple fell, a story tells, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai comforted a grieving student with that verse: acts of lovingkindness atone too.
neighbors.difference: Jewish animal offerings ended with the Temple, and prayer and kindness took their place. Muslims still offer an animal, at Hajj and at Eid, and the meat itself becomes the kindness, shared out.
neighbors.shared: every offering ends up on someone's table, or in someone's heart.

neighbors.heading: a willing mind
neighbors.text: Today men wept because they couldn't join a journey, and the Qur'an lifted the blame. Saint Paul wrote something like it to Christians collecting a gift for the poor. What matters, he said, is the willingness: "For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."
neighbors.difference: Paul is speaking of giving money, not a pilgrimage; Christianity has no journey required of all. In Islam, Hajj stays a duty for whoever is able, and longing counts for those who can't.
neighbors.shared: wanting to give your all counts, even when you can't.

neighbors.heading: the shrine within
neighbors.text: Today people who couldn't make the Hajj shared in it by fasting and by longing. Guru Nanak speaks of a pilgrimage everyone can make. In Japji Sahib he says pilgrimages, discipline, compassion and charity bring only a little merit by themselves; listening, trusting and loving with a humble mind, you bathe at the sacred shrine deep within.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak taught that outward pilgrimage alone earns little, and the true shrine is inside. For Muslims, Hajj stays a real duty for whoever can go, and the heart shares in it when the body can't.
neighbors.shared: the road to God runs through the heart first.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, pauri 21 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: test everything
neighbors.text: Today Aisha tested a report by asking whether it fit the Qur'an. Catholics test claims too. Saint Paul wrote: "But prove all things." The Church teaches that private revelations, even recognized ones, can't add to or correct what Christ revealed. They're judged by whether they fit the faith the Church already holds.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the Church's teaching office, the Magisterium, judges with Scripture and Tradition. Hadith critics were scholars weighing reports against the Qur'an, sound sunnah and each other, with no single office deciding.
neighbors.shared: even good people can mishear; checking is a kind of love.
neighbors.sources: 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 67 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: check it against the teaching
neighbors.text: Today Aisha measured a report against the Qur'an. Before he died, the Buddha gave his monks the same kind of test. If someone says, "I heard this from the Buddha's own mouth," don't accept it or reject it at once. Compare it with the discourses and the discipline. If it doesn't fit, set it aside.
neighbors.difference: For Buddhists, the measure is the Dhamma and the monastic discipline, a teaching to be seen for oneself, with no revealed word of God. In hadith study, the measure is the Qur'an, which Muslims hold is God's own speech.
neighbors.shared: even a trusted voice gets checked against what you know is true.

neighbors.heading: on the roof in the snow
neighbors.text: Today Jabir rode a month to hear one report. The Talmud tells of a young Hillel, too poor to pay the doorkeeper of the study house. So he climbed onto the roof and lay by the skylight to hear the teachers explain the Torah. Snow fell on him through the night. In the morning they found him there and brought him in.
neighbors.difference: Hillel was hungry to hear Torah explained by living teachers. The hadith scholars traveled to hear a report from the one who heard it, keeping the chain back to the Prophet short and sure.
neighbors.shared: some knowledge is worth any cold, any road.

neighbors.heading: keep learning
neighbors.text: Today scholars crossed deserts for a single report, and Moses said he'd march for ages to find a teacher. The Roman philosopher Seneca, already old, wrote that he went to a philosopher's lectures every day. Some laughed at an old man in school. His answer: keep learning as long as you don't know, which, the proverb says, is as long as you live.
neighbors.difference: Seneca sought wisdom for living, by reason. The hadith scholars sought exact words of the Prophet, a sacred trust to be passed on unchanged.
neighbors.shared: you're never too old, or too far away, to learn.

neighbors.heading: one step, a million steps
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said that when you come walking, God comes running. Sikhs know a verse with the same arithmetic. Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh poet and scribe, wrote that if a disciple takes one step toward the Guru's refuge, the True Guru comes forward millions of steps to meet them.
neighbors.difference: In Bhai Gurdas the one who comes forward is the Satguru, the True Guru, whose light Sikhs see as one with God's. In the hadith qudsi, the promise is Allah's own, carried in the Prophet's words.
neighbors.shared: take one small step; you'll be met more than halfway.

neighbors.heading: he came at once
neighbors.text: Today God's answer outran a person's step. The Bhagavata Purana tells of Gajendra, an elephant king caught by a crocodile in a lake. When his strength gave out, he lifted a lotus in his trunk and called to Vishnu. Vishnu came at once, riding Garuda, and pulled him free.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Vishnu comes in a form, on Garuda, to rescue his devotee. In the hadith, Allah has no likeness; the running is read as His mercy outpacing the step, or accepted without asking how.
neighbors.shared: the one you call to is already on the way.

neighbors.heading: grasping the snake
neighbors.text: Today a hadith cut short sounded like the opposite of what it said. The Buddha warned about the same danger. Grasping a teaching wrongly, he said, is like grabbing a water snake by the tail: it turns and bites. Grasp it rightly, by the head, and it's safe. He also called his teaching a raft for crossing, not a thing to carry forever.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's raft is let go of once you've crossed. Muslims hold the Prophet's words as guidance to keep and live by, which is why they read them whole and in their setting.
neighbors.shared: read the whole thing before you decide what it says.

neighbors.heading: how can i, except
neighbors.text: Today hadith were read with their story and a teacher. The book of Acts tells of an official reading Isaiah in his chariot. Philip runs up and asks: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The man answers: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" He invites Philip up, and they read together.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Philip's guidance led to Jesus, whom they see at the heart of all Scripture. In hadith study, the teacher's help is about setting: who asked, what had just happened, and the full report.
neighbors.shared: old words open up when someone reads them with you.

neighbors.heading: for the sake of living well
neighbors.text: Today Muslim jurists asked what the law is for, and named five things it protects. Aristotle asked the same about the city. In his Politics he says a city first comes together for the sake of life, but it keeps going for the sake of living well. Laws, for him, aim at a good life for the people under them.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle reasons from human nature, with no revelation. Al-Ghazali drew the five aims from the revealed law itself, asking what God's commands were protecting.
neighbors.shared: rules are meant to help people live, and live well.

neighbors.heading: the common good
neighbors.text: Today the law had aims: protecting faith, life, mind, family and property. Catholic teaching has a name for its aim: the common good. The Church describes it as the conditions that let people and groups reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily. It rests, the Catechism says, on respect for the person, social well-being, and peace.
neighbors.difference: Catholic teaching roots the common good in human dignity, known by reason and by faith. The maqasid were drawn from reading the shari'ah's own texts, to see what the revealed law protects.
neighbors.shared: a good law leaves people more room to flourish.

neighbors.heading: one truth, many names
neighbors.text: Today honest scholars read the same words two ways, and neither was blamed. An old line in the Rig Veda makes room for the wise to differ too: truth is one, it says, and the sages call it by many names. Hindu thought grew many schools that argue, side by side, about how to read the same old texts.
neighbors.difference: The Vedic line is about naming one reality in many ways. The scholars' difference in Islam is about rulings of practice, read from one Qur'an and one sunnah, with God's oneness never in question.
neighbors.shared: honest people can read the same words and land differently.

neighbors.heading: these and these
neighbors.text: Today the companions split on the road, and neither group was blamed. The Talmud tells of the schools of Hillel and Shammai, who argued for three years. Then a heavenly voice said both were the words of the living God, but the law follows Hillel's school, because they were gentle and taught Shammai's view before their own.
neighbors.difference: In the Talmud, the voice settles practice for one school. In Sunni law the four schools stand side by side, each followed, with no single ruling made for all.
neighbors.shared: you can disagree and still honor the person across from you.

neighbors.heading: a just weight
neighbors.text: Today Abu Hanifa gave away a whole sale's price because a defect went unmentioned. Christians read the same standard in Proverbs: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight." And Jesus asked for plain speech: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay." Honest business is part of a faithful life.
neighbors.difference: Jesus asked for no oaths at all, just a plain yes or no. In the hadith Abu Hanifa lived by, the blessing of a sale comes when both sides speak truly and make things clear.
neighbors.shared: honesty at the counter is a kind of prayer.

neighbors.heading: bread from honest work
neighbors.text: Today a merchant's honesty made him a great scholar. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Nanak eating with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter, instead of at a rich man's feast. Tradition says honest bread gave milk; the bread of cheating gave blood. Gurbani says: one who earns by honest work and gives some of it away knows the path.
neighbors.difference: In Sikh teaching, honest work, kirat karni, goes together with remembering the Name and sharing, three habits of one life. Abu Hanifa's honesty followed the hadith: whoever cheats is not of me.
neighbors.shared: what you earn honestly feeds more than your body.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (paraphrase) · Janamsakhi tradition of Bhai Lalo (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all things are passing
neighbors.text: Today a poem in al-Shafi'i's name said to let the days do what they will, since hard times and good times both pass. The Spanish nun Saint Teresa of Avila kept lines like that, which Longfellow put into English: "Let nothing disturb thee, / Nothing affright thee; / All things are passing; / God never changeth."
neighbors.difference: Teresa finds the steady point in God possessed in prayer: alone God suffices. The poem in al-Shafi'i's name finds it in calm acceptance of the decree, qadar, whatever the days bring.
neighbors.shared: hard days pass; what holds you doesn't.
neighbors.sources: Saint Teresa of Avila, "Santa Teresa's Book-Mark," translated by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

neighbors.heading: the eight winds
neighbors.text: Today a poem said hard times pass and good times pass; neither one stays. The Buddha taught the same about eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. All of them come and go, he said. The wise person sees that, and isn't swept away by any of them.
neighbors.difference: For Buddhists, steadiness comes from seeing that all things are impermanent, with no decree from a creator behind them. In al-Shafi'i's poem, the calm comes from trusting a decree Allah has measured.
neighbors.shared: neither the good days nor the hard ones stay forever.

neighbors.heading: make yourself a teacher
neighbors.text: Today Shia Muslims chose a living scholar to follow in questions of law. The Mishnah gives similar advice. Joshua ben Perachiah said: make for yourself a teacher, and get yourself a friend. Many Jews bring their practical questions, about Shabbat, food or prayer, to a rabbi they trust, who may lean on great decisors past and present.
neighbors.difference: Many Twelver Shia scholars ask followers to choose the most learned living marja'. Jewish communities have no single office like that; people turn to their own rabbi, and rulings of the great decisors can stay in force long after them.
neighbors.shared: nobody has to work out the whole law alone.

neighbors.heading: someone to keep in view
