neighbors.text: Today a shelf held a book of rulings by a living scholar people follow. The Stoic Seneca gave a friend similar advice, borrowed from Epicurus: choose a good person and keep them before your eyes, living as if they were watching. We need someone, he said, to measure our character against.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's guide is a model of character, and can even be someone long dead, like Cato. In the usual Twelver view, one starts by following a living marja', in matters of law, so new questions can be answered.
neighbors.shared: everyone needs someone wiser to look to.

neighbors.heading: every month a good month
neighbors.text: Today a family argued over which night the new moon was seen. Sikhs mark the months too, in poems called Barah Maha, the twelve months, where each month brings its own longing for God. Guru Arjan's ends by saying the months, days and moments are blessed for anyone on whom God's grace falls.
neighbors.difference: In Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, what blesses a month or day is grace and remembrance, not the date itself. For Muslims, the moon sets sacred times like Ramadan, and seeing it begins them.
neighbors.shared: each new month is a fresh chance to turn toward God.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Barah Maha Majh (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: born again, ever new
neighbors.text: Today Muslims looked for the thin crescent to begin and end the fast. Hindu calendars follow the moon too. A Rig Veda hymn says the moon is born again and again, always new, a banner of the days. On Karva Chauth, many Hindu wives fast all day and break the fast only after they see the moon.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindu calendars keep their moon-months in step with the sun by adding a month now and then. The Islamic year stays purely lunar, so Ramadan travels through every season.
neighbors.shared: the moon keeps reminding us we can begin again.

neighbors.heading: milk and water
neighbors.text: Today a stranger joined a row behind an imam of another school. The Buddha once asked three monks living together how they got along. One answered that they lived in harmony, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes. Different bodies, he said, but one mind.
neighbors.difference: The monks' harmony grows from shared training on the path, with no God they bow toward together. In the row, Muslims of different schools stand as one people before one Lord, facing the Ka'ba.
neighbors.shared: you can differ and still stand side by side.

neighbors.heading: that they all may be one
neighbors.text: Today Muslims from different schools stood in one row, shoulder to shoulder. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for his followers: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." Christians from many churches still pray those words, especially when they gather across their differences.
neighbors.difference: Jesus prays for a oneness modeled on his own with the Father, which Christians see within God himself. In the hadith, the row's unity is people standing equal before one God, who has no partner.
neighbors.shared: the person beside you belongs there, whatever their school.

neighbors.heading: whom you eat with
neighbors.text: Today a wedding feast could be one sheep, or just dates and butter on a mat; the meal mattered, not the menu. The philosopher Epicurus, as Seneca passes it on, said much the same: look first at whom you'll eat and drink with, before what you'll eat and drink. A meal alone, he thought, is a lion's or a wolf's life.
neighbors.difference: Epicurus prized company for a calm, happy life. The walimah is a sunnah that announces a marriage, done for Allah's sake; guests are asked to come, and the poor must not be left out.
neighbors.shared: the guest list matters more than the menu.

neighbors.heading: call the poor
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said the worst wedding feast is one where the rich are invited and the poor left out. Jesus gave the same advice at a dinner: "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind." And John's Gospel places his first sign at a wedding in Cana, where the wine ran out.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, marriage is a sacrament, a sign of Christ's love for the Church. In Islam, the nikah is a solemn contract, blessed and celebrated with the walimah.
neighbors.shared: joy is meant to be shared with whoever needs it most.

neighbors.heading: the same in all
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an called animals communities like us, and the Prophet forbade overloading or branding them. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. Many Hindus link that vision to ahimsa, not harming, and extend it to animals, often in what they eat.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus keep ahimsa through a vegetarian diet. Islam permits eating animals slaughtered in God's name, while setting out duties of mercy toward them in life and death.
neighbors.shared: every creature is someone, not something.

neighbors.heading: the enemy's donkey
neighbors.text: Today a camel wept, and the Prophet told its owner to fear God about animals that cannot speak. The Torah asks for the same care: "If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under its burden, thou shalt forbear to pass by him; thou shalt surely release it with him." Rabbis call this tza'ar ba'alei chayim: an animal's pain matters.
neighbors.difference: The Torah even gives the ox and the donkey a Sabbath rest. In the hadith, care is taught case by case: a camel, a bird, a face that must not be branded.
neighbors.shared: an animal's burden is everyone's business.

neighbors.heading: moses and the psalms
neighbors.text: Today Muslims believe in the books given to Musa, Dawud and Isa. Christians carry those older books too: their Bible holds the law of Moses and the Psalms of David beside the Gospels. Luke's Gospel has Jesus say that all things must be fulfilled "which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms."
neighbors.difference: Christians read the Torah and Psalms, as their Bible has them, as fulfilled in Jesus. Muslims believe in those books as first revealed to their messengers, with the Qur'an as the last book and the measure of the others.
neighbors.shared: every age was given words to live by.

neighbors.heading: many voices, one book
neighbors.text: Today Muslims believe God sent books to many messengers. The Sikh scripture gathers many voices too. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the Gurus' hymns beside verses by saints from other paths: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi whose couplets appear near the book's end. Sikhs honor the whole book as their living Guru.
neighbors.difference: The Guru Granth Sahib gathers many saints into one book, honored as the living Guru. Muslims believe in separate books, each sent to its messenger, with the Qur'an as the last.
neighbors.shared: wisdom has been given in many voices, to many peoples.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Sheikh Farid, Ang 1377 onward (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: increase our faith
neighbors.text: Today faith was a battery that rises and falls. Catholics speak of it the same way. In Luke's Gospel the apostles ask Jesus: "Increase our faith." And in Mark, a worried father cries out: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." The Church teaches faith is God's gift, and can grow through prayer and the sacraments.
neighbors.difference: Catholics hold that faith grows through grace, especially in the sacraments. Many Muslim scholars tie its rise to good deeds and its fall to sins, while Hanafi scholars say only its light and fruits change.
neighbors.shared: it's okay if your faith feels low today; it can grow.

neighbors.heading: faith as a faculty
neighbors.text: Today iman was said to grow with good deeds. The Buddha named faith, saddha, as the first of five faculties, with energy, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom. They grow stronger when they're developed, and later teachers added that they balance each other: faith steadied by wisdom, wisdom warmed by faith.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist faith is confidence in the Buddha, his teaching and the community, meant to be tested in experience. Iman is belief in Allah and the unseen, the six articles, held as truth from God.
neighbors.shared: faith isn't a card you hold; it's something you grow.

neighbors.heading: back to the one who gave it
neighbors.text: Today the soul at peace was called home: return unto thy Lord. Jewish scripture speaks of return too. Ecclesiastes says: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." And when news of a death comes, the Mishnah gives Jews a short blessing to say: blessed is the true Judge.
neighbors.difference: Muslims meet a loss with a Qur'an verse: unto Him we are returning. The Jewish blessing praises God as the true Judge, accepting the loss as just even when no one can see why.
neighbors.shared: a life is something given, and it goes back to the giver.

neighbors.heading: returned, not lost
neighbors.text: Today the soul was called home, back to its Lord. A Stoic teacher spoke of return too. Epictetus told his students: never say of anything, I have lost it, but, I have given it back. Has your child died? It was given back. While you have something, he said, care for it the way a traveler cares for an inn.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus offers return as a way to keep the mind steady, and speaks of the giver without describing what comes after. In the Qur'an, the soul itself goes back to its Lord, who welcomes it, content and pleasing.
neighbors.shared: what we love was never ours to keep, only to care for.

neighbors.heading: write it, carry it
neighbors.text: Today each person was handed the book of their own deeds. Guru Nanak speaks of a record too. In Japji Sahib he says virtue and vice aren't just words: the deeds we do again and again are written down, and we carry them with us. What you plant, he says, you eat yourself.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the book is opened on one Day, and Allah counts the good generously. Japji Sahib ties deeds to the coming and going of births, and says the door of release opens by the Creator's grace.
neighbors.shared: every day, you're writing something you'll carry.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, pauri 20; Ang 2, pauri 4 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the scribe of deeds
neighbors.text: Today each person was handed the book of their own deeds. Hindu stories keep a record too. In the Puranas, Chitragupta, the scribe beside Yama, lord of death, writes down the acts of every life. And an Upanishad gives the rule beneath it: as a person acts, so they become. The doer of good becomes good.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the record is read on one Day, and the judge is Allah. In Hindu teaching on karma, deeds ripen across lives, shaping the next birth, and the hope is moksha, release from the round of births.
neighbors.shared: small acts aren't lost; they shape who we become.
neighbors.sources: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.5 (paraphrase) · Chitragupta in the Garuda Purana (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a flower with no scent
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said belief isn't finished when you say it; it has to enter the heart and reach the road. The Buddha said it with a flower. The Dhammapada compares fine words that are never acted on to a bright flower with no scent. Fine words that are lived, it says, are a flower with color and fragrance.
neighbors.difference: Islam begins with belief in Allah, and faith is meant to reach the heart. The Buddha taught no creator to believe in; his teaching is tested by practice, and the fruit he points to is freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: what you believe shows best in what you do next.

neighbors.heading: faith that moves
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said belief isn't finished when you say it, and a hadith put a rock moved off the road among faith's branches. The letter of James says it plainly: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." James pictures someone telling a cold, hungry person, be warmed and filled, and giving nothing.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, faith rests on Jesus, whom they believe is the Son of God, and good works grow from that faith as its fruit. In Islam, faith rests on Allah the One, and good deeds are branches of faith itself.
neighbors.shared: faith shows up in the hands, not only on the lips.

neighbors.heading: the evening ledger
neighbors.text: Today Umar's saying asked for a reckoning each night: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account. The Roman Stoic Seneca kept the same ledger. When the lamp was out and the house was quiet, he wrote, he went over his whole day, word by word and deed by deed, hiding nothing from himself and passing nothing over.
neighbors.difference: Seneca is both judge and defendant: he reviews the day to grow wiser and calmer, with no one else keeping the books. For Muslims, the evening reckoning gets ready for Allah's, and what's wrong is taken to Him in repentance.
neighbors.shared: a day looked at kindly is a day you can learn from.

neighbors.heading: an examination of conscience
neighbors.text: Today Umar's saying asked for a reckoning each night. Catholics keep that ledger too. Saint Ignatius of Loyola taught a daily examen: give thanks for the day's gifts, ask for light, go over the hours, ask pardon for what went wrong, and resolve to amend. The Church asks for an examination of conscience before confession, made in the light of God's word.
neighbors.difference: Catholics bring serious sins they find to a priest in the sacrament of confession, and hear absolution in God's name. In Islam, repentance is made directly to Allah, with no one in between, and a wrong done to people is put right with them.
neighbors.shared: count the gifts first, then the faults, then begin again.
neighbors.sources: St. Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, the general examen (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1454 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the work, not the fruit
neighbors.text: Today the tied camel taught: effort first, then trust. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna something with the same two halves. Your right is to the work, he says, never to its fruits. Don't let the result be your motive, and don't let that turn into doing nothing. Act, and let go of the outcome.
neighbors.difference: Krishna asks Arjuna to act as an offering, letting go of the outcome; in Hindu belief, Krishna is God speaking face to face. In Islam, the trust after effort goes to Allah, beyond every form, who provides.
neighbors.shared: do your part well, then set the result down.

neighbors.heading: commit thy way
neighbors.text: Today the tied camel taught: effort first, then trust. Jewish scripture puts trust in plain words. A psalm sings: "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass." And the Talmud adds a sensible note: don't rely on a miracle. Do your part, and trust God with the rest.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the tied camel comes from the Prophet's own answer, and the Qur'an says Allah loves those who trust. Jewish teaching draws on the Psalms and the rabbis, who weigh how much effort trust asks for.
neighbors.shared: tie the rope, then rest; you were never holding it alone.

neighbors.heading: bigger barns
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said a valley of gold only teaches the want to count. Jesus told a story about it. A rich man's fields did so well that he planned bigger barns and a long rest. That night, the story says, his life was required of him. Before the story, Jesus warned: "a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth."
neighbors.difference: Jesus' story ends with being rich toward God, which Christians hear as following him. The hadith ends with Allah turning to whoever turns, and moves wealth into the soul: richness is richness of the soul.
neighbors.shared: enough is a place in the heart, not a number.

neighbors.heading: greed is a dog
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said a valley of gold only teaches the want to count. Sikh teaching names greed, lobh, among the five thieves that rob the heart, and in one hymn Guru Nanak calls greed a dog. The cure Sikhs point to is santokh, contentment: earning honestly, sharing, and remembering the Name.
neighbors.difference: Sikh teaching counts greed among five thieves and answers it with remembrance of the Name and honest work. The hadith ends greed at the dust of the grave, then opens a door: Allah turns to whoever turns.
neighbors.shared: the want grows with feeding; contentment lets it rest.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Sikh teaching on the five thieves (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: bless us, O Lord
neighbors.text: Today a forgotten bismillah, said late, still covered the whole meal. Catholics name God at the table too. A traditional grace goes: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." It often begins and ends with the sign of the cross.
neighbors.difference: Catholics pray the grace through Christ, whom they believe is God's Son. Bismillah names Allah alone, and the Prophet's table adds the right hand, the near side of the dish, and no complaints about the food.
neighbors.shared: a plate becomes a gift when you remember the giver.

neighbors.heading: eat, remembering why
neighbors.text: Today the adab of eating started with a name. The Buddha taught his monks to start with a reflection. Consider your food wisely, he said: eat not for fun, not for intoxication, not for looks, but to keep the body going, to ease hunger, and to support the holy life.
neighbors.difference: The Buddhist reflection turns attention to why one eats, with no creator to thank. Bismillah turns the meal toward Allah, the giver, so the food becomes a gift received, with thanks to follow.
neighbors.shared: slow down and know what the meal is for.

neighbors.heading: honor, out loud
neighbors.text: Today one word was said three times: your mother. Jewish scripture puts parents in the Ten Commandments: "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." The Talmud makes it practical: give them food and drink, help them dress, help them in and out.
neighbors.difference: The Ten Commandments name the father first; another verse names the mother first, and the rabbis read the two as equal. The hadith names the mother three times before the father, and the Qur'an remembers her carrying the child in weakness upon weakness.
neighbors.shared: the people who carried us are owed our gentlest care.

neighbors.heading: more than feeding
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an asked for not even an uff toward aging parents. Confucius asked for more than support. In the Analects he says people think caring for parents means feeding them. But dogs and horses are fed too. Without reverence, he asks, what's the difference? In the next breath he names the hard part: the look on your face.
neighbors.difference: For Confucius, care for parents is the root of a good life and a well-ordered society, kept through ritual and remembrance. In Islam, kindness to parents comes right after the worship of Allah, and the child's du'a asks God's mercy for them.
neighbors.shared: how we look at our parents is part of how we care.

neighbors.heading: earth, the great mother
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said: if the Hour comes and a seedling's in your hand, plant it. Sikh scripture gives the earth a family name. The closing verse of Japji Sahib says air is the guru, water the father, and earth the great mother of all. Day and night are the two nurses, it goes on, and the whole world plays in their lap.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, people are stewards, khalifa, looking after an earth Allah made, and answerable for it. Japji Sahib speaks of the elements as guru, parents and nurses, a family the One Creator placed around every life.
neighbors.shared: the ground under us deserves the care we'd give family.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, closing shalok (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: my mother, the earth
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said: if the Hour comes and a seedling's in your hand, plant it. A Vedic hymn speaks to the earth herself. In the Atharva Veda's hymn to Prithvi, the singer says: the earth is my mother, I am her son. Some families still say a morning verse asking the earth's pardon before stepping on her.
neighbors.difference: In Hindu worship, the earth is honored as Bhumi Devi, a goddess and mother. In Islam, the earth is Allah's creation, sweet and green, and people look after it as stewards, answerable to Him.
neighbors.shared: you treat the ground differently when you know it holds you.
neighbors.sources: Atharva Veda 12.1.12, the hymn to the earth (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: joy in their joy
neighbors.text: Today a hadith walked into the half-second before typing congratulations. Buddhist teaching has a name for what can fill that gap: mudita, sympathetic joy, being glad at someone else's good fortune. It's one of four boundless states, with loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity. Teachers train it on purpose, starting with someone easy to be glad for.
neighbors.difference: Mudita is trained in meditation, a heart widened step by step, with no creator in view. The hadith ties it to faith itself: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
neighbors.shared: someone else's good news can be yours to celebrate too.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 13, the four boundless states (paraphrase) · Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga IX (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rejoice with them
neighbors.text: Today a hadith walked into the half-second before typing congratulations. Paul's letter to the Romans names both sides of a friend's news: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." And Jesus gave the same measuring stick: "whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them."
neighbors.difference: Jesus' rule is about doing; the hadith is about wanting, what the heart loves for someone else. Christians hear both in the light of Christ's love. Muslims hear the hadith as faith reaching all the way down.
neighbors.shared: want for them what you'd be glad to receive.

neighbors.heading: dyed by your thoughts
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pictured rust on the heart, and repentance as the polish. Marcus Aurelius used a picture of cloth: "Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts." So, he wrote, dye it with good ones, again and again.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, the work is reason and repetition, the mind steering itself. In the hadith, the polish is repentance and asking Allah's forgiveness, and the heart is cleaned by turning back to Him.
neighbors.shared: what we return to every day becomes the color of us.

neighbors.heading: clean of heart
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pictured rust on the heart, and repentance as the polish. Jesus spoke of the heart's shine in a beatitude: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." And a psalm Catholics pray asks for it outright: "Create a clean heart in me, O God."
neighbors.difference: Catholics believe the heart is made clean by God's grace, given through Christ and the sacraments, among them confession. In Islam, the heart is polished as a servant repents and asks Allah's forgiveness directly, wiping the rust day by day.
neighbors.shared: a dulled heart can shine again.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:8 (Douay-Rheims) · Psalm 50:12 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 51:10 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: seven steps, a friend
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said spouses were made so they could find rest in each other, with love and mercy between them. At a Hindu wedding, the couple take seven steps together beside the sacred fire, the saptapadi. With the seventh, an old verse says: be my friend. Tradition counts the marriage as made once that step is taken.
neighbors.difference: In Hindu tradition, the wedding is a sacrament witnessed by the sacred fire, and some hold it as a bond across lifetimes. In Islam, the nikah is a contract with consent and witnesses, and love and mercy are a sign Allah places between the two.
neighbors.shared: a good marriage is a friend to come home to.
neighbors.sources: the saptapadi, as in the Grihya Sutras (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not good to be alone
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said spouses were made from one another, so they could find rest. Genesis begins there too: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him." And the Talmud adds a warm line: a man without a wife lives without joy, without blessing, without goodness.
neighbors.difference: Jewish marriage is called kiddushin, holiness: two people set apart for each other under the chuppah. In the Qur'an, marriage is a contract, and the love and mercy between the two are named as one of Allah's signs.
neighbors.shared: home is where someone is glad you came back.

neighbors.heading: I was sick, and ye visited me
neighbors.text: Today a hadith had God say: I was sick, and you did not visit Me. Jesus tells a strikingly close scene. At the judgment, the King says: "I was sick, and ye visited me." The righteous ask when. He answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
neighbors.difference: In Matthew, the King is Jesus, whom Christians believe is God the Son, present in those who suffer. In the hadith, Allah is not the sick person; whoever visits would find Him with the one who is ill.
neighbors.shared: sitting beside someone sick is never a small thing.

neighbors.heading: serve here, be welcome there
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said a visitor to the sick walks in the garden's harvest. Sikhs call service seva. Guru Nanak sings: serve in the midst of this world, and you'll be given a seat in the Lord's court. Tradition remembers the child Guru, Har Krishan, tending the sick in Delhi during an epidemic, until he caught it himself.
neighbors.difference: In Sikh teaching, seva is selfless service that softens the ego, offered to anyone. In the hadith, visiting is a right of the sick, and the visitor is promised a share of the garden's fruit.
neighbors.shared: showing up is the gift; you don't need the right words.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Guru Har Krishan in Delhi, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the white pall
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet was buried in three plain white sheets, like anyone. At a Catholic funeral, the coffin can be covered with a white pall. The Church's funeral rites say it recalls the white garment of baptism, and shows that all are equal in God's eyes. Ash Wednesday says it too: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return."
neighbors.difference: Catholics see the white as the baptismal robe, a sign of sharing in Christ's rising. In Islam, plain white cloth is the usual custom for burial, and the body is laid in the earth facing the qiblah, to await the Day.
neighbors.shared: at the end, no one is dressed above anyone else.
neighbors.sources: Order of Christian Funerals, General Introduction 38 (paraphrase) · Genesis 3:19 (Douay-Rheims)

neighbors.heading: a house where no one has died
neighbors.text: Today the shroud put everyone in the same white. A Buddhist story says death comes to every house. Kisa Gotami, wild with grief, carried her dead child to the Buddha. Bring me a mustard seed, he said, from a house where no one has died. She knocked on door after door, and found none.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's lesson points to impermanence: whatever is born ends, and clinging brings suffering. In Islam, death is a return to Allah, and the plain white shroud goes into the earth to await the Day of Rising.
neighbors.shared: grief knocks on every door; no one answers it alone.
neighbors.sources: the story of Kisa Gotami, Dhammapada and Therigatha commentaries (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a time to weep
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet wept for his son and called tears mercy. Jewish scripture makes room for tears: "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance." The Talmud even gives grief a calendar: three days for weeping, seven for eulogies, thirty before haircuts and pressed clothes.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, mourning is three days, longer for a widow, and the line is drawn at wailing. The Talmud's calendar runs longer, and it warns against grieving past it, saying, in paraphrase: you are not more compassionate than God.
neighbors.shared: tears for someone you love are not a weakness.

neighbors.heading: weep, but don't wail
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet wept for his son, and the hadith drew its line at wailing. The Roman Stoic Seneca drew nearly the same line, writing to a friend who'd lost a friend. Let the eyes not be dry when we lose someone, he wrote, nor let them overflow. We may weep, but we must not wail.
neighbors.difference: Seneca counsels a measured grief so reason can steer, and finds comfort in remembering the friend gladly. The Prophet called his tears mercy itself, and kept his tongue to what pleases Allah, trusting the loss to Him.
neighbors.shared: you can let the tears come and still keep your words kind.

neighbors.heading: a name from the page
neighbors.text: Today the road ran from the adhan in a baby's ear to the funeral prayer. Sikh life has its rites along the road too, each before the Guru Granth Sahib. A baby is named from a letter of the hymn where the scripture falls open. Couples marry walking around it. And at a funeral, Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime hymn, is sung.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the newborn hears the adhan and the dead are buried facing the qiblah. Sikhs usually cremate their dead, and their rites gather around the Guru Granth Sahib, honored as the living Guru.
neighbors.shared: every turning point in a life can be held in prayer.
neighbors.sources: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on birth, marriage and funeral ceremonies (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the samskaras
neighbors.text: Today the road ran from the adhan in a baby's ear to the funeral prayer. Hindu tradition marks the road with samskaras, rites of passage. At birth, in the old jatakarma, a father touches a little honey and ghee to the baby's lips. Then come naming, first food, first learning, marriage, and at the end, the last rites.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the dead are washed, wrapped in white and buried facing the qiblah. The Hindu last rites, antyeshti, the last offering, give the body to fire, and in Hindu belief the soul moves on toward another birth or toward release.
neighbors.shared: someone carries you in, and someone carries you out.
neighbors.sources: the Grihya Sutras, on the jatakarma and the samskaras (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: awake through the night
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet brought the last ten nights to life, awake in prayer. Buddhist texts remember a night too. Seated under a tree, the Buddha sat through the night, and the texts divide it into three watches. In the first he remembered past lives, in the second he saw beings pass on by their deeds, in the last he awoke.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's awakening came through his own insight, with no revelation from a god. The Night of Power is the night the Qur'an came down from Allah, and Muslims spend it asking Him for pardon.
neighbors.shared: some nights are worth staying awake for.

neighbors.heading: all night in prayer
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet brought the last ten nights to life, awake in prayer and waking his family. The Gospels remember Jesus praying through a night before a great choice: "he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God." In the morning, Luke says, he chose his twelve apostles.
neighbors.difference: Christians believe Jesus prays as the Son to the Father, and their great vigil keeps watch for his rising at Easter. In Islam, the last ten nights look for the Night of Power, when the Qur'an was sent down, and ask Allah's pardon.
neighbors.shared: a quiet night can hold more than a busy day.

neighbors.heading: a citizen of the world
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said people were made nations and tribes to know one another. Old philosophers widened their own map. Asked where he came from, Diogenes the Cynic answered: I am a citizen of the world. Marcus Aurelius, an emperor, wrote that as Antoninus his city was Rome, but as a human being, it was the world.
neighbors.difference: For the philosophers, the shared bond is reason, which every human being has. In the Qur'an, the bond is one Creator, the differences of tongue and color are His signs, and the noblest is the most mindful of Him.
neighbors.shared: a different accent is an invitation to get to know someone.
neighbors.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers 6.63 (paraphrase) · Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.44 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: every tribe and tongue
neighbors.text: Today one row at Friday prayer held a Somali driver, an Indonesian student and a grandfather from Lahore. The Church teaches that catholic means universal, and the Bible has a picture of it: "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues." Catholics pray the Mass in many languages and rites, East and West.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, unity runs through the Church, its sacraments and the Pope, gathered around Christ. In Islam, unity has no single head: it rests on the shahadah, the prayer in Arabic and one qiblah, across many schools.
neighbors.shared: the row is wider than any one language.
neighbors.sources: Revelation 7:9 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 830 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: Gargi asks
neighbors.text: Today a woman named Khawlah argued her case, and a surah opened with her story. An Upanishad keeps a woman's questions too. At King Janaka's court, the learned Gargi questions the sage Yajnavalkya: what is the sky woven on, and what is that woven on? She presses until he warns her not to ask too far, then returns with two more.
neighbors.difference: Khawlah's plea was about her own marriage, and the Qur'an says Allah heard her. Gargi's questions reach for Brahman, the ground of all being, in a debate among scholars. One brings a wrong to be righted, the other a mystery to be searched.
neighbors.shared: asking hard questions out loud is a way of honoring the truth.

neighbors.heading: the daughters speak right
neighbors.text: Today a woman named Khawlah argued her case, and a surah opened with her story. The Torah keeps five sisters who did the same. The daughters of Zelophehad came before Moses: our father died with no sons; why should his name be lost? Moses brought their case to God, and the answer came: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right."
neighbors.difference: In the Torah, the sisters' case widens inheritance for daughters, through Moses. In the Qur'an, Khawlah's plea brings a ruling against a cruel old divorce formula, and the surah is named for her disputing.
neighbors.shared: a woman's question, pressed with courage, deserves an answer.

neighbors.heading: the heavens declare
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pointed at camels, mountains and sky, and called them signs. A psalm Christians pray points the same way: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Some Christian writers, like Francis Bacon, spoke of two books: God's word and God's works, both read to know their author.
neighbors.difference: Christians read creation alongside Scripture, and see its maker most fully revealed in Jesus. In the Qur'an, the word ayah means both a verse and a sign in the world, so reading the sky and reading the book share a name.
neighbors.shared: looking closely at the world can open into wonder.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 19:1 (KJV) · Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning (1605), on the two books (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: skies beyond skies
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an pointed at camels, mountains and sky, and called them signs. Guru Nanak looked up and couldn't finish counting. In Japji Sahib he sings of worlds below worlds, and hundreds of thousands of skies above. Searchers grew weary of searching, he says; try to write it down, and the writing ends first.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an invites people to look, and the Prophet called seeking knowledge a duty. Guru Nanak's hymn stands in awe at a creation too vast to count, and turns the wonder toward the One who alone knows Himself.
neighbors.shared: the more you look, the more there is to see.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib, pauri 22 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: overcome evil by good
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said: repel the evil deed with one which is better. Saint Paul wrote nearly the same to the Romans: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good." And Jesus asked more still, in the Sermon on the Mount: love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you.
neighbors.difference: Jesus' words reach all the way to the enemy: love them, pray for them, and Catholics hear in this the way of the cross. The Qur'an asks for the better answer and holds out a hope: the enemy may become like a close friend.
neighbors.shared: the reply you choose can keep a future open.

neighbors.heading: an old rule
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an said: repel the evil deed with one which is better. The Dhammapada opens with the same refusal. It pictures someone repeating, he abused me, he beat me, and says hatred won't cease in that heart. Then: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."
neighbors.difference: The Buddha speaks of hate as a fire in the one who holds it, and letting go frees that heart. The Qur'an speaks of the other person too: answer with what is better, and the enemy may become like a close friend.
neighbors.shared: hate answered with hate only grows.

neighbors.heading: you were strangers
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet fled his city, and Medina made room. Jewish scripture asks for that room, and gives the reason: "the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." At every Passover, Jews retell their own leaving.
neighbors.difference: The Torah grounds the welcome in a people's memory of slavery and exodus. Muslims remember the Hijra as the Prophet's own flight, and the Ansar who took the migrants in became the picture of a good host.
neighbors.shared: remembering your own journey opens the door for someone else's.

neighbors.heading: the right to visit
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet fled his city, and Medina made room. Immanuel Kant wrote a rule for a peaceful world that starts at the border. A stranger arriving in another land, he argued, has a right not to be treated as an enemy. People share the surface of the earth, he wrote, and at first no one had more right than another to any part of it.
neighbors.difference: Kant describes a minimum that law can guarantee: a right to visit, not to stay. The Qur'an praises the Ansar for something no law can require: preferring the newcomers above themselves, though they were in need.
neighbors.shared: the earth is shared; no one should arrive as an enemy.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Toward Perpetual Peace (1795), third definitive article (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a tenth, and a full plate
neighbors.text: Today a jar on a kitchen shelf made giving regular. Sikhs have a regular gift too: dasvandh, setting aside a tenth of what they earn. Guru Nanak says the one who earns by honest work and gives some of it away knows the path. Langar, the free kitchen where anyone can sit and eat, runs on that giving.
neighbors.difference: Dasvandh is a custom from the Gurus' time, given freely toward the community and its kitchen. In Islam, zakat is a set share owed on wealth, with sadaqah, open and voluntary, beside it.
neighbors.shared: a small gift that keeps coming back shapes the giver.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · the Sikh practice of dasvandh (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: given because it should be
neighbors.text: Today a jar on a kitchen shelf made giving regular. Hindu teaching calls giving dana. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes the purest gift: given simply because giving is right, to someone who can't repay, at the right place and time. An Upanishad adds: give with faith, give with modesty, give with understanding.
neighbors.difference: The Gita grades a gift by the giver's state of mind, as pure, self-seeking or careless. In Islam, a share is owed as zakat, and beyond it sadaqah is open-handed, best given quietly, and multiplied by Allah.
neighbors.shared: how you give matters as much as what you give.

neighbors.heading: tuned like a lute
neighbors.text: Today Salman told a devout friend: give each its right, even sleep. The Buddha once told a monk named Sona much the same. Sona practiced so hard his feet bled, and thought of quitting. The Buddha asked: you played the lute? Too tight, it won't sound. Too slack, it won't either. Tune your effort the same way.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's middle way balances effort so the mind can awaken. Salman's balance gives each its right: Allah, the self and the family each have a claim, and the Prophet said Salman spoke the truth.
neighbors.shared: too tight breaks, too loose won't play: find the tune.

neighbors.heading: rest a while
neighbors.text: Today Salman told a devout friend: give each its right, even sleep. Jesus told his disciples something like it when they were too busy even to eat: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." And about the day of rest he said: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath."
neighbors.difference: Jesus speaks as the one who invites the weary to come to him and rest. In the hadith, the balance comes from a companion, Salman, and the Prophet confirms it: your Lord, your self and your family each have a right.
neighbors.shared: rest isn't a lapse in devotion; it's part of it.

neighbors.heading: we become what we do
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said the most beloved deeds are the constant ones, even if small. Aristotle said character grows the same way. We become just by doing just acts, he wrote, and brave by doing brave ones, and the habits formed from youth make all the difference. One swallow, he said, doesn't make a summer.
neighbors.difference: For Aristotle, steady practice builds a virtue that belongs to the person, the road to a flourishing life. In the hadith, small constant deeds are loved by Allah, and a missed day can begin again with tawbah.
neighbors.shared: small things done every day become who we are.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7 and II.1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: faithful in little
neighbors.text: Today a hadith said the most beloved deeds are the constant ones, even if small. Jesus said: "He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater." Saint Thérèse of Lisieux built her whole way on it: a little way of small things done with great love, like a smile kept for someone hard to like.
neighbors.difference: For Thérèse, the little way is trust in God's mercy, offering small acts to Jesus out of love. In Islam, small constant deeds are loved by Allah, and when one lapses, the Qur'an says: do not despair of His mercy.
neighbors.shared: one small thing, kept, can outlast a big promise.
neighbors.sources: Luke 16:10 (Douay-Rheims) · St. Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: come back with your question
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an was full of questions, and a hadith said the cure for not knowing is asking. A whole Upanishad is built on asking. In the Prashna Upanishad, six seekers come to the sage Pippalada. Live here a year, he tells them, then ask whatever you like; if I know, I'll tell you. Each asks one question.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishads, questions lead inward, toward knowing the Self and Brahman. In the Qur'an, questions are answered by revelation, and asking has manners: ask what you need, of someone who knows, in order to act.
neighbors.shared: a good question is a door, not a doubt.

neighbors.heading: what mean ye?
neighbors.text: Today the Qur'an was full of questions, and a hadith said the cure for not knowing is asking. The Passover Seder is built around a child's questions, and the Torah expects them: "when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service?" The sages added a warning: the bashful person doesn't learn.
neighbors.difference: The Seder sets questions inside a family's retelling of the Exodus, and Jewish learning often studies in pairs, arguing a text aloud. The Qur'an answers questions with revelation, and asks: ask what you need, not what would only trouble you.
neighbors.shared: a question asked out loud keeps learning alive.
